taxonomy.definition: Compound aggregates distort apparent assay potency.
Intrinsic fluorescence or optical interference distorts an assay readout.

taxonomy.specific_cause: Misapplication of Ki and IC50 Parameters
taxonomy.definition: An explanation based on confusing affinity/inhibition endpoints or their substrate/assay dependence.

taxonomy.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
taxonomy.definition: Solubility, hydrophobicity, ionization or other physicochemical limitations. Explicit passive membrane permeability goes to the separate Permeability cause.
Binding multiple targets or off-target pharmacology explains the discrepancy.

taxonomy.specific_cause: Imbalanced Molecular Chameleon Characteristics (Abnormal Conformational Adaptability/Polarity Regulation)
taxonomy.definition: Environment-dependent conformational adaptability or exposed polarity of the compound. Do not confuse compound conformation with target-protein dynamics.
Metabolic conversion, degradation, metabolic activation or active transporter-mediated efflux. Distinct from passive membrane permeability.
Competition/interactions with intracellular substrates, ATP, cofactors or binding partners alter target inhibition.
Target-protein conformational states/dynamics or post-translational modification explain the difference.
Localization, compartmental access or oligomeric/complex state of the TARGET. Compound-only sequestration is not automatically target localization.
Explicit poor passive membrane entry/penetration or passive intracellular access. Use this dedicated cause ahead of the overlapping physicochemical label; active efflux belongs to metabolism_efflux.
Reasons outside the listed taxonomy, insufficiently specific statements, or multiple equally central mechanisms that cannot defensibly receive one primary label.

claims.author_explanation: WM-8014 exhibits relatively high protein binding (97.5%) in cell culture medium containing 10% FCS, which reduces its free active concentration in cellular assays; optimization to WM-1119 reduced plasma-protein binding and increased cellular potency ~9-fold.

evidence.experiment: Determination of protein binding in cell culture medium containing 10% fetal calf serum and mouse plasma
evidence.result: WM-8014 exhibited 97.5% protein binding in medium with 10% FCS, reducing free drug concentration; WM-1119 had reduced protein binding.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of cellular proliferation inhibition IC50 of WM-8014 vs WM-1119 in EMRK1184 cells alongside their biochemical binding affinities
evidence.result: WM-1119 was ninefold more potent in cellular proliferation (IC50 0.25 uM vs 2.3 uM) while biochemical KD values were comparable (2 nM vs 5 nM), attributed to reduced protein binding.

claims.grade_rationale: Authors explicitly measured protein binding (97.5% in 10% FCS medium for WM-8014, and lower protein binding for WM-1119) and showed an associated 9-fold improvement in cellular growth inhibition (IC50 0.25 uM vs 2.3 uM in EMRK1184 cells), while maintaining similar cell-free KAT6A KD (2 nM vs 5 nM). However, no direct controlled causal rescue (such as serum titration testing shifting IC50 in the same assay) was tested for the same compound.

classification.rationale: Serum/plasma protein binding in the cell culture medium (10% FCS) reduces free compound concentration; extracellular serum protein binding is outside the specific taxonomy categories.

insights.text: WM-8014 binds KAT6A with single-digit nanomolar affinity (IC50 8 nM, KD 5 nM) but exhibits micromolar cellular potency in MEFs (IC50 2.4 uM) and EMRK1184 lymphoma cells (IC50 2.3 uM).
The authors identified high serum protein binding (97.5% in culture medium containing 10% FCS) as a primary factor reducing free compound availability in cellular assays.

Structural modification of WM-8014 into WM-1119 decreased protein binding while retaining nanomolar target binding (KD 2 nM), resulting in a ninefold increase in cellular antiproliferative potency (IC50 0.25 uM).

review_notes: CTx-0124143 and WM-2474 were excluded from the compound dataset because neither had paired quantitative cell-free AND cellular potency reported in the main manuscript/figures (CTx-0124143 had only biochemical IC50/KD, and WM-2474 was tested as an inactive control without a numerical cellular IC50).
Supplementary tables (Supplementary Table 1, 2) were referenced in the text but not provided as separate PDF files; all extracted values were obtained from the main text and Extended Data figures.

claims.author_explanation: Poor cellular potency or loss of cellular activity relative to cell-free potency is driven by poor passive cell permeability and high drug efflux, which correlate with high TPSA (≥90 Å) and hydrogen bond donor count (≥1).

evidence.experiment: Correlation between measured Caco-2 Papp / efflux ratio and cellular activity across compounds 51, 55, 74, 75, 85, and 86.
evidence.result: Compounds with high TPSA/HBD and poor permeability (e.g. 55 and 74) had lower cellular potency relative to biochemical potency; optimizing permeability and lowering efflux (85, 86) closed the gap between cell-free and cellular potency.

evidence.experiment: Assessment of 55 cellular activity relative to recombinant potency.
evidence.result: Authors noted that LIMK2 potency for 55 dropped substantially when profiled in cellular assays due to poor permeability.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors quantitatively measured Caco-2 permeability (Papp and efflux ratio) and physicochemical properties (TPSA, HBD, clogD) across the analogue series and demonstrated that Caco-2 permeability correlated well with cellular activities across the series, but they did not perform a controlled causal rescue test (such as co-treating cells with an efflux inhibitor). Thus, this is an association/mechanistic correlation (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: Poor passive cell permeability (driven by high TPSA and HBD count) is explicitly measured and correlated with cellular potency loss, alongside drug efflux.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 74 and 85 are matched structural analogues differing only in the central aromatic ring (pyridine in 74 replaced with phenyl in 85) designed specifically to reduce TPSA and improve cell permeability/efflux.
interventions.description: Switching the pyridine core ring in 74 to a phenyl ring in 85 lowered TPSA from 112 to 99 Å, which significantly improved Caco-2 permeability (Papp increased from 0.9 to 9.4 x 10^-6 cm/s) and reduced efflux ratio (from 60 to 5), leading to enhanced cellular target engagement and p-cofilin inhibition.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Direct matched pair comparison (pyridine 74 vs phenyl 85) evaluating functional cellular p-cofilin reduction alongside enzymatic potency.
interventions.description: Switching the pyridine ring in 74 to a phenyl ring in 85 lowered TPSA and efflux while increasing Caco-2 permeability, improving functional cellular p-cofilin inhibition in SH-SY5Y cells (AlphaLISA pIC50 increased from 6.18 to 7.30).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 74 (NHCH2CH2OH) and 75 (NHCH2CH2OCH3) are matched structural analogues differing by O-methylation of the terminal alcohol, which tests the effect of reducing HBD count on permeability, efflux, and cellular potency.
interventions.description: Capping the terminal hydroxyl HBD of ethanolamine in 74 with a methyl ether in 75 removed one HBD and increased cLogD (1.74 to 2.38), improving Caco-2 permeability (Papp from 0.9 to 8.3 x 10^-6 cm/s) and lowering efflux ratio (60 to 7.5), which improved cellular NanoBRET and AlphaLISA potencies while maintaining similar enzymatic potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 85 (NHCH2CH2OH) and 86 (OCH2CH2OH) are matched structural analogues differing only in the heteroatom linker (NH vs O), directly comparing HBD/TPSA reduction on permeability and cellular activity.
interventions.description: Replacing the ethanolamine NH linker in 85 with an ethylene glycol O linker in 86 removed an HBD and further lowered TPSA (from 99 to 96 Å), increasing Caco-2 permeability (Papp from 9.4 to 15 x 10^-6 cm/s) and reducing efflux ratio (from 5 to 3) while maintaining high cellular NanoBRET and AlphaLISA potency.

coverage.file_name: Baldwin et al. - 2025 - Discovery of MDI-114215 A Potent and Selective LIMK Inhibitor To Treat Fragile X Syndrome.pdf
coverage.label: Table 3
coverage.note: Table 3 reports PAK-phosphorylated enzymatic pIC50, KINOMEscan pKd, NanoBRET pIC50, and AlphaLISA p-cofilin pIC50 for all 6 profiled compounds.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (enzymatic RapidFire pIC50 against PAK1-phosphorylated LIMK1/2 and non-phosphorylated LIMK1/2, and binding affinity pKd via KINOMEscan) and quantitative cellular potency (intracellular target engagement NanoBRET pIC50 for LIMK1/2 in HEK293 cells, and AlphaLISA p-cofilin pIC50 in SH-SY5Y cells) for multiple matched compounds, including 51, 55, 74, 75, 85, and 86.

insights.text: Allosteric type III aryl sulfonamide LIMK inhibitors maintain equipotent enzymatic inhibition against both unphosphorylated and PAK1-phosphorylated LIMK1/2, avoiding the potency drop against PAK1-pLIMK observed with ATP-competitive inhibitors.

Caco-2 cell permeability and efflux ratios strongly modulate cellular potency: compounds with higher permeability and lower TPSA/efflux (such as 85 and 86) translate biochemical potency into cellular target engagement and cofilin dephosphorylation more effectively.
Lead compound MDI-114215 (85) exhibits high kinome selectivity (S35 = 0.01 across 468 kinases) with balanced dual LIMK1/2 activity and excellent cellular target engagement in intact cells.

review_notes: Table 3 provides quantitative values as pIC50 or pKd (-log10 M), which are entered directly with unit '-log10(M)'.

Compounds 57, 71-73, 76-79, and 80-84 have cell-free enzymatic pIC50 in Table 1 or Table 2 but lack cellular potency data in the paper, so they were excluded from the paired dataset in accordance with the scope guidelines.

Parent tool compound 6 (TH-257) has cellular IC50 curves shown in Figure 6 in iPSC-derived neurons, but its biochemical potency is only cited from prior literature (ref 14) rather than measured in this study.

Added non-phosphorylated LIMK1/2 RapidFire enzymatic pIC50 measurements for all 6 paired compounds (51, 55 from p. 8 text; 74, 75, 85, 86 from Tables 1-2), completed biochemical-cellular pairs for all 6 compounds, and fixed and expanded the chemical modification interventions (74->85, 74->75, 85->86) addressing TPSA/HBD-driven permeability and efflux.

claims.author_explanation: The authors propose that the anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic cellular effects of CK2 inhibition are linked to nuclear CK2 activity (e.g., interaction with nuclear chromatin remodeling factor Brg1 and apoptotic regulation in the nuclear matrix), whereas 5a-2 preferentially distributes to the cytoplasm (71% cytoplasmic vs. 16% nuclear in LNCaP cells), which limits its nuclear CK2 inhibition and explains why micromolar concentrations are required for anti-proliferative efficacy despite nanomolar cell-free kinase potency.

evidence.experiment: Subcellular fractionation of LNCaP cells treated with 1 µM 5a-2 for 5 h followed by HPLC-MS/MS quantification of compound levels across four cellular fractions
evidence.result: 71% of intracellular 5a-2 was detected in the cytoplasm and only 16% in the nuclear fraction, in contrast to CX-4945 which was 49% nuclear and 24% cytoplasmic

evidence.experiment: Comparison of cell proliferation EC50 (14.2–39.8 µM), apoptosis induction, and cell migration inhibition between 5a-2 and CX-4945
evidence.result: 5a-2 was less potent than CX-4945 in anti-proliferation and apoptosis (nuclear CK2-dependent processes) but more potent in inhibiting cell migration (cytoplasmic CK2-dependent process)

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured the subcellular distribution of 5a-2 and CX-4945 across four cellular fractions (cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, membrane) by HPLC-MS/MS and correlated nuclear vs. cytoplasmic levels with phenotypic outcomes (proliferation/apoptosis vs. migration). However, no causal rescue intervention (e.g., chemically directing 5a-2 to the nucleus) was conducted to test if redistributing the compound restores cellular anti-proliferative potency.

classification.rationale: The antiproliferative phenotype specifically requires inhibiting the nuclear pool of CK2, while the compound preferentially localizes to the cytoplasm, limiting compartmental target access.

claims.author_explanation: Intracellular target inhibition depends on the free intracellular drug concentration. The authors demonstrated that 5a-2 penetrates cells predominantly by passive diffusion (LogD7.4 = 3.78) and reaches intracellular concentrations of 160.8 to 408.3 nM after treatment with 1 µM extracellular compound, which explains its ability to effectively inhibit intracellular CK2 activity (>75% at 20 µM).

evidence.experiment: Quantitative determination of intracellular concentration of 5a-2 in A431 cells treated with 1 µM compound for 1, 5, and 12 h by HPLC-MS/MS
evidence.result: Intracellular concentration was 160.8 ± 17.5 nM at 1 h, rising to 408.3 ± 55.6 nM at 12 h

evidence.experiment: Temperature-dependent uptake of 1 µM 5a-2 in A431 cells at 37 °C vs. 4 °C for 3 h
evidence.result: Intracellular concentration decreased by 51% at 4 °C, indicating that passive diffusion is the primary mechanism of cellular uptake

claims.grade_rationale: The authors quantitatively measured cellular uptake and intracellular concentration by HPLC-MS/MS at multiple time points and temperatures (37 °C vs. 4 °C), establishing passive diffusion as the primary uptake route. This is a direct mechanistic concentration measurement without an intervention that rescues potency.

classification.rationale: The explanation focuses on passive diffusion across the cell membrane and resulting intracellular concentration driving cellular target inhibition.

insights.text: Indeno[1,2-b]indole 5a-2 exhibits a substantial numerical drop between cell-free CK2 inhibition (IC50 = 25 nM) and cellular proliferation suppression (EC50 = 14.2–39.8 µM across three tumor cell lines).

Compound 5a-2 enters cells primarily via passive diffusion, achieving intracellular concentrations of 160.8 to 408.3 nM after 1 µM extracellular dosing, sufficient to reduce intracellular CK2 activity by >75% at 20 µM.

Subcellular fractionation revealed that 71% of intracellular 5a-2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm and only 16% in the nucleus, providing a mechanistic basis for its weaker anti-proliferative/pro-apoptotic efficacy relative to migration inhibition.

review_notes: Reference compound CX-4945 was evaluated for cellular potency in A431, A549, LNCaP, and HUVEC cells, but its cell-free CK2 IC50 (0.0037 µM) was explicitly cited from Gozzi et al. [38] (Table 1 footnote a). In accordance with the prompt instruction that both observations must be supported by the supplied PDFs and not merely a reference to another paper, CX-4945 is excluded from paired extraction.
Indeno[1,2-b]indoles 5a-1 and 5b-1 were screened only in the biochemical kinase assay (IC50 = 8.17 µM and 9.91 µM, respectively) and excluded from cellular potency determination.

Compound 5b-2 was evaluated for biochemical IC50 (0.047 µM) and tested in intracellular assays at single concentrations (1, 10, 20 µM; % inhibition of Akt phosphorylation and CK2 activity), but no quantitative concentration-response potency (IC50/EC50) was determined in cells.
No controlled causal rescue intervention was performed in this study; hence the interventions array is empty.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of parent Arg-containing lariat 6 with neutral Leu/Phe analogues in CycA FP assay and MDCK permeability assay.
evidence.result: Parent 6 had CycA FP1 IC50 = 0.77 uM but MDCK Papp below LOQ. Neutral replacement in compound 7 regained low MDCK permeability (0.3 x 10^-6 cm/s) with 70-fold loss of affinity, subsequently rescued by hydrophobic tailoring.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of MDCK A-B permeability, Cyclin A/B FP2 IC50, and NCI-H1048 cellular GI50 across neutral macrocycle series in Tables 4-8.
evidence.result: Replacing D-Nva in 26 (CycA IC50 = 0.188 uM, H1048 GI50 = 0.096 uM, MDCK Papp = 2.3 x 10^-6 cm/s) with cyclopropylglycine in 27 (CycA IC50 = 0.177 uM) or cis-D-fluoroproline in 30 (CycA IC50 = 0.132 uM) reduced MDCK Papp to 0.3 x 10^-6 cm/s and degraded H1048 GI50 to 0.458 and 0.176 uM, respectively.

claims.grade_rationale: Supported by direct mechanistic permeability measurements (MDCK Papp and computed ΔGinsert) across parent and neutral macrocycles showing that poor passive permeability drives cellular potency loss (e.g., compound 6 Papp < LOQ; compound 27 vs 26 has equal biochemical IC50 of 0.177 vs 0.188 uM but 8-fold lower MDCK Papp of 0.3 vs 2.3 x 10^-6 cm/s and 4.8-fold worse cellular GI50 of 0.458 vs 0.096 uM), without an isolated non-structural causal rescue.

classification.rationale: Low passive membrane permeability (measured via MDCK Papp) is the primary mechanism explaining the cellular potency loss of the macrocycles, though backbone chameleonicity is also noted as a contributing factor.

claims.author_explanation: Compound 29 had potent cellular activity but exhibited high Caco-2 efflux liability (ER = 55) and modest permeability (0.7 x 10^-6 cm/s). Modifying the N-terminal cap to a spiro-bis-cyclobutyl moiety in compound 34 improved passive permeability (MDCK Papp = 3.6 x 10^-6 cm/s) and reduced efflux liability (ER = 22), enhancing in vitro cellular potency and enabling in vivo antitumor exposure.

evidence.experiment: Measurement of MDCK Papp and bidirectional Caco-2 permeability (A-B, B-A, ER) across N-terminal cap series 29-34.
evidence.result: Spiro-bis-cyclobutyl compound 34 showed MDCK Papp = 3.6 x 10^-6 cm/s and Caco-2 ER = 22, compared to compound 29 with ER = 55 and Papp = 0.7 x 10^-6 cm/s.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured bidirectional Caco-2 permeability (A-B and B-A), calculating efflux ratios (ER) alongside MDCK permeability across N-terminal cap modifications (compounds 29-34), showing correlated reduction in efflux and improved cell activity.

classification.rationale: High Caco-2 efflux liability (ER = 55) is emphasized and measured alongside modest passive permeability to explain cellular potency differences across the series.

claims.author_explanation: Dual Cyclin A/B RxL inhibition is required for optimal synthetic lethality in E2F-driven cancer cell lines, while Cyclin E activity is dispensable; selective activity over Cyclin E and non-transformed WI-38 cells avoids non-specific toxicity.

classification.rationale: Optimal cellular synthetic lethality requires dual inhibition of both Cyclin A and Cyclin B while sparing Cyclin E.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched analogue comparison: compounds 29 and 34 share an identical macrocyclic core and differ only in the N-terminal cycloalkyl cap; however, biochemical potency also improved ~3.3-fold (0.262 to 0.079 uM), confounding purely permeability/efflux-driven rescue.
interventions.description: Modification of the N-terminal cap from trifluoromethylcyclopropyl (29) to trifluoromethyl-spiro-bis-cyclobutyl (34) to reduce Caco-2 efflux liability (ER from 55 to 22) and enhance passive permeability (MDCK Papp from 0.7 to 3.6 x 10^-6 cm/s), improving cellular GI50.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Analogue comparison in Table 5 demonstrating ~100-fold improvement in H1048 GI50 (6.85 to 0.066 uM), driven primarily by improved Cyclin A/B binding affinity and conformational preorganization alongside a 2-fold increase in MDCK permeability (0.5 to 1.0 x 10^-6 cm/s).
interventions.description: Analogue comparison replacing the Abu residue and 3-Cl-Phe of compound 13 with 4-fluoroproline and 2,5-diCl-Phe in compound 19 (via intermediates 15, 17, 18) to rigidify the backbone, eliminate a backbone HBD, and improve target affinity and cellular GI50.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched pair comparison differing by a single ortho-Cl atom on Phe (Table 4 and Table 5).
interventions.description: Addition of a 2-chloro substituent on the 3-chlorophenylalanine ring (compound 13 to 15) to increase lipophilicity and passive MDCK permeability (0.5 to 2.1 x 10^-6 cm/s) while retaining target affinity and cellular activity.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched pair differing by a single N-methyl group on the lysine side chain (Table 6), demonstrating that higher permeability did not improve cellular GI50 when accompanied by a 3-fold loss of Cyclin A affinity.
interventions.description: Nε-methylation of the macrocycle lysine side chain (compound 19 to 20) to boost passive permeability (MDCK Papp from 1.0 to 12.1 x 10^-6 cm/s), which eroded Cyclin A affinity and cellular potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched pair differing only at the tail side chain R (Me vs cyclopropyl, Table 7); larger alkyl chains (23-25) improved permeability but lost biochemical and cellular potency.
interventions.description: Replacement of the tail alanine residue (19) with cyclopropylglycine (26) at the Arg-replacement position to balance passive permeability (MDCK Papp from 1.0 to 2.3 x 10^-6 cm/s) with biochemical and cellular potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched pair differing at the macrocycle turn-inducing linker residue (Table 8) with nearly identical biochemical potency (0.188 vs 0.177 uM), illustrating cellular potency loss driven by reduced passive permeability.
interventions.description: Replacement of the macrocycle linker D-Nva (26) with cyclopropylglycine (27), which retained identical Cyclin A/B biochemical potency but reduced MDCK permeability ~8-fold (2.3 to 0.3 x 10^-6 cm/s) and degraded cellular potency >4-fold.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched pair differing at the macrocycle linker residue (Table 8).
interventions.description: Replacement of D-Nva (26) with Aib (29) in the macrocycle core to improve kinetic solubility (77.3 to 329 uM) and reduce mouse plasma protein binding (99.4% to 93.4%) while maintaining cellular GI50 (0.096 vs 0.092 uM).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched pair differing at the macrocycle linker residue (Table 8), testing the effect of backbone HBD removal vs chameleonic flexibility.
interventions.description: Replacement of D-Nva (26) with cis-D-fluoroproline (30) to eliminate a backbone H-bond donor, which unexpectedly decreased MDCK permeability (2.3 to 0.3 x 10^-6 cm/s) and cellular potency (0.096 to 0.176 uM) despite better biochemical affinity (0.132 uM), attributed to loss of chameleonic IMHBs.

eligibility.reason: The study reports cell-free competitive binding affinity (IC50 in Cyclin A, Cyclin B, and Cyclin E fluorescence polarization assays) alongside cellular antiproliferative potency (GI50 in NCI-H1048 and NCI-H69 SCLC cell lines and WI-38 fibroblasts) for multiple macrocyclic peptide inhibitors (compounds 13, 15, 17-34).

insights.text: Elimination of the canonical charged arginine in the RxL substrate recognition motif was required to achieve passive membrane permeability in macrocyclic Cyclin A/B inhibitors, overcoming a major hurdle for targeting cyclin hydrophobic patches.

Conformational restriction using fluoroproline and tailor-made hydrophobic substitutions in the macrocycle tail restored biochemical affinity lost by arginine elimination, generating nanomolar dual Cyclin A/B inhibitors.
Modifying the N-terminal cap to a spiro-bis-cyclobutyl moiety (compound 34) improved passive permeability and reduced Caco-2 efflux liability relative to earlier analogues.

Inhibition of both Cyclin A and Cyclin B RxL interactions was highlighted as essential to trigger synthetic lethality and antiproliferative activity specifically in RB1-dysregulated cancer cell lines while sparing WI-38 normal fibroblasts.

review_notes: Table footnotes across Tables 6-9 indicate that all compounds in these series have Cyclin B FP IC50 <= 0.020 uM (the assay's limit of quantitation).
Text on page 10 mentions that compound 34 GI50 vs NCI-H1048 was 0.048 uM, whereas Table 9 lists 0.042 uM; the table value was extracted as the primary record and the minor discrepancy documented.
Non-paired compounds (such as 1-5, 6, 8-12, 14, and 16) were excluded from the compound dataset because they lack either cell-free or intact cell quantitative potency in the provided manuscript.

Verified all 20 paired compounds (13, 15, 17-34) across Tables 4-9 and text; completed missing biochemical/cellular pairing links, fixed intervention measurement ID references, added key SAR interventions exploring passive permeability and efflux, and upgraded cl_arginine_permeability to Grade 3 based on direct MDCK Papp measurements.

claims.author_explanation: Poor membrane permeability and intracellular distribution barriers in Leishmania parasites limit compound access to intracellular LmxCLK1, causing a discrepancy between high in vitro affinity/potency and cellular target engagement or phenotypic activity.

evidence.experiment: Electroporation of L. mexicana promastigotes in the presence of K-5 probe compared with passive incubation
evidence.result: Passive incubation yielded minimal BRET signal up to 4 µM, whereas electroporation yielded a robust dose-dependent BRET signal (KD-APP = 810.7 nM), closely matching the cell-free KD (914.6 nM), confirming membrane permeability as the barrier.

evidence.experiment: Screening 380 kinase inhibitors by cell-free DSF vs live-cell promastigote NanoBRET
evidence.result: Compounds with strong in vitro thermal shifts exhibited variable cellular target engagement (e.g., GZD824 ΔTm = 17.4 °C with 46.5% occupancy, WZ8040 ΔTm = 14.8 °C with 60.8% occupancy, and Pelitinib ΔTm = 10.8 °C with negligible cellular occupancy), showing that binding alone does not predict cellular efficacy due to permeability/distribution factors.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly tested this hypothesis using probe K-5: passive incubation gave no cellular target engagement, but physical permeabilization via electroporation completely restored the cellular BRET signal to match in vitro affinity (KD-APP ~ 811 nM vs cell-free KD ~ 915 nM). Furthermore, comparing different kinase inhibitors with similar in vitro thermal shifts showed marked divergence in cellular target occupancy due to differential permeability.

classification.rationale: Poor passive membrane permeability into Leishmania parasites limits access to the intracellular target, which was experimentally rescued by electroporation.

claims.author_explanation: Tracer SV366 demonstrates approximately 5-fold higher potency in intracellular amastigotes than in promastigotes due to stage-specific membrane permeability, intracellular accumulation, or enhanced probe retention within internalized amastigotes, whereas unmodified parent GZD824 exhibits 3-fold lower potency in intracellular amastigotes.

evidence.experiment: NanoBRET saturation and competition assays comparing promastigotes and macrophage-internalized amastigotes
evidence.result: SV366 EC50 was 72.6 nM in amastigotes vs 383.2 nM in promastigotes (~5-fold lower EC50), while GZD824 IC50 shifted from 4.6 µM in promastigotes to 13.0 µM in amastigotes (~3-fold higher IC50).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured target engagement of both SV366 and GZD824 in both promastigote and intramacrophage amastigote stages, observing opposite trends upon fluorophore conjugation, but did not perform a controlled causal rescue or mechanistic trapping experiment.

classification.rationale: Potency differences between promastigotes and intracellular amastigotes are attributed to stage-specific membrane permeability, intracellular accumulation, or retention.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports paired quantitative cell-free biochemical potencies (TR-FRET enzymatic IC50/Ki or purified protein BRET KD/EC50) and quantitative cellular potencies (promastigote and amastigote in-cell NanoBRET target engagement KD-APP/IC50/EC50 and phenotypic viability/killing EC50) for six compounds: K-5, GZD824, staurosporine, WZ8040, WZ3146, and SV366.

insights.text: Cell-free biochemical binding (e.g. thermal stabilization by DSF) does not reliably predict cellular target engagement in Leishmania due to critical membrane permeability and intracellular distribution barriers.

Physical permeabilization by electroporation successfully restores target engagement of a poorly permeable probe to match its in vitro affinity, establishing the parasite membrane as the primary barrier.
Fluorophore conjugation on a shared kinase scaffold (GZD824 vs SV366) altered the relative intracellular target engagement between extracellular promastigotes and macrophage-internalized amastigotes.
The covalent EGFR inhibitor WZ8040 achieves robust target engagement and low-micromolar parasite killing in both promastigotes and macrophage-internalized amastigotes while sparing host macrophages.

review_notes: Recombinant LmxCLK1 enzymatic assays used ATP at 66 µM (10x Km), while cellular NanoBRET reflects competition against intracellular ATP pools.
WZ8040 and WZ3146 are covalent inhibitors; in vitro IC50 values are time-dependent, but kinact/KI could not be reliably determined under assay conditions.

Target validation in Figure 7 included LmxCLK1 overexpression and CLK1/CLK2 null mutants, showing that CLK1 overexpression shifted WZ8040 EC50 3-fold, supporting LmxCLK1 as a functional cellular target.

Added commercial NanoBRET tracer K-5 (cmp_k5) with its cell-free KD (914.6 nM), passive cellular KD-APP (>4.0 µM), and electroporated cellular KD-APP (810.7 nM), linking them to the electroporation intervention (int_electroporation_probe).

Added all additional quantitative measurements from Figures 3, 4, 6E, and 7C-E, including SV366 cell-free EC50 (8.4 nM) and EC80 values, WZ8040 time-dependent pre-incubation IC50 values (0-30 min), THP-1 macrophage cytotoxicity controls, and WZ8040 EC50 values across LmxCLK1-overexpressing, ΔCLK1, ΔCLK2, and Cys-to-Ala mutant lines.

Probe SV363 (GZD824 conjugated to EverFluor590) was tested only in cell-free purified NLuc::LmxCLK1 titration (EC50 > 1 µM, Figure 3B) and was not tested in cellular assays; therefore it is excluded from the paired compound dataset per scope rules.

pairs.rationale: Direct comparison of PRMT5:MEP50 biochemical inhibition against cellular antiproliferative potency in Maver-1 mantle cell lymphoma cells.

claims.author_explanation: The authors observe an ~10-fold shift between biochemical and cell biochemical IC50 values and explain that phenotypic antiproliferative effects manifest slowly over multiple days because even a small amount of residual PRMT5 enzyme turnover is sufficient to maintain substrate methylation, requiring sustained high levels of target inhibition.

evidence.experiment: Time-course proliferation profiling over 12 days and shRNA knockdown of PRMT5 in Z-138 cells comparing SmD3me2s levels to total SmD3
evidence.result: Antiproliferative responses required long incubation times (manifesting over 12 days), and >60% protein knockdown resulted in only 50% substrate methylation reduction, demonstrating that small amounts of residual PRMT5 activity can maintain methylation

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors demonstrate time-dependent proliferation effects and confirm via shRNA knockdown that >60% knockdown only reduces SmD3me2s by 50%, providing mechanistic evidence for the cellular requirement for high inhibition without performing a controlled causal rescue of potency.

classification.rationale: High target vulnerability threshold/residual enzyme turnover (small amounts of residual PRMT5 activity maintain substrate methylation) explains the shift and slow kinetics, which is outside the taxonomy.

insights.text: EPZ015666 is a potent, SAM-uncompetitive and peptide-competitive inhibitor of PRMT5:MEP50 with a biochemical IC50 of 22 nM and Ki of 5 nM.
Cellular antiproliferative activity requires prolonged exposure (12 days), yielding IC50 values of 96 nM in Z-138 and 450 nM in Maver-1 cells.

An average ~10-fold shift is observed between biochemical and cellular methylation IC50 values, consistent with the requirement for sustained and near-complete target inhibition to overcome residual enzyme turnover.

review_notes: EPZ015666 is the only compound in the main text with both quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (IC50 = 22 nM) and cellular potency (IC50 = 96 nM and 450 nM).

Initial HTS hit EPZ007345 (IC50 = 326 nM, Kd = 70 nM) and negative control EPZ019896 (IC50 > 10 µM) lack quantitative cellular potency endpoints in the provided text and were excluded from compound/measurement tables.

Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Figures 1, 9, 10, and 14 contain additional cellular methylation and proliferation IC50 values across multiple cell lines, but supplementary files were not supplied.

claims.author_explanation: SHP099 suppresses MAPK signalling (p-ERK) and cell growth specifically through direct on-target allosteric inhibition of SHP2, as shown by lack of activity in cancer cells expressing the engineered drug-resistant mutant SHP2(T253M/Q257L) or harbouring downstream activating RAS/RAF mutations.

evidence.experiment: Re-expression of wild-type SHP2 vs drug-resistant SHP2(T253M/Q257L) in SHP2-depleted KYSE520 cells treated with SHP099
evidence.result: SHP099 failed to inhibit p-ERK phosphorylation and cell proliferation in cells expressing the double-mutant allele, whereas it inhibited both in cells expressing wild-type SHP2

evidence.experiment: Profiling SHP099 across RTK-dependent vs RAS/RAF-mutated haematopoietic and colorectal cancer cell lines
evidence.result: Cell lines dependent on RTK signalling were sensitive to SHP099, whereas KRAS/NRAS/BRAF-mutated cells were insensitive (IC50 > 20-30 µM)

claims.grade_rationale: The authors perform controlled genetic rescue and resistance tests in both biochemical and cellular contexts: introducing the engineered SHP2(T253M/Q257L) mutant in SHP2-depleted KYSE520 cells prevents SHP099 from inhibiting p-ERK and cell growth, directly isolating target engagement as the causal driver of cellular activity.

classification.rationale: This statement validates on-target allosteric mechanism via drug-resistant mutant rescue and pathway dependence rather than explaining a specific biochemical-to-cellular potency discrepancy.

claims.author_explanation: Cancer cells harbouring constitutively activating downstream RAS or BRAF mutations (such as A2058 with BRAF V600E, or RAS/BRAF-mutated haematopoietic and colorectal lines) are refractory to SHP099 (cellular IC50 > 20-30 µM vs ~0.25 µM p-ERK and ~1.2 µM viability in RTK-driven KYSE520) because constitutive RAS/RAF signalling maintains p-ERK activation and proliferation independently of upstream SHP2 catalytic activity.
claims.category: pathway bypass / target independence (oncogenic RAS/RAF mutations)

evidence.experiment: Transduction of SHP2-dependent SUM52 cells with lentivirus expressing oncogenic KRAS(G12V) followed by dox-inducible SHP2 shRNA depletion (Fig. 1d, Extended Data Fig. 1d)
evidence.result: Exogenous KRAS(G12V) expression restored cellular p-ERK levels and rendered SUM52 cells refractory to SHP2 depletion.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of SHP099 p-ERK inhibition and cellular viability across RTK-driven (KYSE520, MDA-MB-468) vs RAS/BRAF-mutant (A2058, haematopoietic and colorectal panels) cell lines
evidence.result: SHP099 potently inhibited p-ERK (IC50 ~ 0.25 µM) and proliferation in RTK-driven cells but showed no p-ERK or growth inhibition in BRAF V600E A2058 cells (IC50 > 20 µM) or RAS/BRAF-mutant panels (IC50 > 20-30 µM).

claims.grade_rationale: Supported by extensive cell-panel association data (71 haematopoietic and 26 colorectal cell lines, plus shRNA screens across 250 CCLE lines) and controlled genetic intervention showing that exogenous KRAS(G12V) expression in SHP2-dependent SUM52 cells restores p-ERK levels and renders cells insensitive to SHP2 depletion.

classification.rationale: Downstream pathway bypass via constitutively activating RAS or BRAF mutations renders cells refractory to upstream SHP2 inhibition; genetic pathway independence is outside the taxonomy.

claims.author_explanation: Because SHP099 binds the central tunnel at the N-SH2/C-SH2/PTP interface to lock SHP2 in its auto-inhibited conformation, increasing concentrations of activating bidentate phosphotyrosine peptide (2P-IRS-1) shift SHP2 toward the open active state and reduce SHP099 potency tenfold in biochemical assays (and complete removal of the SH2 regulatory domains in SHP2PTP abolishes inhibition, IC50 > 100 µM).
claims.category: allosteric conformational competition / activating ligand level

evidence.experiment: Biochemical titration of activating 2P-IRS-1 peptide concentration in the DiFMUP phosphatase assay with SHP099 vs catalytic-site inhibitor SHP043 (Figure 2d)
evidence.result: Increasing 2P-IRS-1 concentration caused a 10-fold decrease in SHP099 potency (to ~0.25 µM at ~25 µM 2P-IRS-1) but a 6-fold increase in SHP043 potency.

evidence.experiment: Biochemical profiling of SHP099 against isolated SHP2 catalytic domain (residues 230-545) lacking the N-SH2 and C-SH2 domains (Extended Data Table 1)
evidence.result: SHP099 had no detectable inhibitory activity against the isolated PTP domain (IC50 > 100 µM).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly test the effect of titrating the activating 2P-IRS-1 peptide against SHP099 vs the active-site inhibitor SHP043 (Figure 2d), demonstrating a 10-fold loss in SHP099 potency as 2P-IRS-1 increases (whereas SHP043 becomes 6-fold more potent), and corroborate this with co-crystal structure 5EHR and truncation of the SH2 domains (SHP2PTP IC50 > 100 µM).

classification.rationale: SHP099 locks SHP2 in its auto-inhibited conformation, and activating phosphotyrosine peptides shift the target toward the open active conformation, reducing inhibitor potency.

eligibility.reason: SHP099 has quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (SHP2 IC50 = 0.071 µM, Kd = 0.073 µM) and cellular mechanistic potency (p-ERK inhibition IC50 ~0.25 µM in MDA-MB-468 and KYSE520 cells).

insights.text: SHP099 achieves submicromolar cellular target inhibition (p-ERK IC50 ~0.25 µM) that aligns closely with its cell-free biochemical potency (IC50 = 0.071 µM, Kd = 0.073 µM).

Steric clash introduced by the double mutation T253M/Q257L confers >1,000-fold resistance in vitro and completely abolishes p-ERK inhibition and growth suppression in cells, proving an on-target mechanism.
Cellular sensitivity to SHP099 is strictly restricted to RTK-dependent cancers and is bypassed by downstream activating mutations in KRAS or BRAF.

review_notes: SHP099 is the sole compound in the paper with paired cell-free biochemical potency and cellular potency measurements.
Parent hit compound SHP836 (GW286103) has a biochemical IC50 of 5.0 µM reported in Figure 2c, but cellular potency is not reported numerically.
Active-site PTP inhibitor SHP043 is evaluated in biochemical assays across varying IRS-1 peptide concentrations but not in cell potency assays.

Added biochemical measurements for SHP099 at high activating 2P-IRS-1 concentration (Figure 2d) and against the isolated SHP2 PTP domain (Extended Data Table 1), plus cellular measurements in A2058 (p-ERK and proliferation), KYSE520 (5-day CellTiter-Glo proliferation), and engineered KYSE520 cells re-expressing WT or T253M/Q257L SHP2 (Figure 3f).

Added claims and interventions covering (1) on-target SHP2 inhibition validated by the engineered T253M/Q257L resistant mutant, (2) pathway bypass in RAS/BRAF-mutated cells causing loss of cellular activity, and (3) competition with activating 2P-IRS-1 phosphopeptide shifting SHP099 biochemical potency.

claims.author_explanation: Carboxylic acid KDM inhibitors traditionally suffer from poor cellular activity due to high polarity; balancing polarity with lipophilicity and modifying the 6-position vector improved PAMPA permeability, leading to enhanced cellular and MOA potency.

evidence.experiment: Evaluation of cLogD, PAMPA permeability, KDM4C IC50, KYSE-150 proliferation EC50, and H3K36me3 MOA EC50 across compounds 3-6.
evidence.result: PAMPA permeability increased from 18.42 nm/s (3) to 51.50 nm/s (5) and 51.18 nm/s (6), tracking with an increase in cellular antiproliferative potency from 830 nM (3) to 3.5 nM (6) and MOA potency from 560 nM (3) to 1.3 nM (6).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors correlated higher lipophilicity and PAMPA permeability (from 3 to 5 and 6) with improved cellular KYSE-150 EC50 and H3K36me3 MOA EC50 across an analogue series, representing an association/SAR study without dynamic or transporter-controlled rescue.

classification.rationale: High polarity limits passive membrane permeability (measured by PAMPA), and optimizing lipophilicity improved permeability and cellular potency.

claims.author_explanation: High lipophilicity and high plasma protein binding (human PPB = 99.9%) caused a plateau in apparent biochemical IC50 around 40 nM under standard assay conditions (0.2 mg/mL BSA), masking true cell-free potency.

evidence.experiment: KDM4C enzymatic inhibition assay of compound 6 tested under standard BSA (0.2 mg/mL) vs reduced BSA (0.02 mg/mL).
evidence.result: The enzymatic potency of compound 6 shifted from 35 nM (0.2 mg/mL BSA) to 9 nM (0.02 mg/mL BSA).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors performed a controlled intervention on the biochemical assay condition by lowering BSA ten-fold, directly observing a shift in IC50 from 35 nM to 9 nM for compound 6, isolating the protein-binding artifact.

classification.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
classification.rationale: High lipophilicity and non-specific binding to BSA in the biochemical buffer masked true cell-free potency, demonstrated by lowering BSA concentration.

insights.text: Carboxylic acid 2-OG mimetics frequently suffer from poor cell activity; introducing hydrophobic aryl/heteroaryl substituents to increase PAMPA permeability significantly improved cellular antiproliferation and histone mark modulation.

For lipophilic carboxylic acid inhibitors like compound 6, high non-specific binding to assay components (such as 0.2 mg/mL BSA) can artificially right-shift apparent biochemical IC50 values, partially explaining why cellular potency appeared more potent than standard enzymatic potency.
Cellular target engagement confirmed by MS and HTRF against the H3K36me3 mark correlated closely with cell proliferation arrest across the chemical series.

review_notes: Compound 1 (3-(methylamino)isonicotinic acid) and 2,4-PDCA were mentioned with biochemical IC50s (1400 nM and 19 nM, respectively) in Chart 1 and text, but no quantitative cellular potencies were reported for them in this paper; therefore, they were excluded from the paired dataset.

The SI contains additional biological and MS methods, but is not present as a separate PDF in the input files; all extracted values were obtained directly from the main manuscript text, figures, and tables.

Verified all paired compounds (2, 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 5, and 6) against Chart 2, Table 1, Table 2, and manuscript text. Added the remaining censored selectivity measurements (>4,000 nM against KDM2B, KDM3A, KDM3B, KDM6B, and PHF8) from Table 2 for compound 6, additional pairings (low-BSA KDM4C vs KYSE-150 and standard KDM4C vs 3D organoid assays), and chemical modification interventions covering 2a to 3 and the H3K36me3 MOA series.

claims.author_explanation: The authors tested whether cell permeability or intracellular target engagement could explain why compounds 4, 5, and 6 showed higher than expected MM.1S antiproliferation EC50 values (2.2–4.6 uM) relative to biochemical potencies (0.13–0.64 uM). CETSA demonstrated target engagement and stabilization of BRD4 at submicromolar concentrations similar to biochemical potency, ruling out permeability or lack of target engagement as the cause.

evidence.experiment: Isothermal dose-response CETSA measuring BRD4 thermal stabilization in MM.1S cells after 1 h treatment with 4, 5, 6, and (+)-JQ1 across 0.05–25 uM.
evidence.result: Dose-dependent BRD4 stabilization occurred at submicromolar concentrations (0.2–1 uM) comparable to biochemical BRD4 D1 potency, showing intracellular target engagement is achieved at submicromolar concentrations.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly performed an isothermal dose-response CETSA in intact MM.1S cells and observed BRD4 stabilization at submicromolar concentrations matching biochemical potency, concluding that target engagement and permeability cannot explain the reduced antiproliferative activity (Grade 3 mechanistic measurement).

classification.rationale: Poor cell permeability and lack of intracellular target engagement were explicitly tested and ruled out by intact-cell CETSA showing submicromolar BRD4 stabilization.

claims.author_explanation: Selective inhibition of BRD4 D1 alone is insufficient to downregulate c-Myc in MM.1S cells and unexpectedly elevates c-Myc protein levels at submicromolar concentrations matching biochemical BRD4 D1 potency. Downregulation of c-Myc and subsequent antiproliferation occurs only at higher concentrations (>10-fold above biochemical IC50) where other BET bromodomains or off-target kinases may be inhibited.

evidence.experiment: Western blot analysis of c-Myc protein levels in MM.1S cells after 8 h treatment with compounds 4, 5, 6 (0.2–25 uM) and (+)-JQ1 (0.05–5 uM).
evidence.result: Compounds 4–6 induced elevated c-Myc protein levels relative to DMSO control at submicromolar concentrations (0.2–1 uM), whereas c-Myc downregulation occurred only at high concentrations (>10 uM) matching the MM.1S antiproliferation EC50.

claims.grade_rationale: Western blot evaluation of c-Myc protein levels in MM.1S cells after 8 h treatment demonstrated submicromolar elevation of c-Myc rather than repression, mechanistically explaining why submicromolar BRD4 D1 engagement fails to halt proliferation in this c-Myc-dependent line (Grade 3 mechanistic measurement).

classification.rationale: Selective BRD4 D1 inhibition alone fails to repress c-Myc at submicromolar concentrations; antiproliferation occurs only at higher concentrations where other BET bromodomains or off-target kinases are inhibited.

claims.author_explanation: The authors tested whether the observed antiproliferative EC50 values could be attributed to a counter-ion effect by comparing the salt and free-base forms of compound 5.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of MM.1S antiproliferation EC50 between the salt and free-base forms of compound 5.
evidence.result: Salt and free-base forms of 5 gave similar EC50 values, indicating that counter-ion formulation does not explain the observed cellular potency.

claims.grade_rationale: Controlled comparison of salt vs free-base form of compound 5 in the MM.1S proliferation assay ruled out counter-ion formulation effects (Grade 4 intervention test).

classification.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
classification.rationale: A counter-ion/salt formulation effect was tested by comparing salt and free-base forms and was experimentally ruled out.

claims.author_explanation: In discussing why c-Myc downregulation and growth inhibition require high compound concentrations (>10-fold above biochemical BRD4 D1 IC50), the authors state that given their moderate 9–33 fold selectivity for BRD4 D1 and residual p38alpha activity, they cannot rule out effects from inhibiting other BET bromodomains or kinases such as CK1, or drug efflux, although structurally related less-selective inhibitors did not show these effects.

evidence.experiment: Author discussion of potential confounding factors at high compound concentrations (>10-fold above biochemical IC50) in MM.1S cells.
evidence.result: Authors note they cannot rule out contributions from inhibiting other BET bromodomains, off-target kinases (p38alpha, CK1), or drug efflux, while citing prior structurally related less-selective inhibitors that lacked these effects.

claims.grade_rationale: Stated as an unverified caveat/hypothesis that cannot be ruled out without direct efflux or orthogonal rescue testing in this study (Grade 1 statement/hypothesis).

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative biochemical binding potencies (fluorescence anisotropy and AlphaScreen IC50 values) and quantitative cellular antiproliferative potencies (MM.1S cell growth inhibition EC50) for the reference pan-BET inhibitor (+)-JQ1 and BRD4 D1-selective inhibitors 4, 5, and 6.

insights.text: BRD4 D1-selective inhibitors 4, 5, and 6 exhibit submicromolar biochemical affinity (IC50 = 0.13–0.64 uM) but reduced cellular antiproliferative activity (EC50 = 2.2–4.6 uM) in BRD4-dependent MM.1S multiple myeloma cells.

CETSA in intact MM.1S cells demonstrated robust BRD4 stabilization at submicromolar concentrations matching biochemical potency, ruling out poor cell permeability or lack of intracellular target engagement as the cause for the potency gap.

Selective BRD4 D1 inhibition unexpectedly elevates c-Myc protein levels at submicromolar concentrations, with c-Myc downregulation occurring only at concentrations >10-fold higher where off-target BET bromodomains or kinases may be engaged.
Comparison of salt and free-base formulations of lead inhibitor 5 showed comparable cellular antiproliferation EC50 values, ruling out counter-ion effects as the origin of the cellular potency drop.

review_notes: Cellular antiproliferation EC50 values for compounds 4, 5, and 6 are reported in the main text as a collective range (2.2–4.6 uM) with individual curves housed in Supporting Information Figure S14A; this range was faithfully extracted without imputing individual values.
Compounds 1, 2, 3, 7, and 8 from Table 1 were omitted from the dataset because they lacked quantitative cellular potency measurements in the provided main manuscript.

Figure 2B single-dose inhibition datum (61% inhibition at 100 uM for 5 against BRD2 D1) was omitted from measurements because it is a single-concentration percentage rather than an IC50/Kd/potency bound.

Added AlphaScreen biochemical-to-cellular pairs for (+)-JQ1, 4, 5, and 6 alongside the FA pairs, and added the authors' explicit caveat regarding drug efflux and off-target BET/kinase inhibition (p38alpha, CK1) at high concentrations.

claims.author_explanation: The large shift between biochemical potency and cellular cGAMP IC50 in the pyridine carboxylate series (exemplified by compound 21 with h-cGAS IC50 = 36 nM vs THP-1 cell IC50 = 22.9 µM) was attributed to low cell permeability and high active efflux driven by high polarity and the anionic carboxylate moiety.

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 bidirectional permeability and efflux ratio determination
evidence.result: All four tested pyridine carboxylates (15, 18, 20, 21) exhibited Caco-2 Papp A-B < 0.10 x 10^-6 cm/s and ER > 100 (e.g., 18: Papp 0.05, ER 394; 20: Papp 0.05, ER 193; 21: Papp 0.07, ER 137).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured Caco-2 permeability (Papp A-B < 0.10 x 10^-6 cm/s) and efflux ratio (ER > 100) for compounds 15, 18, 20, and 21, confirming extremely poor permeability and high efflux as an endemic property of this series. However, no controlled on/off intervention (e.g. efflux inhibitor rescue in cells) was conducted on these compounds, qualifying this as mechanistic measurement (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: Extremely low passive cell permeability (Caco-2 Papp < 0.10 x 10^-6 cm/s) and high active efflux (ER > 100) due to the anionic carboxylate explain the large cellular potency drop.

claims.author_explanation: In the pyrimidine amide series, introducing a highly basic dimethylamino substituent on compound 31 increased PBS solubility compared to 28 and 30, but came at the expense of Caco-2 permeability (Papp A-B = 0.60 x 10^-6 cm/s) and efflux character (ER = 45), resulting in weaker cellular potency (THP-1 IC50 = 5.01 µM vs 1.87 µM for 30) despite similar biochemical potency.

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 bidirectional permeability and efflux ratio determination for pyrimidine amides 28, 29, and 31
evidence.result: Compound 31 exhibited lower permeability (Papp A-B = 0.60 x 10^-6 cm/s) and higher efflux (ER = 45) compared to 28 (Papp = 7.1, ER = 0.91) and 29 (Papp = 0.91, ER = 20), correlating with a larger biochemical-to-cellular potency shift (0.17 µM to 5.01 µM).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured Caco-2 permeability and efflux ratio alongside biochemical and cellular potencies across matched analogues 28, 29, 30, and 31, showing high efflux (ER = 45) and reduced permeability for 31, which qualifies as a relevant mechanistic measurement without a controlled causal rescue test (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: The explanation and supporting Caco-2 data attribute the cellular potency loss of compound 31 to both reduced passive membrane permeability (Papp A-B = 0.60 x 10^-6 cm/s) and high active efflux (ER = 45) as equally central mechanisms.

claims.author_explanation: Derivative 34 retained similar biochemical and cellular potency (h-cGAS IC50 = 0.037 µM, THP-1 IC50 = 0.56 µM) to 23, but suffered from suboptimal aqueous solubility (PBS solubility = 8.3 µM); replacing the methoxy group with a 2-hydroxyethoxy substituent in 36 while avoiding a basic amine enhanced PBS solubility (167 µM) and improved cellular potency (THP-1 IC50 = 0.06 µM).

evidence.experiment: PBS kinetic/equilibrium solubility and Caco-2 permeability/efflux comparison of 34 and 36
evidence.result: Compound 34 had low PBS solubility (8.3 µM) and THP-1 IC50 = 0.56 µM (h-cGAS IC50 = 0.037 µM), whereas 2-hydroxyethoxy analogue 36 achieved PBS solubility = 167 µM and THP-1 IC50 = 0.06 µM at virtually identical biochemical potency (h-cGAS IC50 = 0.032 µM).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured PBS solubility (8.3 µM for 34 vs 167 µM for 36) and Caco-2 permeability/efflux for both matched analogues, linking the solubility improvement in 36 to its nearly 10-fold improved cellular potency at equivalent biochemical potency (Grade 3).

classification.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
classification.rationale: The explanation attributes the cellular potency difference between matched analogues 34 and 36 directly to aqueous PBS solubility, a core physicochemical property.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Author-discussed series hybridization comparing equipotent biochemical inhibitors 21 (h-cGAS IC50 = 0.036 µM) and 34 (h-cGAS IC50 = 0.037 µM), where the hybridized scaffold improved Caco-2 permeability/efflux (Papp 0.07 -> 2.7, ER 137 -> 1.6) and cellular THP-1 potency (22.9 µM -> 0.56 µM).
interventions.description: Structure-based hybridization replacing the polar pyridine carboxylate metal-binding motif and flexible amide linker of compound 21 with the rigidified tetrahydrocarboline core and 5-methoxy-pyrimidine amide motif of compound 34 to reduce polarity, rotatable bonds, and efflux, and improve cellular potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched molecular pair comparison between 5-methoxy-pyrimidine 34 and 5-(2-hydroxyethoxy)-pyrimidine 36 with identical stereochemistry and biochemical potency (0.037 vs 0.032 µM), increasing PBS solubility from 8.3 to 167 µM and improving THP-1 cellular IC50 from 0.56 to 0.06 µM.
interventions.description: Introduction of a solubilizing neutral 2-hydroxyethoxy group on the pyrimidine amide ring (compound 36 vs 34 and 21) to enhance aqueous solubility without introducing a basic amine, further recovering cellular potency.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports paired quantitative cell-free enzyme inhibition (h-cGAS and m-cGAS IC50) and cellular activity (THP-1 cGAMP and RAW cGAMP IC50) for multiple compounds, including compounds 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 28, 29, 30, 31, 33, 34, and 36.

insights.text: The pyridine carboxylate series achieved high biochemical potency against human cGAS (e.g., compound 21 h-cGAS IC50 = 36 nM), but exhibited a severe drop in cellular potency (THP-1 cGAMP IC50 = 22.9 µM) caused by poor permeability (Papp < 0.10 x 10^-6 cm/s) and high active efflux (ER > 100).

Structure-guided hybridization combining the metal-coordinating motif of the pyridine carboxylates with the tetrahydrocarboline scaffold of compound 23 yielded pyrimidine amides that resolved efflux liability and drastically enhanced cellular cGAMP inhibition.

Optimizing pyrimidine substituents and chirality culminated in lead compound 36, which exhibited balanced nanomolar potency across human and mouse cGAS in biochemical and cellular assays alongside high oral bioavailability in mice.

review_notes: Table 1 contains imide prodrug analogues tested only in the biochemical h-cGAS assay; no cellular potencies are given.

Table 2 contains eight pyridine carboxylate analogues, six of which have paired biochemical and cellular data (including right-censored >33 µM cellular values). Compounds 16 and 17 have 'NA' for THP-1 cellular potency and were omitted from the compound dataset.
Table 3 contains fourteen analogues; eight possess paired biochemical and cellular data, while six (24-27, 32, 35) are marked 'NA' for cellular potency and were omitted.
Compound 36 was additionally profiled in mouse cGAS biochemical and RAW cellular assays (text on page 7), providing an additional paired mouse cross-assay comparison.

Verified all paired compounds across Tables 1-4 and main text; fixed invalid cellular_before_id reference on int_1, added biochemical_after_id/cellular_after_id links, corrected Table 2 R1 substituent descriptions, and added author-attributed claims/interventions regarding basicity-driven efflux (compound 31) and solubility optimization (compound 34 to 36).

claims.author_explanation: Cellular potency disconnect from biochemical potency is driven by target residence time: compounds with prolonged residence time (such as bromine-containing 23 due to a sulfur-halogen bond with Cys490) show significantly improved cellular potency, correlating strongly with residence time (R2 = 0.84) rather than equilibrium binding affinity KD (R2 = 0.55) or ATPase EC50 (R2 = 0.49).

evidence.experiment: SPR single-cycle kinetics and correlation analysis of residence time versus circBRIP1 cellular EC50 across series compounds, alongside crystal structures confirming sulfur-halogen interaction with Cys490.
evidence.result: Compound 23 displayed a 7-fold longer residence time (355 s vs 51 s for 10 and 53 s for 24) and dramatically improved cellular potency (circBRIP1 EC50 = 0.765 uM vs 16.1 uM for 10). Cellular circBRIP1 potency correlated strongly with SPR residence time (R2 = 0.84, P < 0.01) rather than KD (R2 = 0.55).

evidence.experiment: Mechanistic hypothesis and literature support regarding processive molecular motors and drug-target residence time.
evidence.result: Authors note that a molecular motor such as DHX9 that proceeds through a processive reaction mechanism may be more sensitive to inhibitor off-rates, and prolonged residence time leads to a longer-lived pharmacodynamic effect in cells.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors perform mechanistic measurements of kinetics (SPR residence time) and thermal shift across matched analogs (10, 23, 24) showing that off-rate/residence time (355 s vs ~50 s) correlates strongly with cellular potency without substantial change in cell-free ATPase or unwinding affinity. Structural confirmation of the sulfur-halogen bond with Cys490 was obtained by X-ray crystallography, but no controlled on/off rescue intervention (e.g. Cys490 mutation in cells) was conducted.

classification.rationale: Drug-target residence time (binding kinetics/off-rate) is supported by SPR measurements and correlation with cellular potency, which falls outside the specific causes listed in the taxonomy.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 10, 23, and 24 share the exact same 4-phenylthiophene-2-carboxamide core and dianiline scaffold, differing solely in the substituent (H, Br, Me) directed toward the Cys490 thiol.
interventions.description: Introduction of a bromine atom (compound 23) to engage Cys490 in a sulfur-halogen bond compared to unsubstituted 10 or methyl-substituted 24.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 10, 23, and 24 share the identical scaffold and differ only at substituent Z (H, Br, Me). Unlike Br (23, residence time 355 s, circBRIP1 EC50 = 0.765 uM), Me (24) does not increase residence time (53 s vs 51 s for 10) or thermal stability and fails to substantially improve cellular potency (circBRIP1 EC50 = 10.9 uM vs 16.1 uM for 10).
interventions.description: Introduction of a methyl substituent (compound 24) instead of bromine (compound 23) at the position directed toward Cys490 as a non-halogen-bonding steric control relative to unsubstituted compound 10.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 11 and 25 are matched molecular pairs differing only by H vs Br at the Z position pointing toward Cys490, improving circBRIP1 EC50 from 2.11 uM to 0.052 uM.
interventions.description: Introduction of a bromine atom directed toward Cys490 on the pyridyl-thiophene scaffold (comparing compound 11 to brominated analog 25).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 25 (Z = Br) and 26 (Z = Cl) are matched molecular pairs differing only in the halogen atom; chlorine maintains the halogen-sulfur interaction and high cellular potency (circBRIP1 EC50 = 0.062 uM vs 0.052 uM; LS411N IC50 = 0.253 uM vs 0.275 uM).
interventions.description: Halide exchange from bromine (compound 25) to chlorine (compound 26) directed toward Cys490 to maintain the sulfur-halogen bond while reducing molecular weight and lipophilicity.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 21 (Z = H) and 29 (Z = Cl) are matched molecular pairs; while biochemical ATPase EC50 is nearly identical (0.004 uM vs 0.002 uM), addition of the chlorine halogen-bond donor improves cellular circBRIP1 EC50 from 1.28 uM to 0.015 uM.
interventions.description: Introduction of a chlorine atom directed toward Cys490 on the 5-methyl-4-(pyridin-2-yl)thiophene scaffold (comparing non-halogenated compound 21 to chlorinated analog 29).

eligibility.reason: The paper reports cell-free biochemical potency (DHX9 ATPase EC50 and unwinding IC50) alongside cellular potency (circBRIP1 EC50 and LS411N proliferation IC50) for multiple identical compounds (e.g., compounds 1, 8, 9, 10, 11, 23, 25, 26, 29, ATX968, etc.).

insights.text: The compounds act as allosteric partial inhibitors of DHX9 ATPase activity (max inhibition ~70%) but complete inhibitors of RNA helicase unwinding activity.

Cellular target engagement potency (circBRIP1 EC50) correlates significantly more strongly with drug-target residence time measured by SPR (R2 = 0.84) than with equilibrium affinity KD (R2 = 0.55) or biochemical ATPase potency (R2 = 0.49).

A key sulfur-halogen bond between a halogen donor on the compound core and the thiol of Cys490 increases target residence time ~7-fold without altering equilibrium binding affinity, substantially driving cellular potency.
Phenotypic cellular antiproliferative activity selectively targets MSI-H/dMMR CRC cells (LS411N) while sparing MSS/pMMR CRC cells (NCI-H747), mirroring the effect of genetic DHX9 ablation.

review_notes: Compound 5 in Table 1 did not report a circBRIP1 value (indicated by '--') and was excluded from paired extraction.
Compounds 27 and 28 in Table 4 did not report LS411N proliferation IC50 ('--'), but both reported circBRIP1 EC50 and biochemical ATPase EC50, so both were retained.
All reported concentration response curves were derived from 10-point titrations with n >= 2.

Added SPR KD measurements for compounds 1 (apo and with excess ATP, page 2 text) and 10, 23, and 24 (Figure 3, page 5), Table 3 replicate values for compound 10, and text-reported H747 IC50 > 10 uM for ATX968 (page 6).

Added complete biochemical-to-cellular pairing links for all 32 extracted compounds and added matched-pair interventions exploring the Cys490 sulfur-halogen bond (methyl control 24 vs 10, 11 vs 25, Br-to-Cl swap 25 vs 26, and 21 vs 29). Covalent warhead analogs targeting Cys490 mentioned on page 4 were only tabulated in Supporting Information Table S3 (absent from the supplied PDF).

claims.author_explanation: The authors investigated poor membrane permeability as a primary cause for the discrepancy between biochemical IC50 and cellular IC50 values. Peptidomimetics showed 10- to 50-fold lower PAMPA permeability than verapamil. However, the authors explicitly noted that permeability alone does not explain the full ~50-fold discrepancy observed for GD562.

evidence.experiment: Parallel Artificial Membrane Permeability Assay (PAMPA) measuring effective permeability (Pe) of compounds 1c–1k compared to verapamil control.
evidence.result: Compounds 1c–1e showed low permeability values (0.17–0.26 × 10^-6 cm/s), 10- to 50-fold lower than verapamil (8.6 × 10^-6 cm/s).

evidence.experiment: Author evaluation comparing PAMPA permeability metrics to enzymatic and cellular IC50 values.
evidence.result: The authors concluded: 'Based on the PAMPA result, permeability alone did not explain the discrepancy between the biochemical and cellular IC50 values.'

evidence.experiment: Comparison of cLogP, PAMPA permeability, and cellular N-terminal methylation inhibition across C-region hydrophobically modified analogs (1c–1k and DC541).
evidence.result: Higher cLogP correlated with increased PAMPA permeability across the series (1j and 1k reaching 0.9–1.3 × 10^-6 cm/s at cLogP 3.8), and GD562 (cLogP 1.9) achieved ~50 µM cellular IC50 on me3-RCC1 and me3-SET despite 3-fold weaker biochemical potency than DC541 (cLogP 0.7).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors performed direct mechanistic measurements using the PAMPA model on all synthesized analogs, confirming low permeability (0.17 to 0.47 × 10^-6 cm/s for 1c–1f), but noted permeability alone is insufficient to explain the cellular potency deficit (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: PAMPA measurements confirm low passive membrane permeability and show some correlation with cLogP and cellular activity, but the authors explicitly state that permeability alone does not explain the full biochemical-to-cellular discrepancy.

claims.author_explanation: The authors hypothesize that nuclear localization of NTMT1 contributes to the biochemical-to-cellular potency gap, suggesting that compound distribution into the nucleus is required because NTMT1 is predominantly localized in the nucleus.

evidence.experiment: Discussion of future directions proposing fluorescent labeling of GD562 to track cellular distribution.
evidence.result: NTMT1 is predominantly localized in the nucleus, but intracellular/subcellular distribution of GD562 was not experimentally determined.

claims.grade_rationale: Hypothesis based on known target biology from literature without experimental measurement of cellular/nuclear compound distribution in this study (Grade 1).

classification.rationale: The authors hypothesize without experimental testing that the nuclear subcellular localization of the target NTMT1 requires nuclear compound distribution and contributes to the potency gap.

claims.author_explanation: In the design rationale, the authors state that incorporating non-amino acid hydrophobic functional groups at the C-region has the potential to improve the peptidomimetic inhibitor's proteolytic stability in addition to increasing hydrophobicity and membrane permeability.

evidence.experiment: Author design rationale for C-region optimization of peptidomimetic NTMT1 inhibitors.
evidence.result: Authors note that incorporating non-amino acid functional groups at the C-region has the potential to improve proteolytic stability alongside hydrophobicity and permeability.

claims.grade_rationale: Stated as a design hypothesis citing previous peptidomimetic work [15], without experimental measurement of proteolytic or metabolic stability in the current paper (Grade 1).

classification.rationale: The explanation is an untested design hypothesis proposing that C-region modifications improve proteolytic/metabolic stability alongside hydrophobicity and permeability; proteolytic stability is the distinct mechanism highlighted in this reason.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative biochemical IC50 values (NTMT1 SAHH-coupled fluorescence assay) and quantitative cellular IC50 values (inhibition of cellular N-terminal methylation of RCC1/SET in HCT116 cells) for peptidomimetic analogs including 1c (GD560), 1d (GD562), 1e (GD573), 1f (GD564), 1g (GD566), and 1h (GD568).

insights.text: PAMPA permeability assays showed that peptidomimetic NTMT1 inhibitors possess 10- to 50-fold lower passive membrane permeability than verapamil, correlating with their reduced cellular potency.
The authors explicitly concluded that membrane permeability alone does not account for the ~50-fold difference between enzymatic and cellular IC50 values of GD562.
Subcellular compartmentalization was proposed as an explanatory factor, given that NTMT1 is predominantly localized in the nucleus.

GD562 (1d) was identified as the most cell-potent peptidomimetic inhibitor, achieving ~50 µM IC50 on cellular trimethylation of RCC1 and SET in HCT116 cells while retaining submicromolar biochemical IC50 (0.93 µM).

Cellular growth inhibition (GI50) observed for halogenated analogs was confirmed to arise from off-target effects, as compound 1a displayed identical GI50 in wild-type and NTMT1 knockout HCT116 cells.

review_notes: DC541 was excluded from the paired dataset because its cellular IC50 was referenced from previous literature (Chen et al. 2021 [15]) rather than measured de novo in Table 2.
Compounds 1a, 1b, 1i, 1j, and 1k were excluded because quantitative cellular target inhibition IC50 values were either not determined (N.D.) or not evaluated.

Cytotoxicity (GI50) measurements are reported in measurements, but paired analyses are strictly restricted to the on-target cellular N-terminal methylation assay (assay_cellular_me3) since the authors proved that HCT116 growth inhibition is an off-target effect independent of NTMT1.

Corrected compound structure notes and linked Table 1 on PDF page 3 (src_p3_table1) to reflect the actual 2-(naphthalen-1-yl)acetyl-Pro-Lys-R scaffold rather than the misnamed alanine-containing IUPAC string originally in c_1c.

Added the authors' C-region design hypothesis regarding proteolytic stability (claim_proteolytic_stability, Grade 1) and expanded the chemical modification interventions (int_1 through int_5) to cover the full C-region SAR explored to improve hydrophobicity, PAMPA permeability, and cellular potency (linker length variations 1c -> 1d and 1c -> 1e, cyclohexyl replacement 1c/1d -> 1f, and phenyl bromination 1c -> 1g/1h). Additional unpaired analogs (N-methylated 1i and biphenyls 1j, 1k) improved PAMPA permeability (up to 1.3 × 10^-6 cm/s for 1k) but were not tested for cellular target inhibition due to biochemical IC50 > 1 µM (1i, 1j) or off-target cytotoxicity GI50 = 65 µM (1k).

claims.author_explanation: The authors state that although the MTH1 inhibitors are low-nanomolar enzymatic inhibitors, they are only cytotoxic at low micromolar concentrations, noting this may be explained by pharmacokinetic and/or pharmacological properties such as high protein binding or low permeability/efflux in cancer cells.

evidence.experiment: Author explanation in the text for the discrepancy between low-nanomolar enzymatic potency and low-micromolar cellular cytotoxicity.
evidence.result: Authors note: 'although the MTH1 inhibitors are low-nanomolar enzymatic inhibitors they are only cytotoxic at low micromolar concentrations. This is not an uncommon phenomenon and may be explained by pharmacokinetic and/or pharmacological properties such as high protein binding or low permeability/efflux in cancer cells (Extended Data Table 2).'

evidence.experiment: In vitro ADME characterization of plasma protein binding (Rapid Equilibrium Dialysis) and Caco-2 monolayer permeability/efflux.
evidence.result: TH287 exhibited plasma protein free fraction (fu) of 8.0%, Papp A-B of 8.4 x 10^-5 cm/s, and efflux ratio of 0.8; TH588 exhibited fu of 1.7%, Papp A-B of 3.9 x 10^-5 cm/s, and efflux ratio of 0.8.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3. The authors measured in vitro ADME parameters (plasma protein binding, Caco-2 apparent permeability, and efflux ratio; Extended Data Table 2), showing moderate to high protein binding and measurable permeability/efflux, but did not perform a controlled causal rescue (e.g. testing with efflux inhibitors or modulating serum protein concentration) to restore cellular potency to nanomolar levels.

classification.rationale: The authors attribute the potency shift to multiple distinct mechanisms together (high protein binding and low permeability/efflux), supported by ADME measurements, without a single primary cause.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free enzymatic IC50 values against purified human MTH1 and quantitative cellular viability IC50 values across multiple cell lines for compounds TH287, TH588, and TH650.

insights.text: TH287 and TH588 exhibit low-nanomolar enzymatic inhibition against MTH1 across multiple oxidized nucleotide substrates (dGTP, 8-oxodGTP, and 2-OH-dATP), whereas their cellular cytotoxic IC50 values are in the low-micromolar range in cancer cells.

The authors hypothesize that the shift from nanomolar biochemical potency to micromolar cellular cytotoxicity is due to pharmacological and pharmacokinetic factors, citing measured protein binding and Caco-2 permeability/efflux data.
Cellular toxicity of MTH1 inhibitors displays selectivity for cancer cells over primary/immortalized cells (e.g. VH10, BJ-hTERT), which remain viable at concentrations up to >=20 uM.

The poor MTH1 inhibitor TH650 (biochemical IC50 = 2.1 uM) does not reduce viability in any cell line tested (IC50 >= 20 uM), supporting that cellular cytotoxicity correlates with potent MTH1 target inhibition.

review_notes: Scaffold 1 and TH086 were tested in biochemical assays (IC50 = 3800 nM and 3.4 nM, respectively) but lacked quantitative cellular IC50 determinations in the paper, so they were excluded from the compound dataset per inclusion criteria.
Metabolite TH586 had reported MTH1 IC50 (77 nM) in Extended Data Figure 4c but lacked cellular viability IC50 determinations.
The structure of TH650 was corrected in the 2017 Corrigendum (Nature 544, 508), which has been linked via source src_p28_corrigendum_fig1.

Verified all 3 paired compounds (TH287, TH588, TH650), added SPR Kd values (Extended Data Fig. 3g,h), all 17 cell lines from Extended Data Fig. 5j, and SW480 IC50/IC90 labels from Fig. 5e. Confirmed that chemical optimization from TH287 to TH588 targeted liver microsomal/in vivo metabolic stability rather than recovering the biochemical-to-cellular potency dropoff, and no efflux-inhibitor or serum-shift rescue intervention was performed to recover cellular IC50.

claims.author_explanation: Carboxylic acid-containing tricycles (e.g. 18, 22, 55a, 61d, 61j) and polar acid isosteres (tetrazole 33) exhibit zwitterionic character (predominantly charged at physiological pH) or high polarity/low logD, impairing passive membrane penetration and reducing cellular potency relative to neutral primary amides (30, 23, 54i) or more lipophilic zwitterions (55b, 61a, 61f).

evidence.experiment: Measurement of logD (pH 7.4) and matched SAR comparisons of carboxylic acids/isosteres vs carboxamides and polar vs nonpolar alphaD substituents
evidence.result: Polar zwitterionic acids 55a (logD 0.62, NanoBRET 302 nM), 61d (logD 1.42, NanoBRET 164 nM), and 61j (logD 1.04, NanoBRET 71.4 nM) and polar tetrazole 33 (NanoBRET 5846 nM) show large cellular potency dropoffs, whereas neutral amide 54i (logD 2.21, NanoBRET 3.82 nM) and lipophilic zwitterions 55b (logD 2.0, NanoBRET 31.9 nM) and 61f (logD 2.12, NanoBRET 5.56 nM) achieve potent cellular target engagement.

claims.grade_rationale: Supported by explicit physicochemical measurements (logD pH 7.4 across Tables 3-5, pKa = 3.71 and 8.04, and Caco-2 passive permeability in Table 7) combined with matched-pair SAR across multiple series (18 vs 30, 22 vs 23, 55a vs 54i, 55b vs 54e, 61d/61j vs 61a/61f), without a direct non-structural rescue of intracellular potency for a single compound.

classification.rationale: Although driven by zwitterionic character and low logD, the explicit mechanism linking these properties to reduced cellular potency is impaired passive membrane penetration, which belongs to the dedicated permeability category.

claims.author_explanation: Compounds across the bivalent pharmacophore (with and without a carboxylic acid, e.g. 54e, 54i, 61f) are substrates for P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux (ER = 9.1 in Caco-2 and 4.5 in MDCK-MDR1 for 61f), although passive permeability is sufficient in cellular pharmacology assays.

evidence.experiment: Bidirectional permeability in Caco-2 and MDCK-MDR1 cells in the presence and absence of P-gp inhibitor verapamil or BCRP inhibitor novobiocin
evidence.result: 61f showed moderate passive permeability (Papp A-B = 2.8 x 10^-6 cm/s in Caco-2, 5.0 x 10^-6 cm/s in MDCK-MDR1) with efflux ratios of 9.1 and 4.5 that were inhibited by verapamil; similar Caco-2 profiles were observed for 54e and 54i.

claims.grade_rationale: P-gp efflux was directly demonstrated in bidirectional Caco-2 and MDCK-MDR1 transport assays using P-gp inhibitor verapamil and BCRP inhibitor novobiocin, and addressed in vivo using Kolliphor EL (P-gp/solubility enhancer), but efflux inhibitors were not tested for rescuing cellular IC50 in the HCT116 NanoBRET or proliferation assays.

classification.rationale: The explanation focuses on active P-glycoprotein (P-gp) transporter-mediated efflux, demonstrated via bidirectional Caco-2 and MDCK-MDR1 assays with efflux inhibitors.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 22 and 23 are matched analogues with the exact same central amide linker and chloro-biphenyl alphaD group, differing only by CO2H vs CONH2 on the tricycle.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 55a and 55b share the identical tricyclic carboxylic acid and ether-amine linker, differing only in polar vs lipophilic substitution on the alphaD phenyl ring.
