eligibility.reason: The paper evaluates multiple compounds in both cell-free CK2alpha kinase inhibition assays (ADP-Glo) and intact cell target engagement (NanoBRET) and proliferation assays in HCT116 cells.

insights.text: Bivalent engagement of the CK2alpha ATP-binding site and the cryptic alphaD pocket delivers picomolar biochemical potency and high kinome selectivity over off-target kinases such as CLK2 and DAPK3.

Replacing the tricyclic carboxylic acid with a primary carboxamide relieves zwitterionic charge and improves cellular target engagement, but polar acid isosteres such as tetrazole 33 exhibit compromised cellular potency.

Combining a tricyclic carboxylic acid with a lipophilic, nonpolar alphaD motif (e.g. 55b and 61f) allows retention of nanomolar intact-cell NanoBRET target engagement while significantly improving metabolic stability compared to primary amides.

Candidate 61f demonstrates a 9.1 efflux ratio in Caco-2 cells that is sensitive to verapamil, confirming P-gp substrate liability, yet achieves sufficient intracellular exposure to potently suppress p-AKT S129 in tumor cells and in vivo.

review_notes: All 59 compounds with paired quantitative cell-free and cellular potency data across Tables 1-6 (plus human PBMC p-AKT S129 IC50 on p. 18 and SPR Kd values in Table 6) have been extracted, resulting in 131 measurements and 68 biochemical-cellular pairs.

Compounds 21 (Table 2) and Biv5 (p. 2) were excluded because cellular potency was not determined ('ND' or not reported), and literature reference compounds in the Introduction (2, 3, 5, 7, AB668, 8) were excluded as their values are cited from external papers rather than measured in this study (whereas 1, 4, and 6 were experimentally assayed in Table 1).

Both author-attributed explanations for cellular potency dropoff/permeability limitations—(1) zwitterionic charge and high polarity (low logD) of carboxylic acids and tetrazole isosteres impairing passive cell penetration, and (2) P-gp-mediated efflux identified in Caco-2 and MDCK-MDR1 assays—are captured with Grade 3 evidence and 6 interventions covering matched chemical modifications and efflux inhibition.

claims.author_explanation: PROTACs suffer from poor cellular uptake and low intracellular accumulation due to high molecular weight and non-druglike properties. Reversible covalent α-cyanoacrylamide chemistry significantly improves intracellular accumulation and target engagement, hypothesized to occur via reversible reaction with intracellular glutathione acting as a sink to trap the compound inside cells or via cell surface thiol interactions.

evidence.experiment: In-cell target engagement (NanoBRET) and biochemical binding/inhibition comparison for BTK and CRBN, and calculation of K'P,D for RC-1, IRC-1, and RNC-1.
evidence.result: RC-1 showed 3- and 30-fold lower BTK target engagement IC50 compared to IRC-1 and RNC-1, resulting in 6- and 40-fold higher relative intracellular accumulation coefficient K'P,D, while calculated cLogP and PSA were similar.

evidence.experiment: Testing of matched structural control analogues RNC-1-CN-DiMe (reduced double bond) and IRC-1-DiMe (lacking cyano group) in BTK NanoBRET target engagement.
evidence.result: RC-1 maintained ~10-fold lower BTK TE IC50 and ~5-fold higher K'P,D than RNC-1-CN-DiMe and IRC-1-DiMe, demonstrating that enhanced cellular accumulation requires the intact reversible covalent cyano-acrylamide warhead.

evidence.experiment: Artificial membrane permeability measurement using the lipid-PAMPA method.
evidence.result: None of the compounds (RC-1, IRC-1, RNC-1) were detected on the receptor side, with total recovery rates of only 20-30%, indicating the assay was unsuitable due to compound retention on lipids/plastics.

evidence.experiment: Hypothesis that rapid, reversible reaction with intracellular glutathione (~1-10 mM) acts as a sink to trap cyano-acrylamide compounds inside cells.
evidence.result: Stated as a mechanistic hypothesis based on prior literature, noting it could be tested in future work by measuring target engagement at varied GSH levels.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors synthesized matched control compounds lacking the cyano group or double bond (IRC-1-DiMe, RNC-1-CN-DiMe) and showed that the cyano-acrylamide moiety specifically confers higher relative intracellular accumulation (K'P,D) and in-cell target engagement in both BTK and CRBN NanoBRET assays. However, lipid-PAMPA permeability measurements failed due to high compound sticking/low recovery, and the proposed intracellular glutathione trapping mechanism remains a hypothesis that was not causally tested by perturbing cellular GSH levels in this paper.

classification.rationale: While poor PROTAC uptake is the background problem, the specific mechanism explaining improved intracellular accumulation and potency of the cyano-acrylamide warhead is reversible covalent interaction with intracellular glutathione (or surface thiols), supported by matched control analogues.

eligibility.reason: The study reports both cell-free biochemical binding (Kd by DiscoverX or fluorescence quenching) / enzymatic kinase inhibition (IC50) and cellular potencies (in-cell target engagement IC50 by NanoBRET, cell viability IC50, and BTK degradation DC50) for the same compounds, including RC-1, IRC-1, RNC-1, and control compounds.

insights.text: PROTACs exhibit substantial cellular target engagement drops relative to cell-free binding due to poor membrane permeation and intracellular accumulation associated with high molecular weight.

Introducing an alpha-cyanoacrylamide reversible covalent warhead (RC-1) provides a multi-fold enhancement in relative intracellular accumulation (K'P,D) and in-cell target engagement compared to irreversible or noncovalent counterparts.
Matched structural analogues lacking the cyano group or having a reduced Michael acceptor double bond lose the intracellular accumulation advantage, confirming the warhead's specific chemical role.
High target engagement enables RC-1 to act as a dual-functional inhibitor and degrader, maintaining kinase pathway inhibition even when cellular degradation is incomplete.

Physical permeability methods like lipid-PAMPA and cell-lysate drug extraction gave poor recovery and surface-binding artifacts, making live-cell NanoBRET target engagement a preferred operational readout.

review_notes: DD-03-171 and MT-802 were evaluated in cell viability and BTK NanoBRET assays (Fig. 2f and 3d), but no quantitative cell-free biochemical binding or enzymatic inhibition data were reported for them in this paper, so they were excluded from compound-level extraction.
FLT3 degraders (RC-FLT3, IRC-FLT3, RNC-FLT3) in Fig. 3g,h only had in-cell CRBN NanoBRET data without cell-free biochemical potency, so they were also excluded.
Lipid-PAMPA experiments on RC-1, IRC-1, and RNC-1 yielded undetectable concentrations on the receiver side and low recovery (20-30%), so no quantitative permeability coefficient could be extracted.

Table 1 lists RC-Ctrl BTK TE IC50,TE as 0.059 µM and RC-1 as 0.043 µM (matching Fig. 3c), whereas separate head-to-head NanoBRET runs in Fig. 3d report 0.047 µM for RC-Ctrl and 0.059 µM for RC-1, and Fig. 3f reports 0.033 µM for RC-1; all distinct reported values were retained.

Added direct BTK Kd vs BTK TE IC50,TE pairs (used by the authors to compute K'P,D in Table 1), Mino cell viability pairs, and mechanistic control interventions (RNC-1-CN-DiMe and IRC-1-DiMe vs RC-1, IRC-1 vs RC-1, and CRBN TE comparison).

claims.author_explanation: The authors explain that early potent compounds (such as 11 and 18) failed to activate the cellular NF-κB pathway despite achieving cellular target engagement in CETSA because they exhibited partial inhibitory efficacy (<50-66%) and faster off-rates. Optimizing the compounds for high maximal inhibitory efficacy (87-95%) and a slow off-rate (prolonged target occupancy preventing physiological ubiquitin competition) was required to translate biochemical potency into cellular pathway activity in compound 21.

evidence.experiment: SPR single-cycle kinetic analysis and SPR ubiquitin competition assay comparing compounds 18 and 21 on immobilized USP21
evidence.result: Compound 21 exhibited a slower off-rate and longer complex half-life than compound 18, and resisted ubiquitin displacement much more effectively at 1 uM competitor concentration.

evidence.experiment: Cellular NF-κB dual-luciferase reporter assay across compounds 11, 17-22 at 10 uM
evidence.result: Only compounds with high biochemical efficacy and slow off-rate (20 and 21) robustly activated NF-κB, while compound 18 (faster off-rate, lower efficacy) and 11 (partial efficacy) showed minimal or no activation.

evidence.experiment: Intact-cell HiBiT CETSA at 49 °C for compounds 11 and 17-22 (at 50 and 100 uM) and Caco-2 permeability/efflux profiling across Table 4 analogues
evidence.result: Compound 11 and compound 18 achieved strong intracellular USP21 thermal stabilization in CETSA despite failing to activate NF-κB at 10 uM, showing that intracellular binding occurs at high concentrations; however, compound 18 also had low Caco-2 permeability (Papp = 14 nm/s, ER = 14) and partial biochemical efficacy (66-74%), whereas compound 21 combined high permeability (Papp = 42 nm/s, ER = 0.7), full biochemical efficacy (87-95%), and slow off-rate.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors provide extensive mechanistic measurements (biochemical efficacy percentages, SPR association/dissociation kinetics, ubiquitin displacement competition curves, and HiBiT CETSA) demonstrating that compound 21 has prolonged target residence time and outcompetes ubiquitin better than compound 18, correlating with cellular functional activity. However, no controlled on-target causal rescue or modulation in a single system was performed.

classification.rationale: The explanation centers on achieving full inhibitory efficacy and a slow off-rate to prevent displacement/competition by physiological ubiquitin in cells, supported by SPR ubiquitin competition and kinetic assays.

interventions.comparison_rationale: The authors explicitly trace the optimization campaign from compound 11 through compounds 17 and 18 to compound 21 (BAY-805) to overcome the lack of cellular NF-κB reporter activity. Because compounds 11, 17, and 18 were only tested at single concentrations in cellular assays (inactive at 10 uM in NF-κB; tested at 50/100 uM in CETSA) and lack quantitative cellular EC50 values, before-measurement IDs are left null in accordance with schema rules.
interventions.description: Analogue optimization from compound 11 (R4 = Me, R2 = CH2OMe) via compound 17 (R4 = CF3, R2 = CH2OMe) and compound 18 (R4 = CF3, R2 = CH2OH) to compound 21 / BAY-805 (R4 = CF3, R2 = isobutyl), which increased maximal biochemical inhibitory efficacy (from 26-59% in 11 and 66-74% in 18 to 87-95% in 21), slowed the dissociation off-rate from USP21 (resisting ubiquitin displacement), improved Caco-2 permeability/efflux (Papp = 42 nm/s, ER = 0.7), and restored cellular NF-κB pathway activation (EC50 = 17 nM).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched enantiomeric pair (22 vs 21) with identical physicochemical properties (logD7.5 = 3.6, efflux ratio = 0.7) profiled head-to-head across biochemical and cellular dose-response assays as a target-engagement specificity control.
interventions.description: Stereochemical comparison between the inactive (S)-enantiomer negative control BAY-728 (compound 22) and the eutomer (R)-enantiomer chemical probe BAY-805 (compound 21), demonstrating stereospecific biochemical inhibition, intracellular CETSA target stabilization, and cellular NF-κB pathway activation.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (hUSP21 HTRF and Ub-rhodamine IC50 values) and quantitative cellular potency (HiBiT CETSA EC50 and NF-κB dual-luciferase reporter EC50 values) for the chemical probe BAY-805 (compound 21) and its enantiomeric negative control BAY-728 (compound 22).

insights.text: Intracellular target engagement (measured by HiBiT CETSA) alone was insufficient to trigger cellular pathway activation (NF-κB reporter); compounds with partial biochemical efficacy or rapid dissociation rates failed to activate the pathway.
Compound 21 (BAY-805) achieved low nanomolar potency across both peptide-substrate and full-ubiquitin biochemical assays (HTRF IC50 = 6 nM, Ub-Rhod IC50 = 2 nM) with high maximal efficacy (87-95%).

Biophysical competition assays revealed that compound 21's slow off-rate effectively outcompeted endogenous ubiquitin binding to USP21, which translated to robust cellular target engagement (CETSA EC50 = 95 nM) and cellular pathway activation (NF-κB EC50 = 17 nM).
The (S)-enantiomer BAY-728 (compound 22) demonstrated >2000-fold lower biochemical potency and lacked significant cellular target engagement (CETSA EC50 > 100 uM), serving as a negative control.

review_notes: Compounds 11 and 17-20 were key intermediates in the authors' optimization of biochemical efficacy, residence time, and cellular NF-κB activity (Tables 3-4, Figures 2-7). However, because their cellular profiling was reported only as bar graphs at single/fixed concentrations (10 uM for NF-κB reporter in Figures 2C and 5; 50 and 100 uM for HiBiT CETSA in Figures 3B and 4) without quantitative cellular EC50 determinations or numerical bounds, they are excluded from the paired compound dataset per eligibility rules and documented in claims and interventions.

Cell proliferation across Jurkat, Molm-13, A549, MDA-MB-231, and U2OS tumor cell lines was reported as IC50 > 30 uM for compounds 21 and 22, representing phenotypic viability safety profiling rather than target-mediated cellular efficacy.

Added biophysical SPR Kd measurement (2.2 nM) and corresponding cellular pairs for BAY-805 (compound 21), as well as intervention records capturing the medicinal chemistry optimization from compounds 11/17/18 to 21 and the matched enantiomeric control comparison (22 vs 21).

claims.author_explanation: Test compounds generally show substantially weaker cellular activity than biochemical activity; some compounds with potent biochemical activity displayed weak activity in cells, which the authors suggest might be explained by low permeability into cells. Conversely, 36a likely owes its remarkably small shift between biochemical and cellular data to its good cell permeability properties and absence of efflux.

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 bidirectional permeability measurement compared with the shift between biochemical BCAT1/2 IC50 and cellular BCAA IC50 across compounds 35, 35a, 36, and 36a.
evidence.result: Compounds with higher efflux (e.g. 35, ER=11.1; 35a, ER=6.2) showed larger shifts from biochemical to cellular IC50 in U-87 MG cells (e.g. 35a: 90 nM biochem vs 2.7 uM cellular), whereas 36a (ER=0.5, Papp A-B=252 nm/s) showed a small shift (31 nM biochem vs 358 nM cellular).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors propose cellular permeability as an explanation for the biochemical-to-cellular potency drop and correlate it with Caco-2 permeability data across the series (Grade 2, associative SAR). However, intracellular compound concentration was not directly measured in the target cells (not Grade 3 or 4).

classification.rationale: The explanation and supporting Caco-2 data combine passive cell permeability and active efflux (efflux ratios) to explain the biochemical-to-cellular shifts across the series.

claims.author_explanation: Strong loss of compound 36a potency was observed in the biochemical BCAT1 assay in the presence of 2% bovine serum albumin or human serum albumin (shifting IC50 into the micromolar range). High plasma protein binding limits unbound compound concentration and partially contributes to lack of efficacy in in vitro assays containing serum albumin (such as proliferation assays with 10% FCS).

evidence.experiment: Biochemical BCAT1 assay in the presence or absence of 2% BSA or HSA, alongside plasma protein binding equilibrium dialysis.
evidence.result: The IC50 of 36a shifted from ~31 nM to the micromolar range upon addition of 2% serum albumin; equilibrium dialysis showed high plasma protein binding with fu of 0.14% (mouse) and 0.055% (rat).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly measured the effect of adding 2% BSA or HSA to the cell-free biochemical assay, showing an IC50 shift from nanomolar to micromolar, and directly measured plasma protein binding (fu = 0.14% in mouse, 0.055% in rat) (Grade 3). However, cellular rescue by manipulating serum protein in the functional BCAA assay was not presented.

classification.rationale: High serum albumin / plasma protein binding reducing free drug concentration in assay media is experimentally supported by BSA/HSA shift and dialysis assays, but extracellular serum binding falls outside the listed taxonomy causes.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched pair of M-helical atropisomers differing specifically by the 1'-substituent (nitrile in 35a vs chloro in 36a) on the same core scaffold.
interventions.description: Chemical modification replacing the 1'-nitrile group with chlorine (35a to 36a) in the annulated naphthyl series to decrease compound acidity (pKa 4.8 to 5.7), abolish efflux (ER 6.2 to 0.5), and enhance cell permeability (Papp 42 to 252 nm/s), resulting in improved cellular potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched molecular pair of racemic naphthyl pyrimidinediones differing only by 1'-CN (35) vs 1'-Cl (36) tested in the same BCAT1 biochemical and U-87 MG cellular assays.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison replacing the 1'-nitrile substituent in racemic annulated compound 35 with a 1'-chloro substituent in racemic compound 36, reducing active efflux (ER from 11.1 to 1.1) and increasing Caco-2 permeability (Papp A-B from 13 to 137 nm/s), which improved cellular potency in U-87 MG (5 uM to 1.8 uM) and MDA-MB-231 (5 uM to 1 uM) despite weaker biochemical potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched molecular pair of M-helical atropisomers (35a vs 36a) evaluated in the BCAT2 biochemical assay and BCAT2-expressing MDA-MB-231 cellular BCAA assay.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison replacing the 1'-nitrile group with chlorine in the M-helical atropisomer (35a to 36a), evaluated on BCAT2 and MDA-MB-231 cells (high BCAT2 expression), reducing the biochemical-to-cellular potency dropoff.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Author-discussed matched pair (36a vs 43) differing by 1'-Cl vs 1'-H; note that 36a is a single M-helical atropisomer whereas 43 is not separated into atropisomers.
interventions.description: Removal of the 1'-chlorine atom from active probe 36a (BAY-069) to generate negative control 43 (BAY-771), which retains high Caco-2 permeability (Papp A-B = 275 nm/s, ER = 0.62) and moderate pKa (5.2) while losing biochemical BCAT1 potency (31 nM to 6500 nM) and cellular U-87 MG potency (358 nM to 6200 nM).

eligibility.reason: The paper provides both quantitative cell-free biochemical IC50 values (BCAT1 and BCAT2) and quantitative cellular IC50 values (measuring BCAA/leucine consumption in U-87 MG and MDA-MB-231 cells) for multiple compounds, including 35, 35a, 35b, 36, 36a (BAY-069), 36b, 43 (BAY-771), and reference compound A.

insights.text: Annulation of the central benzonitrile to a naphthalene ring, accompanied by replacing the cyano substituent with a chlorine atom (36a/BAY-069), modulated compound pKa (from 4.7-4.8 to 5.7) and abolished active efflux (ER dropped from 6.2 to 0.5), leading to strong apical-to-basolateral permeability (Papp = 252 nm/s) and a very small biochemical-to-cellular potency shift.

The pyrimidinedione core forms an acidic pharmacophore whose pKa critically modulates target binding, but high acidity and polarity also correlate with increased active efflux and poor cellular penetration across the early series.

Addition of 2% serum albumin to the biochemical BCAT1 assay shifted the IC50 of 36a from 31 nM to the micromolar range, in line with very high plasma protein binding (fraction unbound 0.14% in mouse and 0.055% in rat), which the authors suggest limits unbound compound concentrations in cell-based assays containing serum.

Atropisomerism around the single bond connecting the naphthalene and pyrimidinedione cores leads to dramatic stereospecific target engagement: the M-helical atropisomers 35a and 36a are significantly more potent than the corresponding P-helical enantiomers 35b and 36b.

review_notes: Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, and Table 4 report extensive biochemical SAR (BCAT1 and BCAT2 IC50 values) and Caco-2 permeability data for benzonitrile pyrimidinediones, but none of these compounds have quantitative cellular IC50 values reported in the manuscript prose or tables.
Compound 1 is mentioned in text as having 'low micromolar activity in the cellular mechanistic assay (data not shown)', but lacking a numerical potency value, it is not eligible as a paired compound.
Compound 33 is noted as having 'showed no cellular mechanistic activity (assays see below)', but no bound or numerical IC50 is reported.
Compounds 37, 37a, and 37b in Table 5 have biochemical IC50s reported, but no cellular IC50 values are provided (they are omitted from Table 6).
Reference compound A has biochemical IC50 values reported on page 1 (BCAT1 = 81 nM, BCAT2 = 21 nM) and cellular IC50 values reported in Table 6 footnote (U-87 MG = 5.3 uM, MDA-MB-231 = 564 nM).

In Table 5, compound 36 has BCAT2 IC50 listed as 1160 nM, whereas in Table 6 it is listed as 1.2 uM (rounded); compound 36b has BCAT1/BCAT2 IC50s listed as 2320 nM / 2680 nM in Table 5 and 2.3 uM / 2.7 uM in Table 6.

Proliferation assays in U-87 MG, MDA-MB-231, SEM, CAL-51, HCC-33, and NCI-H2110 cells (10% FCS) for 36a (BAY-069) and compound A are described on page 11 as failing to inhibit cell proliferation (referencing Supporting Information Table S5 and Figure S18, not in main PDF), with no numerical IC50 values or bounds provided in the main manuscript.

The biochemical BCAT1 IC50 shift of 36a in the presence of 2% BSA or HSA is described on page 11 as shifting 'to the micromolar range' (referencing Supporting Information Figure S17), without an exact numerical IC50 in the main text.

claims.author_explanation: The authors state that the primary limitation in translating biochemical potency to cellular target engagement and in vivo exposure was high topological polar surface area (TPSA), which correlated with elevated Caco-2 efflux ratios and lower apparent permeability. Reducing molecular weight allowed removal of polarity and lowering of TPSA, reducing efflux and improving cellular exposure.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of biochemical TR-FRET IC50 and cellular NanoBRET IC50 between bridged N-acetyl piperazines (6 and 7, TPSA 105) and bridged morpholines (4 and 5, TPSA 94)
evidence.result: Compounds 6 and 7 suffered a 20- to 30-fold drop from TR-FRET IC50 (0.9, 1.9 nM) to cellular NanoBRET IC50 (26.9, 41.0 nM), and exhibited high Caco-2 efflux ratios (45 and 26), whereas 4 and 5 maintained better cellular potency (10.7, 12.5 nM) with lower efflux ratios (3.0, 3.5).

evidence.experiment: Bidirectional Caco-2 permeability and efflux ratio profiling of azetidine analogues with matched lipophilicity but divergent TPSA (10 vs 12)
evidence.result: Compound 10 (TPSA 94, log D 2.7) displayed high permeability (15 x 10^-6 cm/s) and low efflux ratio (1.4), whereas compound 12 (TPSA 108, log D 2.6) showed poor permeability (2.8 x 10^-6 cm/s) and high efflux ratio (22), showing that TPSA rather than log D dictates efflux in this series.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors provide in vitro Caco-2 bidirectional permeability and efflux ratio measurements across multiple chemical series (Tables 2, 4, 6) showing that higher TPSA correlates with high efflux ratios and wider potency gaps (e.g., bridged piperazines 6 and 7 vs morpholines 4 and 5, or 12 vs 10). However, the paper performs no controlled causal rescue with an efflux transporter inhibitor (such as verapamil or elacridar) in intact cells.

classification.rationale: The primary mechanism emphasized by the authors and Caco-2 experiments is high TPSA driving elevated active efflux ratios (and lower apparent permeability), where reducing TPSA reduced efflux and improved cellular target engagement.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Direct structural analogue comparison within the 4-membered cyclic amine pyrimidine series with isolated modification of the 3-substituent.
interventions.description: Modification of the azetidine 3-position substituent from 3-cyano (12) to 3-methoxy (10) to decrease TPSA (108 to 94) while maintaining similar log D (2.6 to 2.7), reducing efflux and improving cellular potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Series-level structural optimization comparing the most potent bicyclic pyrimidine 8 with the optimized low-MW 5-chloro-6-fluoropyridine 17.
interventions.description: Downsizing from the bicyclic morpholine-pyrimidine series (8) to substituted pyridines (17, CCT374705) to reduce molecular weight and TPSA (114 to 68), reducing efflux (18 to 2.3) and improving unbound exposure.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Direct analogue comparison on the same tricyclic quinolinone core replacing the 2-pyrimidine cyclic amine substituent, though bridged morpholine 4 also improves biochemical affinity (2.9 to 1.4 nM).
interventions.description: Replacement of the cis-3-hydroxy-5-methylpiperidine of CCT373567 with a morpholine ring (3) and bridged morpholine (4), reducing TPSA from 104 to 94 A^2, improving Caco-2 permeability (<3 to 3.3 and 6.7 x 10^-6 cm/s), lowering efflux ratio (>16 to 6.0 and 3.0), and improving cellular NanoBRET IC50 (25.9 to 15.3 and 10.7 nM).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched bicyclic 3,8-bridged series on the identical pyrimidine-tricyclic quinolinone scaffold comparing N-acetylpiperazine 6 with morpholine 4.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison between bridged N-acyl piperazines (6, 7; TPSA 105 A^2, Caco-2 ER 45 and 26) and bridged morpholines (4, 5; TPSA 94 A^2, Caco-2 ER 3.0 and 3.5), where removing the polar N-acyl piperazine moiety reduces TPSA and efflux and improves cellular NanoBRET potency (from 26.9-41.0 nM to 10.7-12.5 nM).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Analogue comparison on the same core; cellular improvement is partly driven by higher biochemical affinity (1.3 vs 2.9 nM) as well as intramolecular H-bonding.
interventions.description: Introduction of a larger endo-hydroxy-bridged morpholine bicycle (8, endo-3-oxa-9-azabicyclo[3.3.1]nonan-7-ol) hypothesized to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond and fill the pocket, improving cellular NanoBRET IC50 from 25.9 nM (CCT373567) to 4.5 nM despite high TPSA (114 A^2) and remaining efflux (ER 18).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Direct matched pair in the 4-aminopyridine series replacing 5-CN, 6-Cl (14) with 5-Cl, 6-F (17) to lower TPSA and efflux.
interventions.description: Replacement of the 5-cyano-6-chloropyridine of CCT372064 (14, TPSA 92 A^2, Caco-2 A-B 2.5, ER 28) with 5-chloro-6-fluoropyridine in CCT374705 (17, TPSA 68 A^2, Caco-2 A-B 17, ER 2.3), lowering TPSA to eliminate efflux and improve permeability while preserving biochemical (4.8 vs 6.0 nM) and cellular (12 vs 22 nM) potency.

eligibility.reason: The study reports cell-free biochemical potency (BCL6 TR-FRET IC50) and cellular potency (cellular NanoBRET IC50, MSD degradation DC50, and DLBCL proliferation GI50) for multiple matching tricyclic quinolinone analogues.

insights.text: Intracellular target engagement (NanoBRET IC50) correlated tightly with topological polar surface area (TPSA): higher TPSA provoked elevated Caco-2 efflux ratios and wider cell-free to cellular potency drops.

Bridged piperazine analogues (6 and 7) suffered a substantial loss in cellular target engagement compared to morpholine counterparts (4 and 5), matching their higher TPSA (105 vs 94) and elevated efflux ratios (26-45 vs 3.0-3.5).

Downsizing from 6-membered pyrimidine heterocycles to 4-membered azetidines and 5,6-substituted pyridines reduced MW and TPSA, effectively mitigating efflux and enabling sustained in vivo free concentrations above the cellular IC90.

claims.author_explanation: Upregulation of P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1) in multidrug-resistant Ph+ leukemia cells (K562/Dox) mediates active drug efflux, decreasing intracellular concentration and causing a loss of cellular antiproliferative potency for P-gp substrates like bosutinib; reducing P-gp efflux by optimizing the molecular dipole and hydrogen-bond donor acidity restores cellular efficacy in resistant cells.

evidence.experiment: Quantitative flow cytometry and Western blot for P-gp protein expression in K562-vehicle control versus K562/Dox cells.
evidence.result: K562/Dox cells showed an ~8-fold increase in P-gp expression by flow cytometry (412 vs 49 P-gp/cell) and a strong 170 kDa P-gp band on Western blot compared to wild-type K562 cells.

evidence.experiment: Determination of MDCKII-MDR1 bidirectional apparent permeability and efflux ratios for bosutinib, 14a, and 16a.
evidence.result: Bosutinib is a strong P-gp substrate with an MDCKII-MDR1 efflux ratio of 28.3, whereas 14a and 16a display substantially lower efflux ratios (6.0 and 5.4, respectively) and improved A-to-B permeability.

evidence.experiment: 72 h antiproliferative IC50 determination in K562 vs K562/Dox (P-gp overexpressing) cells.
evidence.result: Bosutinib suffered a ~1360-fold loss of antiproliferative potency in K562/Dox cells (IC50 shift from 0.0086 nM to 11.7 nM), whereas 16a suffered only an ~4-fold resistance shift (IC50 8.1 nM in K562 to 34.8 nM in K562/Dox).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured P-gp expression in K562 vs K562/Dox cells using quantitative flow cytometry and Western blot, determined in vitro transcellular permeability and efflux ratios in MDCKII-MDR1 cells, and evaluated antiproliferative shifts. However, they did not perform a controlled causal rescue using a chemical P-gp inhibitor (such as elacridar or verapamil) in the K562/Dox proliferation assay, relying instead on structural modification (SAR).

classification.rationale: The loss of cellular potency in resistant cells is explicitly attributed to active efflux mediated by upregulated P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1), supported by expression, MDCKII-MDR1 efflux, and proliferation data.

eligibility.reason: The paper provides quantitative biochemical IC50 values against BCR-ABL1 and cSRC kinases (Figure 4A) alongside quantitative cellular antiproliferative IC50 values in K562 and K562/Dox leukemia cells (Figure 5) for compounds 14a, 16a, and the reference inhibitor bosutinib.

insights.text: Compound 16a incorporates a 5-chloro-6-methoxypyridin-2-ylamino moiety that minimizes the molecular dipole through internal dipole cancellation with the 3-carbonitrile group, resulting in an MDCKII-MDR1 efflux ratio of 5.4 compared to 28.3 for bosutinib.
In patient-derived Ph+ K562 cells, 16a exhibits nanomolar antiproliferative potency (IC50 = 8.1 nM) matching its subnanomolar biochemical BCR-ABL1 activity.

In multidrug-resistant K562/Dox cells overexpressing P-glycoprotein, 16a experiences only an ~4-fold loss of antiproliferative potency (IC50 = 34.8 nM), whereas bosutinib suffers an ~1360-fold loss of potency (IC50 shifting from 0.0086 nM to 11.7 nM).

Direct NMR measurement of Abraham ANMR values and absence of 1J(NH-F) scalar coupling demonstrated that the reduced P-gp efflux of ortho-fluoro analogues is not mediated by intramolecular N-H...F hydrogen bonds.

review_notes: Bosutinib biochemical data in Figure 4A is noted in the caption as originating from reference 34, but was retained because bosutinib was included in the same table and served as the direct reference benchmark alongside newly synthesized 14a and 16a in Figure 5.

Compounds 5a, 8a, 12a, 13a, and 15a had biochemical IC50 values in Figure 4A but were not profiled in the cellular proliferation assay in Figure 5, so they were excluded from the paired dataset per scope instructions.
Imatinib had cellular antiproliferative IC50 values in Figure 5 but no biochemical kinase IC50 values in Figure 4A, so it was excluded.

Added BCR-ABL1 H396P biochemical assay and measurements from Figure 4A for paired compounds bosutinib, 14a, and 16a, completed before/after measurement links in interventions, added matched-pair comparison 14a -> 16a and K562 vs K562/Dox assay comparison, and added missing source src_p4_text.

claims.author_explanation: Disulfiram is rapidly metabolized in cells to diethyldithiocarbamate (DTC). DTC thiol activity against cellular targets is substantially enhanced by complexation with copper (Cu2+), likely because Cu2+ increases the electrophilicity of DTC thiols. In the absence of copper, disulfiram and DTC show lower cellular potency (~8-22 µM); adding copper gluconate restores cellular potency 24- to 44-fold to ~0.4 µM, matching cell-free liposome leakage potency.

evidence.experiment: Literature citation of disulfiram pharmacokinetics and DTC-copper complexation mechanism
evidence.result: Disulfiram is rapidly metabolized in cells to DTC, and DTC anti-cancer/biological activity is enhanced by copper complexation.

evidence.experiment: In vitro liposome leakage assay of disulfiram and DTC with and without copper gluconate
evidence.result: Copper gluconate only weakly enhanced potency in liposomes (C-23 IC50 went from 0.30 ± 0.01 µM to 0.20 ± 0.01 µM; DTC went from 1.66 ± 0.10 µM to 0.77 ± 0.09 µM), attributed to high intrinsic Cys191 reactivity.

evidence.experiment: Concentration-response pyroptosis cell death assay in LPS-primed THP-1 cells with disulfiram or DTC +/- copper gluconate
evidence.result: Addition of Cu2+ decreased the cellular IC50 of disulfiram 24-fold to 0.41 ± 0.02 µM and DTC 44-fold to 0.49 ± 0.01 µM, matching their cell-free liposome leakage potencies.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors conducted controlled causal rescue experiments in cells and liposomes: adding copper gluconate specifically enhanced cellular potency ~24-fold for disulfiram and ~44-fold for DTC to align with cell-free values, while copper only weakly affected cell-free liposome leakage. Although confirmed in cellular assays and in vivo sepsis protection, intracellular copper-DTC complex concentrations were inferred rather than directly quantified inside the cells (Grade 4).

classification.rationale: The explanation involves cellular metabolic conversion of disulfiram to DTC and subsequent activation/complexation with copper ions, supported by copper supplementation rescuing cellular potency.

eligibility.reason: Quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (liposome leakage and caspase activity IC50s) and quantitative cellular potency (pyroptosis inhibition IC50s) were measured for disulfiram (C-23) and its metabolite diethyldithiocarbamate (DTC).

insights.text: Disulfiram (C-23) potently inhibits GSDMD pore formation in cell-free liposomes (IC50 0.30 µM) by covalently attaching a diethyldithiocarbamate moiety to Cys191.
Disulfiram cellular potency is substantially weaker (~8-10 µM) than liposome leakage potency, which the authors attribute to rapid intracellular metabolism to diethyldithiocarbamate (DTC).
Supplementation with copper gluconate rescues the cellular potency of both disulfiram and DTC to ~0.4-0.5 µM, closely aligning cellular activity with cell-free liposome leakage potency.

In addition to directly inactivating GSDMD Cys191, disulfiram directly inhibits inflammatory caspases (caspase-1 IC50 0.15 µM, caspase-11 IC50 0.73 µM), indicating a multi-target mechanism in cellular inflammasome inhibition.

review_notes: C-23 (disulfiram) and DTC met the inclusion criteria with quantitative IC50 values in both cell-free biochemical liposome leakage and intact cell pyroptosis assays.

Bay 11-7082 has explicit biochemical IC50s/Kd in Extended Data Fig. 6 (liposome leakage WT IC50 = 6.81 µM, C38A = 11.87 µM, C191A = 13.46 µM, GSDMD-3C = 20.3 µM, GSDMA3-3C = 22.2 µM; MST Kd = 35.6 µM; caspase-1 IC50 = 0.15 µM; caspase-11 IC50 = 1.96 µM) and 8-point 2-fold concentration-response bar charts (0.3125-40 µM) for cellular pyroptosis in Fig. 4c,d, from which half-maximal concentrations (~3.5 µM in THP-1 canonical pyroptosis and ~25 µM in iBMDM non-canonical pyroptosis) were extracted as graph_estimate records.
Disulfiram analogues C-23A1 through C-23A12 in Extended Data Fig. 5 have biochemical IC50s in liposomes, but lack reported cellular IC50 values (only bar charts are shown in ED Fig. 5d,e).

claims.author_explanation: Much of the wide variation and apparent loss of potency in live-cell NanoBRET assays relative to permeabilized cells reflects differential intracellular unbound exposure (Kpuu < 1) resulting from extensive non-specific binding, rather than differences in intrinsic E3 ligase binding recognition.

evidence.experiment: Direct comparison between RBA (IC50,live / IC50,permeabilized) and 1/Kpuu, and regression between IC50,permeabilized and IC50,intracellular (IC50,external * Kpuu)
evidence.result: RBA varied with 1/Kpuu with a slope of 0.85 (95% CI 0.44–1.26, R2 = 0.74), and IC50,perm tracked IC50,intracellular across >2 orders of magnitude (slope 0.90, R2 = 0.78, p = 0.08).

evidence.experiment: Measurement of total cellular accumulation (Kp) and cellular unbound fraction (fu,cell) to determine Kpuu across the PROTAC panel
evidence.result: Unbound intracellular concentrations were lower than external dosing concentrations by an average of 2.1-, 14-, and 21-fold for pomalidomide-, thalidomide-, and VHL-based PROTACs, respectively.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors quantitatively validated the exposure penalty using two fully independent orthogonal techniques: mass-balance determination of physical Kpuu (via Kp and fu,cell) and in-assay permeabilization (RBA). IC50,permeabilized agreed quantitatively with Kpuu-corrected IC50,intracellular (slope 0.90, R2 = 0.78), and RBA matched 1/Kpuu (slope 0.85, R2 = 0.74).

classification.rationale: The loss of live-cell potency is attributed to low intracellular unbound exposure (Kpuu < 1) caused by extensive non-specific intracellular binding/sequestration of the compound, which is outside the specific taxonomy categories.

claims.author_explanation: Extending the alkyl linker in dBET1 (11) to dBET6 (12) dramatically improves membrane permeability and intracellular unbound accumulation (Kpuu), narrowing the live-to-permeabilized potency gap (RBA drops from 10 to 2.5) despite near-identical intrinsic CRBN affinity.

evidence.experiment: NanoBRET dose-response curves in live vs permeabilized cells and Caco-2 permeability measurement for matched pair dBET1 (11) and dBET6 (12)
evidence.result: Compounds 11 and 12 display similar intrinsic IC50,perm (63 vs 79 nM), but 12 shows ~189-fold higher Papp (64.4 vs 0.34 x 10^-6 cm/s), ~3-fold higher Kpuu (0.080 vs 0.027), and 3.2-fold higher live-cell potency (197 vs 636 nM).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors compare matched analogues (11 vs 12) differing solely by linker length and observe identical intrinsic permeabilized-cell potency alongside divergent live-cell potency, Kpuu, and Caco-2 permeability; however, this is an analogue comparison rather than a dynamic rescue intervention.

classification.rationale: The matched-pair comparison of dBET1 and dBET6 attributes the narrowed live-to-permeabilized cell potency gap primarily to a dramatic improvement in membrane permeability and resulting intracellular unbound accumulation.

claims.author_explanation: Passive membrane permeability contributes to cellular target engagement within individual E3 ligase classes, and more lipophilic alkane linkers improve permeability and Kpuu in CRBN-based PROTACs (whereas VHL-based PROTACs benefit from more hydrophilic linkers for passive permeability), but passive permeability alone is an incomplete predictor of the cellular potency dropoff because it does not capture intracellular nonspecific binding and sequestration.

evidence.experiment: Modified Caco-2 apical-to-basolateral passive permeability assay with pre-incubation and efflux inhibitor cocktail (quinidine, benzbromarone, sulfasalazine) compared against live-cell NanoBRET IC50
evidence.result: Passive Caco-2 permeability correlated moderately with live-cell NanoBRET IC50 within E3 ligase classes (R2 = 0.39 for pomalidomide, 0.48 for thalidomide, 0.62 for VHL) and increased in CRBN matched pairs with alkane vs polar/PEG linkers (e.g., 5 vs 4: 18.4 vs 0.54 x 10^-6 cm/s).

evidence.experiment: Correlation analysis between passive Caco-2 permeability and physical intracellular unbound exposure (Kpuu) or total accumulation (Kp) across the full PROTAC panel
evidence.result: Passive Caco-2 permeability correlated only weakly with NanoBRET IC50 across the full dataset (R2 = 0.21) and showed no correlation with Kpuu (R2 = 0.09) because intracellular binding (fu,cell) decouples membrane permeation rates from unbound intracellular concentrations.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly measured passive Caco-2 permeability (with efflux inhibitors) alongside Kp, fu,cell, and Kpuu across the panel and matched linker pairs, demonstrating moderate within-class correlations with live-cell IC50 (R2 = 0.39-0.62) but weak overall correlation (R2 = 0.21) and no correlation with Kpuu (R2 = 0.09).

classification.rationale: Passive membrane permeability is shown to correlate moderately with cellular potency within E3 ligase classes, but correlates weakly overall and fails to predict Kpuu due to intracellular nonspecific binding.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative target engagement potencies in both intact live cells (IC50,external) and digitonin-permeabilized cells (IC50,perm) for 12 PROTACs and 2 control compounds engaging CRBN or VHL, alongside intracellular exposure (Kpuu) and Caco-2 permeability.

insights.text: Apparent cellular target engagement IC50 values for PROTACs vary widely when referenced to external concentrations, but this spread is largely driven by differences in intracellular unbound exposure (Kpuu) rather than intrinsic E3 ligase recognition.

Recalculating target engagement IC50 values using measured intracellular unbound exposure (Kpuu) narrows the apparent potency spread across the PROTAC panel from ~4000-fold to ~150-fold, in quantitative agreement with intrinsic affinity directly measured in digitonin-permeabilized cells.

Independent LC-MS/MS physical exposure measurements (1/Kpuu) and bioluminescent target engagement shifts (RBA) recover the exact same intracellular exposure penalty quantitatively across >2 orders of magnitude (slope 0.85, R2 = 0.74).

Passive Caco-2 permeability alone is a poor surrogate for target-site exposure because it reflects membrane transit rates without capturing extensive intracellular non-specific binding and accumulation.

For the matched pair dBET1 and dBET6, extending the alkyl linker confers ~189-fold higher passive permeability and ~3-fold higher Kpuu, explaining a 3.2-fold higher live-cell target engagement potency despite near-identical intrinsic CRBN affinity.

review_notes: Table 2 reports 20 PROTACs and 2 small-molecule controls (lenalidomide and VH298). Exactly 12 PROTACs and the 2 controls have both live-cell (IC50,external) and permeabilized-cell (IC50,perm) quantitative potencies, fulfilling the inclusion scope.
PROTACs 3, 6, 7, 8, 10, and 13 were only characterized in live cells (IC50,perm marked as NAj) and were excluded from compound and measurement extraction in accordance with scope instructions.
PROTACs 19 and 20 showed no competition within the tested concentration range in live cells and were not evaluated in permeabilized cells; they are excluded.

PROTACs 16 and 17 have both live-cell and permeabilized-cell IC50 values, allowing RBA calculation, but fu,cell and Kpuu could not be determined due to buffer concentrations falling below the limit of quantitation.

The digitonin-permeabilized NanoBRET assay removes the intact plasma membrane barrier, directly reporting intrinsic affinity for the tagged E3 ligase, and serves as the cell-free biochemical comparator in this study.

Added claim_3 and matched-pair analogue interventions (int_2: dBRD9 vs dBRD9-A; int_3: compound 2 vs 1; int_4: compound 15 vs MZ-1) to comprehensively capture the authors' analysis of passive Caco-2 permeability and linker polarity effects alongside intracellular unbound exposure (Kpuu).

limitations: Cellular proliferation is a phenotypic readout that reflects overall cell viability and EGFR signalling inhibition rather than direct intracellular target engagement.
Asymmetric dimer formation of EGFR in intact cells renders allosteric inhibitor binding less effective in cellular contexts without dimerization disruption.

limitations: Cellular activity is driven primarily by targeted protein degradation through CRBN recruitment rather than direct catalytic kinase inhibition.

limitations: Cellular antiproliferative effect is mediated by degradation rather than pure enzymatic inhibition.
Cellular potency is influenced by membrane permeability and ternary complex formation.
pairs.rationale: JBJ-07-038 was evaluated in the cell-free EGFR L858R/T790M HTRF assay and in Ba/F3 cells transformed with EGFR L858R/T790M.

limitations: Mechanism of cellular action involves PROTAC-mediated degradation rather than simple biochemical inhibition.
Phenotypic proliferation measurement reflects multiple steps including cellular entry, CRBN binding, ubiquitination, and degradation.
pairs.rationale: JBJ-07-200 was tested against purified EGFR L858R/T790M in the HTRF kinase assay and in EGFR L858R/T790M-dependent Ba/F3 cell proliferation.

limitations: Both biochemical IC50 (~110 nM) and cellular proliferation IC50 (> 10 uM) are read from Figure 2A and 2C graphs.

N-methylation of the glutarimide ring abolishes CRBN binding, preventing EGFR degradation and demonstrating that allosteric binding alone without dimer disruption or degradation is insufficient for cellular antiproliferative activity.
pairs.rationale: Negative control compound control-DDC-01-163 was evaluated in the purified EGFR L858R/T790M HTRF biochemical assay and in the EGFR L858R/T790M Ba/F3 cell proliferation assay.

claims.author_explanation: Allosteric EGFR inhibitors such as EAI001 and JBJ-07-149 suffer from reduced cellular antiproliferative potency as single agents because EGFR asymmetric dimer formation renders one of the allosteric pockets harder to occupy; disruption of dimerization (e.g., by cetuximab) is required to restore potent cellular inhibition.

evidence.experiment: Proliferation assay of EGFR L858R/T790M Ba/F3 cells treated with JBJ-07-149 alone or in combination with cetuximab
evidence.result: JBJ-07-149 showed poor single-agent anti-proliferative activity (EC50 = 4.9 uM) but potent activity in the presence of cetuximab (EC50 = 0.148 uM)

evidence.experiment: Conversion of JBJ-07-149 into CRBN-recruiting PROTAC DDC-01-163 versus N-methylated CRBN-inactive negative control (control-DDC-01-163) in EGFR L858R/T790M Ba/F3 cells
evidence.result: DDC-01-163 degraded mutant EGFR and potently inhibited cell proliferation (EC50 = 0.096 uM) despite 45-fold weaker biochemical inhibition (IC50 = 45 nM vs 1.1 nM), whereas control-DDC-01-163 bound EGFR biochemically (~110 nM) but could not engage CRBN or inhibit cell proliferation (> 10 uM).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors explain the loss of single-agent cellular potency of JBJ-07-149 based on prior structural/mechanistic work on asymmetric dimers and demonstrate experimentally that co-treatment with cetuximab restores potent anti-proliferative activity (EC50 shifts from 4.9 uM to 0.148 uM).

classification.rationale: The reduced single-agent cellular potency is caused by the target's oligomerization state—specifically EGFR asymmetric dimer formation occluding one allosteric pocket—supported by combination rescue with the dimerization-disrupting antibody cetuximab.

claims.author_explanation: PROTAC degraders frequently exhibit poor membrane permeability due to high molecular weight and hydrogen bond donors/acceptors. The presence of a free phenolic hydroxyl group in JBJ-07-038 reduces cellular permeability and intracellular CRBN engagement; replacing the hydroxyl with fluorine (JBJ-07-200) improves cellular CRBN engagement and antiproliferative activity despite lowering biochemical binding affinity.

evidence.experiment: Cellular competition-based assay evaluating displacement of BRD4BD2-directed CRBN ligands and restoration of BRD4BD2-GFP signal
evidence.result: JBJ-07-200 showed superior intracellular CRBN engagement compared to JBJ-07-038, and JBJ-04-125-02-based degraders showed less potent rescue due to the free hydroxyl group

evidence.experiment: Comparison of biochemical IC50 and cellular anti-proliferative EC50 between JBJ-07-038 (OH) and JBJ-07-200 (F)
evidence.result: JBJ-07-200 had weaker biochemical affinity (IC50 = 390 nM vs 19 nM) but superior cellular antiproliferative potency (EC50 = 0.15 uM vs 0.48 uM) and superior EGFR degradation

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly measured intracellular CRBN engagement using a cellular competitive degradation assay (BRD4BD2-GFP rescue) and compared JBJ-07-038 and its fluorinated analogue JBJ-07-200, showing improved cellular CRBN engagement and antiproliferative activity for the fluorinated analogue despite a 20-fold drop in biochemical kinase affinity. This represents an analogue comparison supported by a relevant intracellular engagement assay.

classification.rationale: The explanation attributes reduced cellular potency and intracellular CRBN engagement of JBJ-07-038 to poor membrane permeability from a free phenolic hydroxyl group, supported by analogue comparison and cellular CRBN engagement assays.

insights.text: Parent allosteric EGFR inhibitor JBJ-07-149 exhibits potent biochemical kinase inhibition (IC50 = 1.1 nM) but poor single-agent anti-proliferative activity (EC50 = 4.9 uM) due to asymmetric EGFR dimer formation; addition of the dimerization-disrupting antibody cetuximab rescues cellular potency to 0.148 uM.

Conversion of an allosteric inhibitor into a PROTAC degrader (DDC-01-163) bypasses the requirement for cetuximab, yielding potent cellular growth inhibition (EC50 = 0.096 uM) despite a 45-fold loss in biochemical kinase inhibitory potency compared to JBJ-07-149.

Cellular membrane permeability critically impacts PROTAC efficacy: replacing the phenolic hydroxyl in JBJ-07-038 with a fluorine atom in JBJ-07-200 reduces biochemical kinase affinity by 20-fold but enhances intracellular CRBN engagement and improves antiproliferative EC50 from 0.48 uM to 0.15 uM.

Allosteric EGFR degrader DDC-01-163 retains potent cellular activity against osimertinib-resistant tertiary mutations L858R/T790M/C797S (EC50 = 0.041 uM) and L858R/T790M/L718Q (EC50 = 0.028 uM), which are refractory to standard ATP-competitive inhibitors.

review_notes: Extracted all 5 compounds with both cell-free biochemical (HTRF) and cellular (Ba/F3 proliferation) potency data in the main paper: JBJ-07-149, DDC-01-163, control-DDC-01-163 (graph estimates from Fig 2A and 2C), JBJ-07-038, and JBJ-07-200.

JBJ-04-125-02 (structure in Fig 1B), lenalidomide (Fig 2B), and osimertinib/gefitinib/afatinib (Fig 6A, 7A) do not have paired biochemical and cellular potency values reported in this PDF and are therefore excluded from the paired compound list.
Table S1 (SAR of linkers 11g, 11k, 11m-q) and Figures S1-S3 are in the Supplementary Information, which is not part of the supplied PDF.

compounds.structure_notes: Cyclic peptide 30 containing pyridine amino acid X90, 4-chlorophenyl, ethyl side chain (Abu), and cyclized via linker L1 with thiol building blocks. Fully depicted in Fig. 5d and Fig. 6a.

conditions: 10 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, 0.005% (w/v) Tween-20, pH 7.4
assays.description: FP competition assay determining the displacement of fluorescein-labeled Nrf2 peptide probe from recombinant human Keap1 Kelch domain (residues 321–609) under reducing conditions.
assays.principle: Fluorescence polarization competition binding assay

conditions: HEK293 cells expressing firefly luciferase under Nrf2/ARE response element control
High-glucose DMEM with 10% FBS, 100 U/ml penicillin, 100 µg/ml streptomycin
assays.description: Cellular reporter assay measuring Nrf2 pathway activation triggered by inhibition of Keap1-mediated Nrf2 degradation in HEK293-ARE cells.
assays.principle: Nrf2/ARE responsive luciferase reporter activation

limitations: Cell-free assay measures competitive displacement from purified Kelch domain over 15 min, whereas the cellular assay measures transcriptionally mediated luciferase accumulation over 14 h.
Cellular activity is subject to membrane permeation, intracellular active efflux, and nonspecific binding.
pairs.rationale: Both assays assess modulation of the Keap1-Nrf2 protein-protein interaction; the cell-free FP assay directly quantifies binding affinity to the recombinant human Keap1 Kelch domain, while the HEK293-ARE reporter assay measures downstream cellular Nrf2 transcriptional activation resulting from Keap1-Nrf2 complex inhibition.

claims.author_explanation: The authors explain that active efflux by efflux pumps (efflux ratio > 90 across Caco-2 monolayers) reduces the intracellular levels of peptide 30, accounting for its lower activity in cells (IC50 ~ 50 µM) compared to in vitro binding affinity (Ki = 53 nM).

evidence.experiment: Bidirectional Caco-2 cell monolayer transport assay measuring apical-to-basal and basolateral-to-apical apparent permeability (Papp) of compound 30.
evidence.result: Apical-to-basal Papp was below the detection limit (Papp = 0.07 x 10^-6 cm/s limit) while basolateral-to-apical Papp was 6.6 x 10^-6 cm/s, demonstrating an efflux ratio > 90.

evidence.experiment: PAMPA assay measuring passive artificial membrane permeability of peptide 30.
evidence.result: Peptide 30 showed passive artificial membrane permeability of Papp = 1.2 x 10^-6 cm/s.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors measured mechanistic transport parameters (bidirectional Caco-2 permeability and PAMPA) specifically for compound 30, observing high asymmetric transport (efflux ratio > 90). However, they did not perform a controlled causal rescue (e.g., repeating the cellular assay with an efflux inhibitor).

classification.rationale: The explanation specifically cites active efflux by efflux pumps (measured via bidirectional Caco-2 transport) as the cause for reduced intracellular levels and lower cellular potency of peptide 30.

claims.author_explanation: The authors attributed the complete lack of cellular activity of precursor macrocycles (22–24) to limited membrane permeability from polar H-bond donors, and investigated passive membrane permeability as a potential explanation for peptide 30's lower cellular activity relative to biochemical binding, finding that after replacing asparagine with pyridine (X90), peptide 30 had decent passive membrane permeability (PAMPA Papp = 1.2 x 10^-6 cm/s) sufficient for cellular activity while efflux remained the primary barrier.

evidence.experiment: PAMPA passive artificial membrane permeation assay on untagged cyclic peptide 30.
evidence.result: Peptide 30 displayed decent passive membrane permeability (Papp = 1.2 x 10^-6 cm/s), indicating that passive permeation was sufficient to achieve cellular activity and that active efflux (efflux ratio > 90 in Caco-2) rather than passive impermeability was the main cause of the remaining cellular dropoff.

evidence.experiment: Chloroalkane penetration assay (CAPA) in HeLa cells comparing CA-tagged precursor 23a-CA and its backbone N-methylated analog 23b-CA.
evidence.result: 23a-CA showed moderate cytosolic penetration (CP50 = 0.58 ± 0.04 µM), whereas removing one H-bond donor by N-methylation in 23b-CA improved permeability ~6-fold (CP50 = 0.091 ± 0.009 µM), supporting polarity/H-bond donors as the barrier to cell entry.

evidence.experiment: Substitution of the polar asparagine residue in macrocycle 23 (Ki = 10.3 nM, inactive in cells up to 80 µM) with H-bond-donor-free pyridine amino acid X90 (Ppa) to yield cyclic peptide 30.
evidence.result: Peptide 30 retained nanomolar Keap1 affinity (Ki = 53 ± 5 nM) with reduced polar surface (2 H-bond donors, TPSA = 203 Å^2) and gained dose-dependent cellular activity in HEK293-ARE reporter cells (IC50 ~ 50 µM).

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors directly measured passive membrane permeability for peptide 30 via PAMPA (Papp = 1.2 x 10^-6 cm/s) and evaluated cytosolic penetration of CA-tagged precursor analogs (23a-CA and 23b-CA) via CAPA, guided by SAR replacing the polar asparagine with pyridine X90 to unlock cellular activity in 30. However, precursor peptide 23 lacked a numerical cellular potency bound, and changing the side chain alters both target affinity and physicochemical properties (`mechanism_isolated=false`).

classification.rationale: Passive membrane permeability was supported as the barrier for precursor macrocycles (22-24) via CAPA and SAR, but evaluated and ruled out as the primary barrier for modified peptide 30 (which had adequate PAMPA permeability while efflux remained the main issue).

eligibility.reason: Peptide 30 was evaluated for both cell-free Keap1 binding affinity (Ki = 53 ± 5 nM in an FP competition assay) and cellular activity in HEK293-ARE luciferase reporter cells (IC50 ~ 50 µM).

insights.text: De novo screening of a 15,360-member fully random cyclic peptide library generated by combinatorial SPPS and acoustic nanoliter diversification successfully yielded uncharged sub-kDa inhibitors of the challenging Keap1-Nrf2 PPI.

Linker exploration and macrocyclization improved biochemical binding affinity approximately 1,000-fold to low nanomolar Ki values (e.g., peptide 23 Ki = 10.3 nM), but potent polar macrocycles remained inactive in cells due to poor membrane permeability.

Engineering out hydrogen-bond donors by substituting the polar asparagine side chain with a pyridine amino acid (X90) yielded cyclic peptide 30, which retained high Keap1 affinity (Ki = 53 nM) while substantially lowering polarity (TPSA 203 Å2, two HBDs).

Cyclic peptide 30 achieved intracellular target engagement in HEK293-ARE reporter cells (IC50 ~ 50 µM); the right-shift relative to biochemical Ki was attributed by the authors to active efflux, supported by a Caco-2 efflux ratio > 90.

review_notes: Only compound 30 satisfied the inclusion criteria of having both a quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (Ki = 53 ± 5 nM) and a quantitative cellular potency (IC50 ~ 50 µM) reported in the paper.

Earlier macrocycles (22, 23, 24, 28) and library 5 analogs (29, 31, 32) were tested in the HEK293-ARE reporter assay up to 80 µM but showed no activity above negative control levels without reported numerical bounds; they were therefore excluded from the paired dataset.

Two interventions exploring and addressing the membrane permeability barrier were recorded: (1) replacement of the polar asparagine side chain in macrocycle 23 with pyridine amino acid X90 to yield cell-active peptide 30 (before-measurement IDs null because 23 lacked a numerical cellular bound), and (2) backbone N-methylation of 23a-CA to 23b-CA in an exposure-only CAPA cell penetration assay, which improved cytosolic access ~6-fold (CP50 from 0.58 µM to 0.091 µM) but abolished Keap1 binding. No efflux inhibitor intervention was performed to rescue the Caco-2 efflux observed for peptide 30.

CAPA (chloroalkane penetration assay) was utilized to measure cell penetration (CP50) of CA-tagged derivatives (23a-CA, 23b-CA, Pep5-CA, Trp-CA), but CAPA measures cytosolic access rather than intracellular target inhibition potency.

claims.author_explanation: Linear all-D peptide dPMI-δ and certain stapled/double-stapled analogues (dPMI-δ(2-9), dPMI-δ(5-9), and double-stapled dPMI-δ(1-5,9-12)) bind Mdm2 with high affinity biochemically (sub-micromolar to low nanomolar Kd) but fail to activate p53 in cells because they lack membrane permeability.

evidence.experiment: Testing linear dPMI-δ, stapled analogues, and stitched dPMI-δ(1-5-12) in HCT116 p53 reporter, LDH leakage, and counter-screen assays.
evidence.result: Linear dPMI-δ and stapled dPMI-δ(2-9), dPMI-δ(5-9) showed no p53 activation and no LDH leakage up to 50 µM despite sub-micromolar/nanomolar Mdm2 binding; stitched dPMI-δ(1-5-12) showed potent on-target p53 activation (EC50 = 4 µM) without LDH release.

evidence.experiment: Testing inhibition of p53(1-52)-Mdm2 interaction in a yeast two-hybrid growth assay.
evidence.result: Stitched dPMI-δ(1-5-12) completely prevented yeast growth expressing p53/Mdm2 at 12.5 µM while having no effect on control kinetochore Csm1-Dsn1 interaction; linear dPMI-δ and double-stapled dPMI-δ(1-5,9-12) showed no effect.

evidence.experiment: Incubation of linear and stapled all-D peptides in whole cell homogenate and human plasma for 4 hours to test proteolytic stability (Fig. S5).
evidence.result: Over 90% of linear and stapled all-D peptides remained intact after 4 h in both whole cell homogenate and human plasma, ruling out proteolytic degradation as the cause of cellular inactivity.

evidence.experiment: Prior study cited by authors (Liu et al., ref. 47) delivering linear dPMI-δ into cells using nano-carriers.
evidence.result: Linear dPMI-δ lacked intrinsic cell permeability and activity on its own, but activated p53 in cells when delivered intracellularly using nano-carriers.

claims.grade_rationale: Authors demonstrated that linear dPMI-δ and double-stapled dPMI-δ(1-5,9-12) bind Mdm2 tightly in FP and SPR but lack cellular activity in the p53 reporter assay (EC50 >50 µM and 34.6 µM, respectively), cause no LDH release, and fail in a yeast 2-hybrid intracellular assay, whereas the stitched analogue enters cells and engages the target (SAR and multi-assay association/characterization).

classification.rationale: The failure of linear and certain stapled peptides to activate p53 in cells despite high biochemical Mdm2 affinity is attributed to a lack of membrane permeability, supported by cellular reporter, yeast two-hybrid, stability assays, and prior nano-carrier delivery studies.

claims.author_explanation: For certain stapled peptides (dPMI-δ(1-5) and dPMI-δ(6-10)), apparent cellular p53 reporter activity is confounded by non-specific plasma membrane disruption rather than genuine intracellular target engagement, as evidenced by matching EC50 values for p53 reporter activation and LDH leakage.

evidence.experiment: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assay and counter-screen assay in HCT116 cells under identical conditions (16 h, 2% FBS).
evidence.result: dPMI-δ(1-5) and dPMI-δ(6-10) induced LDH release with EC50 of 24 µM and 18.5 µM, close to their reporter EC50 values, whereas dPMI-δ(5-12) and stitched dPMI-δ(1-5-12) caused no LDH leakage (>50 µM).

claims.grade_rationale: Authors conducted an LDH release assay under identical conditions to the p53 reporter assay, showing that dPMI-δ(1-5) (p53 EC50 13.7 µM, LDH EC50 24 µM) and dPMI-δ(6-10) (p53 EC50 30.3 µM, LDH EC50 18.5 µM) cause membrane leakage, demonstrating that apparent cellular activity reflects membrane lysis rather than selective target engagement.

classification.rationale: Apparent cellular reporter activity is explained as an artifact of non-specific plasma membrane lysis/disruption (measured by LDH leakage) rather than true intracellular target engagement, which falls outside the specific taxonomy labels.

eligibility.reason: The study reports quantitative cell-free binding affinities (Kd by FP and SPR against Mdm2 and Mdm4) and quantitative cellular potencies (EC50 in a p53-responsive β-lactamase reporter assay in HCT116 cells) for the same series of linear, stapled, and stitched all-D peptides and the control peptide ATSP-7041.

insights.text: Stapling an all-D linear peptide can restore or impart cellular permeability, but staple position critically affects whether intracellular target engagement or non-specific plasma membrane lysis dominates.

Apparent cellular activity in reporter gene assays must be evaluated alongside membrane integrity (LDH release) and counter-screen assays to distinguish bona fide intracellular PPI inhibition from cytotoxicity resulting from membrane disruption.

A stitched bicyclic architecture (dPMI-δ(1–5–12)) achieved clean intracellular target engagement and activation of p53 (EC50 = 4 µM) without detectable membrane leakage, whereas the double-stapled analogue remained cell-impermeable despite 1.5 nM biochemical affinity.

review_notes: Table 1 lists 'dPMI-δ(5v12)' in the column heading, which is clearly a typographical error for dPMI-δ(5–12) as confirmed in the text and subsequent tables.

All 11 peptides across Tables 1-4 (linear dPMI-δ, 6 single-stapled analogues, stitched dPMI-δ(1-5-12), stitched scrambled control, double-stapled dPMI-δ(1-5,9-12), and control ATSP-7041) and all 66 measurements across Mdm2 FP, Mdm2 SPR, Mdm4 FP, cellular p53 reporter, LDH release, and counter-screen assays were extracted and verified against the tables.
High detergent (0.1% Tween-20) caused an affinity shift in FP due to micellar sequestration (Table S1, in SI), but standard data with 0.001% Tween-20 from main text tables were extracted.

claims.author_explanation: The authors hypothesize and provide multi-assay evidence that poor cellular permeability caused by the peptidic SelK degron moiety severely limits intracellular drug availability and cellular potency of KLHDC2-recruiting PROTACs, requiring sub-nanomolar to low nanomolar biochemical affinity to achieve even micromolar cellular degradation and proliferation inhibition.

evidence.experiment: NanoBRET cellular target engagement assay measuring displacement of fluorescent tracer from WEE1-nanoluciferase in intact HEK-293T cells comparing KYH1872, the small-molecule PROTAC ZNL-02-096, and their respective kinase warheads (YHJ1039 and AZD1775).
evidence.result: Intracellular WEE1 target engagement by KYH1872 was ~300-fold less efficient than by ZNL-02-096, despite comparable target engagement by their isolated kinase warheads, attributing poor cellular potency to the peptidic SelK moiety.

evidence.experiment: CRBN target engagement assay using HEK-293T cells expressing a BRD4-BD2-GFP reporter to test whether appending the SelK peptide to thalidomide (KYH2605) abrogates intracellular CRBN engagement compared to free lenalidomide.
evidence.result: KYH2605 failed to engage cellular CRBN, whereas lenalidomide engaged CRBN efficiently, verifying that the SelK peptide impedes cellular permeability.

evidence.experiment: Transwell Caco-2 bidirectional permeability assay measuring apparent permeability (Papp) and efflux ratios for KYH1872, parental SelK peptide (35), and kinase inhibitor YHJ1039.
evidence.result: Caco-2 permeation assays confirmed that the SelK peptide confers low membrane permeability to KYH1872.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors performed relevant mechanistic measurements (nanoBRET cellular target engagement showing ~300-fold weaker WEE1 engagement than small-molecule PROTAC ZNL-02-096, lack of cellular CRBN engagement by a SelK-thalidomide conjugate KYH2605, and transwell Caco-2 permeability assays), directly demonstrating that the SelK peptide moiety impairs cellular entry. However, no controlled rescue restoring cell permeability to functional PROTACs was demonstrated.

classification.rationale: Poor cellular potency of KLHDC2-recruiting PROTACs is attributed to poor cellular membrane permeability caused by the peptidic SelK degron moiety, supported by NanoBRET, CRBN engagement, and Caco-2 permeability assays.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports cell-free biochemical binding affinities (KD by TR-FRET against recombinant KLHDC2) and quantitative cellular potencies (cell viability EC50 and HiBiT / Western blot degradation DC50 in MOLM-14 cells) for the same peptide-conjugated PROTAC compounds (KYH1872, KYH1996, KYH1886, and KYH2293).

insights.text: Peptide-based KLHDC2 PROTACs (e.g., KYH1872) achieve sub-nanomolar to low nanomolar biochemical affinity (<2 nM) for the E3 ligase KLHDC2, but display micromolar cellular potency (EC50 ~1-3 uM for proliferation; DC50 ~0.3-1.3 uM for kinase degradation).

The primary cause of the large biochemical-to-cellular potency gap is poor cellular permeability conferred by the peptide degron (SelK fragment), as demonstrated by nanoBRET cellular target engagement (~300-fold weaker than small-molecule PROTAC ZNL-02-096), lack of cellular CRBN engagement by thalidomide-SelK conjugate KYH2605, and Caco-2 permeability data.

Tight biochemical binding to KLHDC2 (<20 nM threshold) is essential for cellular activity; weakening KLHDC2 binding by stereocenter inversion (KYH2011, KD = 155 nM) or C-terminal tetrazole substitution (KYH2293, KD = 68.5 nM) abolishes or markedly impairs kinase degradation and cell viability.

Kinase degradation by KYH1872 is on-mechanism and dependent on cullin neddylation, as pretreatment with the NAE inhibitor MLN4924 rescued degradation of WEE1 and CDK4 in both Western blotting and HiBiT assays.

review_notes: Compounds YHJ1039 (parent kinase inhibitor) and DB0625 (CRBN-based degrader) were excluded from compounds/pairs because cell-free KLHDC2 binding data were not tested/reported for them.

KYH2011 is reported as 'n.d.' in Table 1 and Table 3, but Figure 3D explicitly plots its 72 h MOLM-14 proliferation dose-response curve up to 10 uM (10^-5 M) with >75% proliferation remaining, allowing extraction of a censored cellular EC50 > 10 uM paired with its biochemical KD of 155 nM.

No controlled intervention rescued cellular permeability of the SelK peptide degron, but matched SelK peptide analogue comparisons (KYH1886, KYH1996, KYH2293 vs KYH1872) are recorded in interventions with mechanism_isolated=false. Additionally, SelK-thalidomide conjugate KYH2605 (39) was tested as a cellular-only permeability probe in the CRBN engagement assay.

claims.author_explanation: Covalent targeting of CDK7 at cysteine 312 by the acrylamide of THZ1 provides sustained, irreversible inhibition and dramatic cellular potency in sensitive cancer lines, whereas the reversible analogue THZ1-R exhibits lower biochemical binding affinity and markedly reduced antiproliferative potency that rapidly washes out.

evidence.experiment: LanthaScreen Eu Kinase Binding Assay over 20, 60, and 180 min incubation
evidence.result: THZ1 showed time-dependent increase in CDK7 inhibitory potency (IC50 shifted from 15.6 nM to 3.2 nM), whereas THZ1-R showed time-independent potency (~146 nM), indicative of covalent inactivation.

evidence.experiment: Ectopic expression of Flag-CDK7 wild type versus C312S mutant in HeLa S3 cells treated with THZ1
evidence.result: Expression of C312S mutant CDK7 restored RNAPII CTD Ser 5/7 phosphorylation and gene expression of sensitive transcripts (MYC, KLF4, ID1, GATA2), whereas wild-type CDK7 did not rescue.

evidence.experiment: Cellular compound washout experiments evaluating antiproliferative effects in Jurkat and Loucy cells
evidence.result: THZ1 antiproliferative effects were impervious to washout (Jurkat IC50 55 nM continuous vs 99 nM washout), whereas THZ1-R potency was substantially lost upon washout (IC50 shifted from 2,008 nM to 5,600 nM).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors perform mass spectrometry mapping of the covalent adduct to C312, engineer a C312S point mutant CDK7 that prevents irreversible binding and rescues RNAPII phosphorylation and gene expression, and contrast THZ1 against reversible THZ1-R across biochemical and cellular washout assays.

classification.rationale: The difference in biochemical and cellular potency/washout durability between THZ1 and THZ1-R is explained by covalent irreversible binding to C312 versus reversible binding, a mechanism not covered by a dedicated taxonomy label.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free CDK7 binding potencies (LanthaScreen Eu kinase binding assay) and cellular antiproliferative potencies across multiple cell lines for both THZ1 and its reversible analogue THZ1-R.

insights.text: THZ1 achieves exceptional potency and selectivity for CDK7 by covalently modifying a unique cysteine residue (C312) positioned outside the canonical kinase domain.
Saturating the acrylamide to generate THZ1-R eliminates covalent reactivity, resulting in a marked drop in biochemical binding affinity and a dramatic loss of cellular antiproliferative potency.

Cellular washout experiments show that THZ1 antiproliferative effects and CDK7 inhibition are impervious to compound removal, while THZ1-R activity is reversible and substantially diminished following washout.

Ectopic expression of Flag-tagged CDK7 C312S, but not wild-type CDK7, rescues RNAPII CTD phosphorylation and gene transcription in the presence of THZ1, demonstrating that C312 is the critical determinant of cellular pharmacology.

review_notes: Flavopiridol and Staurosporine are included in Extended Data Figure 9e, f as reference antiproliferative compounds, but no cell-free biochemical potency values are reported for them in this main text/extended data PDF, so they were excluded from the paired compound extraction.

Supplementary tables referenced in the text (such as Supplementary Table 1 listing known CDK7 inhibitors and Supplementary Table 4 detailing the 1,000 cancer cell lines panel) are not present in this 16-page article file.

pairs.rationale: Both assays directly measure p300 catalytic acetyltransferase activity; the cell-free TR-FRET assay measures acetylation of a histone H4 peptide by p300-BHC, and the cellular high-content microscopy assay measures endogenous H3K27 acetylation, a known selective mark placed by p300/CBP in PC-3 cells.

limitations: Cellular H3K27Ac reflects combined p300 and CBP catalytic activity in intact PC-3 cells rather than isolated CBP activity alone.
pairs.rationale: CBP and p300 are paralogous HATs that both catalyze cellular H3K27Ac in PC-3 cells; pairing CBP-BHC TR-FRET IC50 with cellular H3K27Ac EC50 evaluates the biochemical-to-cellular shift for the CBP paralog.

claims.author_explanation: A-485 is an acetyl-CoA-competitive catalytic inhibitor of p300/CBP, as evidenced by X-ray co-crystallography overlapping the acetyl-CoA binding site and a linear increase in biochemical IC50 with increasing acetyl-CoA concentration, which explains cellular potency modulation by physiological acetyl-CoA levels.

evidence.experiment: Enzymatic p300 activity assay determined at increasing concentrations of acetyl-CoA substrate.
evidence.result: The activity assay IC50 for p300 inhibition by A-485 increased linearly with increasing concentrations of acetyl-CoA.

evidence.experiment: X-ray crystal structure of human p300 HAT domain in complex with A-485 at 1.95 A resolution compared to acetyl-CoA bound structures.
evidence.result: Co-crystal structure shows the A-485 binding site directly overlaps with that of acetyl-CoA in the catalytic pocket.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors demonstrated competitive inhibition through linear IC50 dependence on acetyl-CoA concentrations (Fig. 2d) and high-resolution co-crystal structure showing active-site overlap with acetyl-CoA (Fig. 2a-c).

classification.rationale: Cellular potency modulation is explained by competition with endogenous physiological acetyl-CoA at the catalytic pocket of p300/CBP, supported by linear IC50 shifts with increasing acetyl-CoA and co-crystallography.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (TR-FRET IC50 and SPA IC50 for p300/CBP) and quantitative cellular potency (high-content microscopy EC50 for inhibition of histone acetylation H3K27Ac in PC-3 cells) for the catalytic inhibitor A-485.

insights.text: A-485 is a potent catalytic p300/CBP inhibitor with low nanomolar cell-free potency (IC50 9.8 nM against p300, 2.6 nM against CBP) that translates to cellular target engagement (EC50 73 nM for H3K27Ac reduction in PC-3 cells).

The compound competitively inhibits p300 with respect to acetyl-CoA, as confirmed biochemically by linear dependence of IC50 on acetyl-CoA concentration and structurally by X-ray co-crystallography at 1.95 A resolution.

Cellular inhibition of the target mark H3K27Ac is highly selective over other histone marks such as H3K9Ac (EC50 > 10,000 nM) and correlates with stereospecificity, as the inactive control diastereomer A-486 shows negligible biochemical and cellular activity.

review_notes: A-486 (compound 5) is the inactive diastereomer/control analog; its cell-free IC50 is >10,000 nM (p300) and >50 uM (SPA), but in the cellular assay it is simply described as 'inactive' without a numerical bound, so it was excluded from paired compounds per the instruction that 'inactive' without a numerical bound is not a numerical potency.

Earlier series members (Compound 1, Compound 2, Compound R) have biochemical SPA IC50 values reported in Figure 1a, but cellular potency values for these compounds are located in Supplementary Tables not included in the provided PDF.

Cell proliferation EC50 values across 124 cell lines (Figure 3c) and 5 prostate lines (Extended Data Figure 5f) are displayed as graphical bar plots referencing Supplementary Table 10, with no numerical values stated in the text.

Verified biochemical acetyl-CoA titration (Fig. 2d) as an assay_condition intervention demonstrating that increasing acetyl-CoA from ~0.16 uM to 10 uM linearly shifts A-485 p300 IC50 from ~4 nM to ~52 nM, closely approaching the cellular H3K27Ac EC50 of 73 nM. Also noted that the authors attribute differences between cellular target engagement (H3K27Ac EC50 = 73 nM in PC-3) and cellular antiproliferative sensitivity across tumor lines (Fig. 3c, Extended Data Fig. 5f) to lineage-specific transcriptional addiction (e.g., AR+ vs AR- status) rather than differences in cellular target inhibition.
