Both values represent ranges across multiple mutant variants/cell lines
pairs.rationale: Biochemical PRC2/EZH2 Ki_app (0.5-3 nM) compared to 6-day cellular growth IC50 (28-861 nM) in the six most sensitive EZH2-mutant DLBCL cell lines.

limitations: Phenotypic proliferation readout vs biochemical enzyme inhibition
pairs.rationale: Biochemical PRC2/EZH2 Ki_app compared to 6-day cellular growth IC50 in Jiyoye (wild-type EZH2 Burkitt lymphoma cell line).

limitations: Lack of cellular growth sensitivity reflects biological independence from EZH2 catalytic activity rather than failure of target engagement
pairs.rationale: Biochemical PRC2/EZH2 Ki_app compared to 6-day cellular growth IC50 (>1.3 uM) in generally insensitive Burkitt and Hodgkin's lymphoma lines.

claims.author_explanation: Inhibition of H3K27me3 is maximal by 48 h, but phenotypic inhibition of proliferation takes several days (maximal after 2-7 days depending on cell line) because downstream transcriptional activation of silenced PRC2 targets, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis require prolonged EZH2 inhibition.

evidence.experiment: Time-course analysis of H3K27me3 loss and growth inhibition in Pfeiffer and KARPAS-422 cells over 1 to 8 days of GSK126 exposure
evidence.result: H3K27me3 loss began before 24 h and was maximal after 2 days; anti-proliferative response required 2 days in Pfeiffer and 6-7 days in KARPAS-422 for maximal potency

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured the kinetics of target mark inhibition (H3K27me3) versus cell proliferation, cell cycle, and apoptosis over 1-8 days, showing that target inhibition precedes phenotypic growth arrest without need for higher drug concentrations once sufficient exposure duration is reached.

classification.rationale: The delay between rapid cellular target mark inhibition (H3K27me3) and phenotypic proliferation arrest is explained by the slow biological kinetics required for downstream transcriptional reactivation, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis.

claims.author_explanation: Despite potent cellular H3K27me3 inhibition across all tested DLBCL cell lines (IC50 = 7-252 nM) independent of EZH2 mutation status, wild-type EZH2 lines (such as Toledo) and some mutant lines show poor anti-proliferative potency (growth IC50 > 1.3 uM) because co-occurring genetic alterations override dependence on EZH2 activity or compensatory epigenetic mechanisms (such as H3K9, H4K20 or DNA methylation) dampen transcriptional reactivation of silenced target genes.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of cellular H3K27me3 inhibition (ELISA/Western blot), gene expression profiling (Affymetrix microarray and qRT-PCR), and 6-day proliferation across sensitive EZH2-mutant DLBCL lines versus insensitive WT EZH2 Toledo cells.
evidence.result: GSK126 inhibited H3K27me3 in both WT and mutant lines (IC50 7-252 nM, P = 0.27), and 2 uM GSK126 caused near-complete H3K27me3 loss in Toledo cells but induced minimal transcriptional changes (only 23 upregulated probe sets and no TXNIP/TNFRSF21 induction) and no growth inhibition.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly demonstrate via H3K27me3 ELISA, Western blot, microarray profiling, and qRT-PCR that GSK126 achieves near-complete target engagement (H3K27me3 loss) in insensitive Toledo cells at 2 uM, yet fails to induce target gene transcription or growth arrest (Grade 3 mechanistic measurement). The specific identity of the overriding genetic alterations or compensatory chromatin marks (H3K9, H4K20, DNA methylation) remains an untested hypothesis.

classification.rationale: The lack of anti-proliferative response despite potent cellular H3K27me3 inhibition in certain cell lines is attributed to biological pathway independence (co-occurring genetic alterations or compensatory epigenetic mechanisms), which is outside the taxonomy.

insights.text: GSK126 is an S-adenosyl-methionine-competitive inhibitor of PRC2 that inhibits wild-type and mutant EZH2 methyltransferase activity with Ki_app between 0.5 and 3 nM in cell-free assays.
In intact lymphoma cells, GSK126 reduces the repressive histone mark H3K27me3 with an IC50 of 7-252 nM within 48 hours, showing a modest drop in apparent potency relative to cell-free Ki.
Phenotypic growth inhibition requires prolonged exposure (2 to 7 days), with sensitive DLBCL cell lines exhibiting 6-day growth IC50 values between 28 and 861 nM.

review_notes: Only GSK126 has paired biochemical and cellular potency values reported in the main text of this paper.
A biochemical hit compound was noted with Ki_app = 700 nM, but without structural details, cellular activity, or a formal compound identifier.

Individual cell line growth IC50 values for the 46 lines in Figure 2a are tabulated in Supplementary Table 5, which was not part of the primary manuscript PDF; reported numerical values in the main text (HT = 516 nM, Jiyoye = 232 nM, sensitive range = 28-861 nM) were captured.

Added GSK126 biochemical EZH1 Ki_app (89 nM), cellular growth IC50 bound (>1.3 uM) for insensitive Burkitt/Hodgkin's lymphoma cell lines, and Figure 2b time-course growth IC50 graph estimates (Day 1 vs Day 3/7 in Pfeiffer and KARPAS-422).

Added the authors' explanation for lack of phenotypic anti-proliferative potency in insensitive DLBCL cell lines despite full cellular H3K27me3 target engagement (compensatory epigenetic silencing via H3K9/H4K20/DNA methylation or overriding co-occurring mutations, Grade 3), and added two assay_condition interventions capturing the time-course recovery of growth IC50 from Day 1 to Day 3/7 in Pfeiffer and KARPAS-422 cells.

claims.author_explanation: Inclusion of 10% FCS in the cellular culture medium shifts the IC50 of VER-246608 for p(Ser293)E1alpha suppression from 266 nM (0% FCS) to 1.45 uM (10% FCS), and reduced serum conditions enhance anti-proliferative potency.

evidence.experiment: MSD ELISA measuring p(Ser293)E1alpha in PC-3 cells treated with VER-246608 in 0% FCS versus 10% FCS.
evidence.result: IC50 was 266 nM in 0% FCS compared to 1.45 uM in 10% FCS.

evidence.experiment: Sulforhodamine B cell mass determination after 120 h treatment in 10% FCS versus low serum (0.5% FCS) or serum-free (0% FCS) conditions.
evidence.result: VER-246608 demonstrated enhanced growth inhibitory efficacy under reduced serum conditions, achieving complete growth suppression in 0% or 0.1% FCS.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly measured the biomarker IC50 in PC-3 cells with 0% vs 10% FCS (Table 1), demonstrating an ~5.5-fold loss of potency in 10% serum. Furthermore, 120 h proliferation assays in multiple cancer cell lines (PC-3, SW-1088, UM-22B, MEF) confirmed increased anti-proliferative efficacy under serum-depleted conditions.

classification.rationale: The shift in cellular potency is explained by the presence of 10% fetal calf serum (FCS) in the culture medium versus serum-free/low-serum conditions; serum effects/binding are not explicitly represented by a single taxonomy cause.

claims.author_explanation: Supraphysiological D-glucose and nutrient abundance in standard culture media maintain elevated intracellular pyruvate and allow compensatory transamination from L-alanine via ALAT, buffering against the anti-proliferative and metabolic effects of PDK inhibition.

evidence.experiment: Measurement of media L-lactate, glucose consumption, intracellular pyruvate, and extracellular L-alanine in PC-3 cells in standard vs glucose/glutamine-depleted media.
evidence.result: VER-246608 reduced L-lactate, glucose consumption, and intracellular pyruvate levels only under nutrient-depleted conditions.

evidence.experiment: Combination index (CI) analysis and potentiation of the ALAT inhibitor beta-chloro-alanine by VER-246608 in PC-3 cells.
evidence.result: Synergism was observed (CI < 0.9) and 20 uM VER-246608 potentiated beta-chloro-alanine cytotoxicity by 1.8-fold.

evidence.experiment: MSD ELISA measuring p(Ser293)E1alpha in PC-3 cells treated with 5, 10, and 20 uM VER-246608 for 6 h and 24 h in normal vs low-serum (LS) and very-low-glucose/low-glutamine (VLG+LGn) media (Figure 5A, 5B).
evidence.result: Apparent cellular potency for p(Ser293)E1alpha suppression was increased under austere conditions (LS and VLG+LGn) compared to normal media.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors demonstrated that glycolytic attenuation and cytostasis occur only under glucose- or nutrient-depleted media, measured intracellular pyruvate and alanine depletion, and demonstrated synergistic cell growth inhibition when combining VER-246608 with the ALAT inhibitor beta-chloro-alanine.

classification.rationale: Standard culture media nutrient abundance (glucose) and compensatory metabolic pathways (ALAT transamination) buffer against the metabolic and anti-proliferative effects of PDK inhibition, representing metabolic pathway buffering outside the taxonomy.

claims.author_explanation: Nov3r fails to elicit functional cellular anti-glycolytic and anti-proliferative activity because lipoamide-site inhibition yields sub-maximal (~60%) suppression of p(Ser293)E1alpha and PDK activity, whereas disruption of the glycolytic phenotype requires >88% biomarker ablation.

evidence.experiment: Concentration-dependent suppression of p(Ser293)E1alpha by Nov3r in PC-3 cells up to high concentrations.
evidence.result: Suppression plateaued at approximately 60% reduction, with no reduction in L-lactate or glucose uptake and no cytotoxicity up to 80 uM.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors demonstrated that Nov3r reaches a plateau at ~60% suppression of p(Ser293)E1alpha and sub-maximal PDK-1 inhibition in vitro, and showed that >88% reduction in phosphorylation is required to reduce L-lactate or glucose consumption.

classification.rationale: The lack of functional cellular anti-glycolytic and anti-proliferative activity is explained by sub-maximal (~60%) target/biomarker inhibition from allosteric lipoamide-site binding, whereas >88% ablation is required for phenotypic effect.

claims.author_explanation: Competition for pyruvate from lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), due to its cytoplasmic localization and frequent over-expression in cancer cells, may limit the amount of pyruvate available to the mitochondrial PDC even when PDC is fully activated by PDK inhibition.

evidence.experiment: Author hypothesis in Discussion citing literature on LDH-A overexpression in cancer.
evidence.result: States that cytoplasmic LDH competition for pyruvate may limit substrate availability for PDC even when fully dephosphorylated.

claims.grade_rationale: Proposed by the authors in the Discussion (citing reference [34]) as an additional explanation for why D-glucose depletion and near-complete (>88%) p(Ser293)E1alpha ablation are required to observe glycolytic inhibition; not directly tested with LDH perturbations in this study.

classification.rationale: The authors hypothesize that cytoplasmic LDH competes with the mitochondrial PDC complex for the substrate pyruvate, limiting metabolic flux even when PDK is inhibited; this metabolic pathway substrate diversion is untested here and outside the taxonomy.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free enzyme functional and binding potencies (DELFIA IC50, FP IC50, ITC Kd) and intact cellular target engagement IC50 values (Meso Scale Discovery ELISA measuring p(Ser293)E1alpha inhibition in PC-3 cells) for the small-molecule PDK inhibitors VER-246608 and Nov3r.

insights.text: VER-246608 is a potent ATP-competitive pan-isoform PDK inhibitor (biochemical IC50s 35-91 nM across PDK1-4) that engages intracellular PDK and suppresses PDC E1alpha phosphorylation in intact PC-3 cells (IC50 = 266 nM in 0% FCS).
Inclusion of 10% FCS causes an ~5.5-fold drop in cellular biomarker potency for VER-246608 (IC50 shifts from 266 nM in 0% FCS to 1.45 uM in 10% FCS).

Cellular anti-proliferative and anti-glycolytic effects of PDK inhibition require austere conditions (depletion of serum or glucose/glutamine) and an exceptionally high target inhibition threshold (>88% suppression of E1alpha phosphorylation).

Under nutrient-rich conditions, cancer cells buffer pyruvate loss through compensatory deamination of L-alanine via alanine aminotransferase (ALAT); co-inhibition of ALAT synergistically restores sensitivity to VER-246608.

The lipoamide-site inhibitor Nov3r binds PDK potently in vitro but achieves only sub-maximal (~60%) suppression of cellular E1alpha phosphorylation, failing to cross the threshold required for metabolic disruption or cytostasis.

review_notes: Table 1 lists p(Ser293)E1alpha (0% FCS) IC50 for Nov3r as 5 nM (n=3), whereas page 4 text quotes 55 nM for the same assay. The table value of 5 nM was preserved in the measurements table.

The analogue VER-246520 is mentioned in the main text (pages 5 and 7) as having comparable potency, but its numerical potency data are located in Supplementary Table S2, which was not included in the provided main PDF.

Sulforhodamine B cell mass determinations in Figure 4 and Supplementary Table S1 are reported as single-concentration percentages of control or condition shifts, rather than full fitted GI50/IC50 curves.

Other compounds mentioned in the paper lack paired biochemical and cellular potency data in the main PDF: VER-246520 (potency data in absent Supplementary Table S2), DCA (literature background only), Pfz3 (crystallization ligand only, page 11), VER-160364 (FP probe, Kd = 30 nM on PDK-1, page 11), and VER-246550 (40 uM lysis buffer additive, page 13).

claims.author_explanation: The reduced potency of ester 56 for the inhibition of EGFR phosphorylation (pIC50 5.3) and growth inhibition (pGI50 < 5.0) relative to its in vitro potency (pIC50 8.1) is likely a consequence of its increased reactivity and competitive reaction with glutathione in a cellular environment.

evidence.experiment: Author explanation of potency discrepancy citing literature on covalent warhead reactivity and competitive reaction with intracellular glutathione
evidence.result: Ester 56 loses 2.8 log units from cell-free EGFR binding (pIC50 8.1) to cellular pEGFR inhibition (pIC50 5.3)

claims.grade_rationale: Authors propose that high chemical reactivity towards intracellular nucleophiles (glutathione) reduces cellular potency relative to cell-free potency, citing literature on warhead reactivity and citing in vitro reaction profiles.

classification.rationale: The potency drop from cell-free to cellular assays for ester 56 is attributed to high chemical reactivity and competitive inactivation/conjugation with intracellular glutathione, which represents metabolic/chemical transformation in cells without direct experimental testing on 56 in the supplied evidence.

claims.author_explanation: Acrylate conjugate 53 achieves higher cellular antiproliferative activity (pGI50 5.3) compared to ester 56 (pGI50 < 5.0) in part due to reduced Michael acceptor reactivity from the 5FU beta-substituent, and also due to the intracellular addition-elimination release of cytotoxic 5FU upon covalent binding to EGFR.

evidence.experiment: Intact protein mass spectrometry after incubation of WT EGFR with compound 53
evidence.result: Observed adduct mass corresponding to initial adduct (+502 Da) and lower mass peak corresponding to loss of 5FU (+372 Da)

evidence.experiment: 19F NMR addition-elimination reaction of 53 with N-acetyl-L-cysteine methyl ester and glutathione
evidence.result: Rapid release of 5FU with t1/2 ca. 5 min and complete release within 1 h

evidence.experiment: A431 growth inhibition assay comparing compound 56 alone vs 56 combined with equimolar 5FU
evidence.result: Co-administration of 56 and 5FU increases potency to pGI50 6.2 mimicking the released cytotoxic effect

claims.grade_rationale: Authors support the hypothesis with mechanistic NMR thiol-addition elimination kinetics, mass spectrometry demonstrating covalent EGFR adduct formation and 5FU release for 53, media stability assays showing release is EGFR-dependent, and combination growth curves of inhibitor plus free 5FU.

classification.rationale: The enhanced cellular antiproliferative activity of conjugate 53 is explained by attenuated Michael acceptor reactivity (reducing off-target thiol inactivation) and target-mediated intracellular chemical cleavage/release of cytotoxic 5FU.

claims.author_explanation: Acrylamide conjugate 57 showed little inhibition of cellular EGFR phosphorylation (pIC50 5.6) and no antiproliferative effects (pGI50 < 5.0) despite biochemical EGFR inhibition (pIC50 7.3) and covalent adduct formation in vitro, which the authors discuss alongside its significantly slower retro-Michael release of 5FU compared to acrylate ester 53.

evidence.experiment: Intact protein mass spectrometry after incubation of WT EGFR with acrylamide 57
evidence.result: Demonstrated clear covalent adduct (+501 Da) with negligible release of 5FU (+371 Da), indicating a much slower retro-Michael addition than ester 53

evidence.experiment: 19F NMR reaction of acrylamide 57 with N-acetyl cysteine
evidence.result: No evidence of 5FU release even after 24 h, in contrast to complete release within 1 h for acrylate 53

claims.grade_rationale: Authors perform intact-protein mass spectrometry and 19F NMR thiol-reaction experiments on 57 showing covalent EGFR adduct formation with negligible 5FU elimination compared to acrylate ester 53, linking warhead electronics (amide vs ester) to payload release and cellular activity.

classification.rationale: The lack of cellular antiproliferative activity for acrylamide 57 compared to acrylate 53 is linked to its failure to undergo retro-Michael elimination and release active 5FU after covalent adduct formation, supported by MS and NMR reaction studies.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free biochemical potencies (WT EGFR pIC50 by TR-FRET) and cellular potencies (inhibition of pEGFR by HTRF and antiproliferative pGI50 in A431 cells) for compounds 2 (dacomitinib), 53, 56, and 57.

insights.text: Appending 5-fluorouracil as a leaving group to the beta-position of an acrylate ester warhead (compound 53) allows covalent binding to wild-type EGFR with concomitant release of the cytotoxic payload via an addition-elimination mechanism.

The release of the cytotoxic payload upon cysteine addition depends strongly on the electronics and geometry of the Michael acceptor: acrylate esters (53) undergo rapid elimination, whereas acrylamides (57) form stable adducts without significant payload release.

Acrylate ester 56 exhibits high biochemical potency against EGFR (pIC50 8.1) but markedly reduced cellular potency (pEGFR pIC50 5.3), attributed to high reactivity and competitive scavenging by intracellular thiols such as glutathione.

Conjugate 53 maintains cellular EGFR target engagement (pEGFR pIC50 7.8) and translates into increased antiproliferative activity (pGI50 5.3) compared to ester 56 (pGI50 <5.0), consistent with combined EGFR inhibition and intracellular 5FU release.

review_notes: Table S1 in the Supporting Information was mentioned in the main text as reporting potent EGFR inhibition for compounds 49-51, but the SI PDF was not provided. Compounds 49-51 lacked paired cellular data in the main text.

Potency values are reported as negative logarithm molar values (pIC50, pGI50). All numerical values, inequalities, and standard deviations were extracted verbatim from Figure 5 labels and the associated text.
Compound 56 and compound 57 had censored pGI50 values (<5.0) in the 72 h A431 cell growth assay.

Verified all paired compounds (2, 53, 56, 57), measurements, claims, and interventions against the PDF text and inspected figures (Figures 5 and 6). Fixed source reference in eligibility and added coverage and intervention records for completeness.

evidence.result: BAY-405 kinase inhibition shifted from IC50 = 11 nM (at 10 uM ATP) to IC50 = 56 nM (at 1 mM ATP), confirming ATP competition.

evidence.experiment: Co-crystal structure determination of BAY-405 in complex with MAP4K1 kinase domain
evidence.result: X-ray crystallography confirmed BAY-405 binds directly to the ATP binding site in an ATP-competitive manner.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3. The authors tested the ATP competition hypothesis directly for lead compound BAY-405 by measuring kinase inhibition at low (10 uM) and high (1 mM) ATP concentrations, observing an IC50 shift from 11 nM to 56 nM, and validating an ATP-competitive binding mode by X-ray crystallography, confirming ATP competition contributes to potency shifts, although this was not a cellular rescue experiment.

classification.rationale: The discrepancy between biochemical binding and cellular potency is attributed to competition with high physiological intracellular ATP, supported by enzymatic assays at low vs high ATP and X-ray crystallography.

claims.author_explanation: The discrepancy between biochemical and cellular IC50 is partially attributed to the potential impact of protein binding in the assay medium (1% FCS) for this lipophilic chemical series.

evidence.experiment: Equilibrium dialysis plasma protein binding assay for BAY-405 across multiple species
evidence.result: Unbound fraction (f_unbound) was 3.49% (human), 1.39% (mouse), 2.52% (rat), and 0.75% (dog), demonstrating high protein binding.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3. The authors hypothesize that serum protein binding in the cell assay medium reduces free compound concentration, supporting this with equilibrium dialysis plasma protein binding measurements for BAY-405 (f_unbound = 3.49% in human, 1.39% in mouse), though no varying-serum rescue experiments were conducted in the cellular assay.

classification.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
classification.rationale: The biochemical-to-cellular potency shift is partially attributed to high protein binding in the assay medium (1% FCS) due to the lipophilic nature of the chemical series, supported by equilibrium dialysis plasma protein binding measurements.

eligibility.reason: The manuscript reports quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (MAP4K1 binding competition IC50 and enzymatic kinase IC50) and quantitative cellular potency (inhibition of pSLP76 phosphorylation in Jurkat cells and human primary PBMCs) across a series of azaindole derivatives.

insights.text: Azaindole MAP4K1 inhibitors demonstrate a consistent ~100-fold drop from cell-free binding affinity (low nM) to intracellular pSLP76 target engagement (submicromolar to low micromolar).
The authors attribute this potency drop primarily to physiological ATP competition in intact cells and serum protein binding in the cell culture medium.
Kinase assays at 10 uM versus 1 mM ATP verified that BAY-405 is an ATP-competitive active site inhibitor, with IC50 increasing from 11 nM to 56 nM at high ATP.
High plasma protein binding was confirmed across preclinical species (e.g., human f_unbound = 3.49%), consistent with reduced free drug exposure in serum-containing assays.

review_notes: Compound 36 in Table 6 was excluded because its cellular pSLP76 IC50 was not determined (n.d.).
Compounds 2-10 and 12 in Tables 1-2 were excluded because no cellular IC50 was reported for them in the main text tables.

For compound 30, identical cellular pSLP76 IC50 values (1.02 µM) were reported in Table 5 (Jurkat cells) and Table 6 (PBMCs); both have been recorded to reflect the distinct assay assignments given in the respective table footnotes.

Added high-ATP (1 mM) biochemical kinase IC50 (56 nM) for BAY-405 (38), phenotypic PBMC IFN-gamma EC50 values (212 nM with PGE2, 111 nM with TGF-beta) from Figure 4B/C, corresponding pairs, and the ATP-shift assay-condition intervention exploring the biochemical-to-cellular potency dropoff.

claims.author_explanation: Compounds in the initial series bearing highly basic amine substituents (calculated pKa > 10) and polar pyrazine head-groups suffered from poor membrane permeability (MDCK Papp = 0.4-2.7 x 10^-6 cm/s), limiting their cellular activity. Reducing head-group polarity (5 to 6) and attenuating amine pKa and lipophilicity via beta-oxygen inductive effects (such as the 5-amino-1,3-dioxanyl moiety in 11 and 12) improved permeability and cellular potency.

evidence.experiment: MDCK apparent permeability (Papp, A-to-B flux at 10 uM) and cellular pMEK IC50 across compounds with high vs lowered pKa
evidence.result: Compounds with high pKa (>10) showed poor permeability (Papp = 0.4 - 2.7 x 10^-6 cm/s), whereas introducing lower-pKa groups such as the 5-amino-1,3-dioxane (12) improved Papp to 2.4 x 10^-6 cm/s and pMEK IC50 to 69 nM.

evidence.experiment: N-methylation of the primary amine in compound 12 to give compound 13 to reduce H-bond donors and further increase permeability
evidence.result: N-methylation (13) did not improve permeability (MDCK Papp decreased from 2.4 to 0.4 x 10^-6 cm/s) and gave similar cellular potency (pMEK IC50 = 57 nM vs 69 nM for 12, with Ki = 1.9 nM vs 3.7 nM).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured transcellular permeability (MDCK Papp) across compounds alongside calculated pKa and observed that lowering basicity while maintaining or improving Papp corresponded with improved cellular activity (pMEK IC50). However, no causal rescue intervention (e.g., permeabilizing cells or efflux transporter modulation) was conducted to isolate permeability directly; this represents correlative SAR and in vitro permeability measurements.

classification.rationale: The limited cellular activity of initial compounds is explicitly attributed to poor membrane permeability (measured by MDCK Papp) driven by high amine basicity (pKa > 10) and polarity, which improved upon lowering pKa.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched molecular pair differing only by a single ring nitrogen in the R3 head-group (pyrazine in 5 vs pyridine in 6); biochemical Ki remained equipotent (1.9 vs 2.1 nM) while MDCK Papp increased from 0.4 to 1.2 x 10^-6 cm/s and cellular pMEK IC50 improved from 124 nM to 45 nM.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 5, 8, and 9 share R1 = Et and R3 = 5-methylpyrazin-2-yl; removing the basic amine markedly increased MDCK Papp (from 0.4 to 21.0 and 10.6 x 10^-6 cm/s) but severely compromised PAK1 biochemical binding (Ki = 64 and 66 nM) and cellular potency (IC50 = 980 and 813 nM).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched molecular pair sharing R1 = Me and R3 = 5-methylpyrazin-2-yl; lowering cpKa from 10.4 (7) to 6.9 (10) improved MDCK Papp from 0.4 to 3.5 x 10^-6 cm/s, though weaker biochemical potency (Ki = 19 nM vs 7.4 nM) resulted in weak cellular potency (pMEK IC50 = 399 nM).
interventions.description: Analogue comparison replacing the basic (trans-4-aminocyclohexyl)methyl R2 group of compound 7 with a lower-pKa (morpholin-2-yl)methyl extension in compound 10.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Exact matched pair sharing R1 = Et and R3 = 5-methylpyrazin-2-yl; introducing the two ring oxygens lowered cpKa from 10.4 to 7.7 and cLogP from 4.5 to 2.4, improving MDCK Papp from 0.4 to 1.7 x 10^-6 cm/s and narrowing the biochemical-to-cellular gap (Ki = 8.0 nM, pMEK IC50 = 148 nM).
interventions.description: Analogue comparison replacing the basic (trans-4-aminocyclohexyl)methyl R2 moiety of compound 5 with a (cis-5-amino-1,3-dioxan-2-yl)methyl moiety in compound 11 to attenuate pKa and cLogP via beta-oxygen inductive effects.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Author-described optimization step combining the low-pKa dioxane R2 motif of 11 with the less polar methylpyridine R3 head-group and 2-MeNH R1 group, improving MDCK Papp from 1.7 to 2.4 x 10^-6 cm/s, biochemical Ki from 8.0 to 3.7 nM, and cellular pMEK IC50 from 148 to 69 nM. insights.text: Highly basic amine extensions designed to engage ribose-pocket Asp/Asn residues caused low cellular permeability (MDCK Papp around 1-2 x 10^-6 cm/s) and high hERG channel inhibition.
Completely removing the basic amine moiety abolished biochemical potency by over an order of magnitude (compounds 8 and 9 vs 5 and 6), demonstrating its essential role in binding.

Incorporating an atypical 5-amino-1,3-dioxanyl group reduced amine basicity via beta-oxygen inductive effects while retaining key hydrogen-bonding interactions, resulting in balanced cellular biomarker activity and reduced off-target liabilities.

review_notes: Figure 3A reports kinase selectivity profiling of compound 12 against 235 kinases with IC50 values against 7 other kinases, but compound 12 was already fully paired with PAK1 biochemical and cellular data.

Figure 4 and Figure 5 report mouse in vivo PK and PD (pMEK suppression in H292 NSCLC xenografts) for compound 12; in vivo efficacy data do not constitute concentration-based in vitro cellular potencies.

Verified all 14 paired compounds across Tables 1 and 2 against the page images, corrected R-group structural descriptions (including pyrazine vs pyridine R3 assignments in 7-11 and R2 substituent identities in 1, 5-15), and added all author-discussed chemical modification interventions exploring permeability and pKa (5->6, 5->8/9, 7->10, 5->11, 11->12, 7->12, and 12->13).

claims.author_explanation: DT2216 binds BCL-2 with high affinity in cell-free assays but cannot induce BCL-2 degradation or efficiently kill BCL-2-dependent RS4;11 cells because it cannot form stable {BCL-2:DT2216:VCB} ternary complexes in live cells.

evidence.experiment: Live-cell NanoBRET assay measuring BCL-2:VCB ternary complex formation in 293T cells.
evidence.result: DT2216 failed to produce a NanoBRET signal between BCL-2 and VCB in live cells.

evidence.experiment: Western blotting of BCL-2 protein levels after DT2216 treatment in RS4;11 and MOLT-4 cells.
evidence.result: DT2216 did not induce degradation of BCL-2 in cells.

evidence.result: Pre-treatment with VHL-032 caused no significant IC50 change for DT2216 in RS4;11 cells (212 ± 27.4 nM vs 326 ± 11 nM), confirming lack of functional VHL-dependent ternary complex activity against BCL-2 in live cells.

claims.grade_rationale: Authors demonstrated high cell-free BCL-2 binding (Table 2) and in vitro AlphaLISA ternary complex formation, but absence of live-cell ternary complex by NanoBRET assay (Figure 4E), lack of BCL-2 degradation by Western blot (Figure 2), and absence of VHL-032 competition effect on RS4;11 viability (Figure 5A).

classification.rationale: Failure of a PROTAC to form a stable intracellular ternary complex with the target and E3 ligase in live cells is outside the specific taxonomy categories.

claims.author_explanation: Tethering the linker from the cyclohexenyl methyl group enables formation of stable {BCL-2:PROTAC:VCB} ternary complexes in live cells, which enhances BCL-2 inhibition without degradation and leads to potent RS4;11 cell killing in an E3 ligase-dependent manner.

evidence.experiment: NanoBRET assay in live 293T cells expressing HiBit-BCL-2, LgBit, and HaloTag-VHL.
evidence.result: PZ703b generated prominent dose-dependent BRET signals reflecting stable ternary complex formation in live cells.

evidence.experiment: RS4;11 cell viability assay with PZ703b in the presence or absence of 10 uM VHL ligand VHL-032.
evidence.result: Co-treatment with VHL-032 caused a 20-fold activity loss for PZ703b (IC50 shifted from 11.3 nM to 209 nM).

evidence.experiment: Co-immunoprecipitation of BCL-2 and Bim in RS4;11 cells treated with PZ703b with or without VHL-032.
evidence.result: PZ703b disrupted BCL-2:Bim interaction, and pre-treatment with VHL-032 blocked this disruption, confirming VHL engagement is required for cellular BCL-2 inhibition.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors demonstrated live-cell ternary complex formation by NanoBRET (Figure 4E), disruption of BCL-2:Bim interaction by co-IP (Figure 5B), and causal rescue/loss of potency upon pharmacological intervention by competing VHL binding with VHL-032 (Figure 5A, 5C), which shifted PZ703b IC50 by ~20-fold and blocked BCL-2:Bim disruption.

classification.rationale: Enhancement of cellular potency via intracellular PROTAC-mediated ternary complex formation with an E3 ligase is outside the specific taxonomy categories.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports cell-free AlphaScreen displacement binding affinities (Kd/Ki) against BCL-XL and BCL-2 (both with and without VHL/VCB) alongside cell viability IC50 values (in MOLT-4, RS4;11, and human platelets) and cellular degradation DC50 values for ABT-263, DT2216, PZ703a, and PZ703b.

insights.text: Tethering the VHL E3 ligase ligand to the pro-R methyl group on the cyclohexene core of ABT-263 generated PZ703b, which maintains potent BCL-XL degradation (DC50 14.3 nM) while potently inhibiting BCL-2 without degrading it.

Cell-free binary binding affinities to BCL-2 do not predict cellular activity: DT2216, PZ703a, and PZ703b possess similar BCL-2 Kd values (1.2-2.3 nM), but PZ703b is 19-fold and 37-fold more potent than DT2216 and PZ703a in killing BCL-2-dependent RS4;11 cells.
NanoBRET and co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that enhanced BCL-2 inhibition by PZ703b requires formation of a stable {BCL-2:PROTAC:VCB} ternary complex in live cells.

Pharmacological competition with excess free VHL ligand (VHL-032) shifts PZ703b cellular potency in RS4;11 cells from 11.3 nM to 209 nM and blocks BCL-2:Bim disruption, proving that VHL recruitment causally enhances intracellular BCL-2 inhibition.

PZ703b preserves platelet-sparing selectivity (platelet IC50 0.96 uM vs MOLT-4 IC50 15.9 nM, ~100-fold difference) due to low platelet VHL expression, avoiding thrombocytopenia typical of parent warhead ABT-263.

review_notes: Table 1 tests 13 compounds, but only ABT-263, DT2216, PZ703a, and PZ703b were profiled in cell-free binding assays in Table 2.
Table 2 reports displacement binding data as Kd values; methods describe them as Ki values fitted from competitive displacement AlphaScreen.
Figure 5A reports additional IC50 values in RS4;11 cells under VHL-032 competition: DT2216 (326 ± 11 nM), PZ703a (1041 ± 38 nM), and PZ703b (209 ± 17.6 nM).
PZ703b-NC (negative control epimer on the VHL hydroxyproline) showed negligible activity in cells and was excluded from pairs due to absent cell-free binding values in Table 2.

Verified all paired compounds (ABT-263, DT2216, PZ703a, PZ703b), added missing source src_fig5_c, extracted the quantitative VHL-032 competition cellular IC50 measurements from Figure 5A (m_dt2216_rs411_vhl032_ic50, m_pz703a_rs411_vhl032_ic50, m_pz703b_rs411_vhl032_ic50), linked before/after intervention IDs, and added interventions covering the linker attachment site redesign (DT2216 vs PZ703b) and stereochemical configuration (PZ703a vs PZ703b in RS4;11).

claims.author_explanation: Cellular activities in the NanoBRET assay were on average an order of magnitude lower than biochemical potencies, but correlated well with TR-FRET biochemical potency, consistent with most benzimidazolones having high cell permeability (PAMPA > 20 x 10^-6 cm/s) and solubility.

evidence.experiment: Correlation analysis of TR-FRET biochemical IC50 versus NanoBRET cellular IC50 across n=175 benzimidazolone analogues.
evidence.result: A linear correlation (R2=0.62, n=175) was observed, with cellular activities consistently positioned above the unity line, indicating cellular potencies were on average an order of magnitude lower than biochemical potencies.

evidence.experiment: PAMPA permeability assay at pH 7.4.
evidence.result: Compounds 36, 37, and 27 showed PAMPA permeability values of 48, 6, and 19 x 10^-6 cm/s, respectively; 75% of benzimidazolones displayed PAMPA permeability > 20 x 10^-6 cm/s.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors observe an ~1-order of magnitude shift between biochemical (TR-FRET) and cellular (NanoBRET) potency across the chemical series (Figure 7D, n=175) and report passive permeability (PAMPA) and solubility measurements that correlate with cellular entry, but do not perform a causal rescue test (e.g. efflux inhibition or permeabilization). This corresponds to a mechanistic measurement/association (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: The authors evaluate passive membrane permeability (PAMPA) and solubility to explain the relationship between biochemical and cellular potency.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free biochemical potency (TR-FRET IC50) and cellular potency (NanoBRET IC50 and InCELL Hunter EC50) for the same benzimidazolone compounds (compounds 36, 37, and 27) in Table 1 and Figure 6B.

insights.text: Cellular potency in the full-length BCL6/SMRT NanoBRET assay was consistently approximately one order of magnitude lower than biochemical TR-FRET potency across 175 benzimidazolone analogues.

The orientation and placement of protein tags substantially affected cellular PPI assay sensitivity: tagging BCL6 C-terminally with NanoLuc and SMRT C-terminally with HaloTag yielded robust concentration responses, whereas N-terminal HaloTagging of BCL6 showed minimal inhibition.

Cellular target engagement was verified early using an InCELL Hunter assay with a truncated BCL6 BTB domain (residues 14-135), whereas full-length BTB domain (residues 1-135) failed to generate an assay window.

review_notes: Only compounds 27, 36, and 37 have fully tabulated quantitative biochemical and cellular potencies in the main text (Table 1). Additional analogues mentioned in Figure 7D (n=175) and Table S3 are located in the Supplementary Information, which is not part of the primary PDF.

Compound 25 has biochemical potency reported in the text (TR-FRET IC50 = 2.1 ± 0.1 µM) and was tested in InCELL Hunter at a single concentration (30 µM, Figure 6A), but lacks a quantitative cellular EC50/IC50 value, so it was excluded from paired compounds.

claims.author_explanation: Introducing polarity at R4 to eliminate hPXR activation (such as the cyanopyrimidine heterocycle in 10 or hydroxyl group in 9) decreased overall permeability, increased the efflux ratio, or led to poor cellular potency despite potent enzymatic inhibition.

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 cell permeability assay measuring Papp [A-B] and Papp [B-A] to calculate efflux ratio, alongside cell-free enzymatic IC50 and HT1080 cellular 2-HG IC50.
evidence.result: Compound 9 showed decreased Papp (1.9 x 10^-6 cm/s) and increased efflux ratio (26) compared to AGI-14100 (Papp 14.2 x 10^-6 cm/s, efflux ratio 2.3); compound 10 had a ~42-fold weaker cellular potency (297 nM) relative to enzymatic potency (7 nM); compound 11 showed very low Papp (0.19 x 10^-6 cm/s) and very high efflux ratio (129). AG-120 restored high permeability (15 x 10^-6 cm/s) and low efflux ratio (2), maintaining 8 nM cellular IC50.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured both Caco-2 permeability (Papp) and efflux ratios alongside enzymatic and cellular IC50 values across an SAR series, showing clear association between increased polarity/efflux and cellular potency drop (e.g. compound 10: Enz IC50 7 nM vs Cell IC50 297 nM). However, no rescue experiment with an efflux inhibitor was performed.

classification.rationale: Both decreased passive permeability (Papp) and increased active efflux (efflux ratio) are co-equally supported by Caco-2 data to explain the cellular potency drop.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 10, 11, and AG-120 share the core scaffold and were directly designed in parallel/series to address the same polarity, permeability, and hPXR liabilities.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison: Replacing one of the C-F bonds at R3 with an embedded nitrogen atom in the ring (AG-120) instead of modifying R4 with highly polar groups (compound 10), or appending sulfonamide (compound 11), to balance low hPXR activation with high permeability, low efflux ratio, and balanced enzymatic and cellular potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 9 and 10 are matched molecular pair analogues differing only by a CH-to-N substitution in the R4 heteroaryl ring (cyanopyridine vs cyanopyrimidine).
interventions.description: Analogue comparison: Transitioning from the cyanopyridine heterocycle in 9 to the more polar cyanopyrimidine heterocycle in 10 at R4 to abolish hPXR activation resulted in a marked loss of cellular potency (from 1 nM to 297 nM) despite maintaining enzymatic potency (10 nM vs 7 nM).

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compound 11 and AG-120 share the identical core and R4 substituent, differing only at the R3 aromatic ring modification used to tune polarity, permeability, and efflux.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison: Replacing the polar R3 sulfonamide-substituted phenyl ring in compound 11 with a 2-fluoropyridin-3-yl ring in AG-120 reduced tPSA (from 166.0 to 118.2 A^2), restored Caco-2 permeability (Papp from 0.19 to 15 x 10^-6 cm/s), and eliminated high efflux (efflux ratio from 129 to 2) while maintaining potent enzymatic (11 nM vs 12 nM) and cellular (13 nM vs 8 nM) activity.

insights.text: Introduction of excessive polarity at R4 to eliminate hPXR activation (such as the cyanopyrimidine heterocycle in 10) significantly degraded cellular potency relative to enzymatic potency, coinciding with reduced permeability.

Modifying R3 by incorporating a nitrogen atom directly into the aromatic ring (pyridine in AG-120) maintained single-digit nanomolar enzymatic and cellular potency while simultaneously achieving high permeability and a low efflux ratio.
AG-120 demonstrates consistent single-digit to low double-digit nanomolar potency against both recombinant mutant IDH1 enzymes and endogenous mutant IDH1 across diverse tumor cell lines.

review_notes: Compound 5 from Table 1 had Cell IC50 recorded as 'ND' and was excluded from the paired compound dataset as required by scope instructions.
Table 1 and Table 2 both list AGI-14100 with the same potency values (Enz IC50 = 6 nM, Cell IC50 = 1 nM); these were consolidated into a single compound record referencing both tables.

Primary cellular IC50 in Table 1 and Table 2 was assayed using the HT1080 cell line endogenously expressing mIDH1-R132C, while biochemical IC50 was assessed against mIDH1-R132H homodimer; authors note R132H and R132C have equivalent inhibitor sensitivity, confirmed by AG-120 profiling in Table 3.
No explicit SMILES strings were provided in the text; provided_smiles is therefore left null for all compounds.

Verified all compounds in Tables 1-3, structure notes for AG-120, and added matched analogue interventions (9 to 10 and 11 to AG-120) documenting how polarity, permeability, and efflux changes across R3 and R4 explored and resolved the cellular potency dropoff.

claims.author_explanation: The disparity between biochemical and cellular activities for early phenylalanine amide analogues (such as 4g) was attributed to an ATP-competitive inhibition mode: because intracellular ATP levels (~millimolar) are much higher than the 500 uM ATP used in the cell-free assay, cellular potency was compromised. Switching to an ATP-uncompetitive inhibition mode (as observed in 6d) eliminated this competition and significantly improved cellular activity.

evidence.experiment: Steady-state kinetic studies of 4g and 6d assessing inhibition mode with respect to ATP concentration.
evidence.result: Compound 4g was confirmed to be ATP-competitive and suffered an apparent >17-fold drop from biochemical IC50 (0.36 uM) to SKOV-3 cellular IC50 (6.2 uM). In contrast, 6d was uncompetitive with ATP and exhibited an SKOV-3 IC50 of 0.094 uM close to its biochemical IC50 of 0.022 uM.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors conducted detailed mechanistic steady-state kinetic experiments demonstrating that 4g is ATP-competitive whereas 6d is ATP-uncompetitive, correlating directly with the retention of cellular potency for 6d. However, no controlled causal rescue directly altering intracellular ATP levels was performed in the cellular assay; the evidence relies on mechanistic kinetic characterization coupled with analogue comparison.

classification.rationale: The biochemical-to-cellular potency drop is explained and kinetically supported by competition with high intracellular ATP concentrations for ATP-competitive vs uncompetitive inhibitors.

claims.author_explanation: Reasoning that the lack of cellular activity of the initial benzoic acid fragment hit 2 (CENP-E IC50 = 6.7 uM, no detectable cellular effect at 40 uM) might be due to poor membrane permeability related to the presence of the negatively charged carboxylate group, the authors replaced the carboxylate with neutral amide derivatives (such as phenylalaninamide 3g).

evidence.experiment: Replacement of the carboxylic acid of hit 2 with amino acid amide derivatives (e.g., 3g) to address hypothesized poor carboxylate permeability.
evidence.result: Phenylalanine methylamide 3g maintained biochemical potency (CENP-E IC50 = 6.5 uM, similar to 2 at 6.7 uM; carboxylic acid analogue 3k was 10-fold weaker at 61 uM), but 3g still showed no measurable antiproliferative activity in SKOV-3 cells at 25 uM (IC50 > 25 uM).

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 1: The authors state a medicinal chemistry hypothesis attributing the lack of cellular activity of carboxylic acid 2 to poor permeability of the carboxylate moiety. No membrane permeability measurements are reported, and simple replacement of the carboxylate with a methylamide (3g) retained biochemical potency (6.5 uM) but did not yet achieve measurable cellular potency (SKOV-3 IC50 > 25 uM) until further side-chain optimization.

classification.rationale: Authors hypothesized that poor membrane permeability of the negatively charged carboxylate caused the lack of cellular activity, though neutral amide replacement alone was inconclusive.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Table 4 directly compares C-terminal modifications starting from lead amide 4l to narrow the 10-100-fold biochemical-to-cellular potency differential; 6d shares the core scaffold and 4-tert-butylimidazol-2-yl side chain (with imidazole N-Me) and was tested in identical CENP-E and SKOV-3 assays.

interventions.description: Matched one-carbon homologation of the C-terminal group from hydroxymethyl (6b) to hydroxyethyl (6d) on the identical N-methyl-4-tert-butylimidazol-2-yl scaffold (6), which improved SKOV-3 cellular potency >11-fold (from 1.1 uM to 0.094 uM) with only a ~2-fold change in biochemical IC50 (from 0.043 uM to 0.022 uM).

interventions.description: Reduction of the C-terminal N-methylamide of 4l (R1 = CONHCH3, R2 = H) to a hydroxymethyl group in 6a (R1 = CH2OH, R2 = H) as part of C-terminal exploration to narrow the biochemical-to-cellular potency differential, yielding modest improvements in both biochemical (0.19 to 0.056 uM) and cellular (4.4 to 2.7 uM) potency.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative biochemical IC50/Ki values against human CENP-E ATPase activity alongside quantitative cellular antiproliferative IC50 values (in SKOV-3 and Colo205 cell lines) across multiple matched small-molecule analogues including 4g, 6d, and clinical candidate GSK923295 (1).

insights.text: The disparity between cell-free and cellular potencies observed for initial phenylalanine amide analogues was traced to their ATP-competitive mode of inhibition, as intracellular ATP concentrations (~millimolar) greatly exceed the 500 uM ATP used in the biochemical assay.

Modifying the C-terminus to a hydroxyethyl group (as in 6d) altered the kinetic mechanism to ATP-uncompetitive, successfully mitigating intracellular ATP competition and bridging the gap between biochemical and cellular potency.

Binding to CENP-E exhibits strict stereochemical bias: the (S)-enantiomer 5a was >400-fold more active than (R)-enantiomer 5b in the cell-free assay, and only 5a induced the characteristic mitotic spindle misalignment phenotype in cells, confirming on-target mechanism.

The optimized clinical candidate GSK923295 (1) is an uncompetitive inhibitor with respect to both ATP and microtubules, achieving nanomolar potency in cell-free Ki and in tumor cell line antiproliferation.

review_notes: Fragment hit 2 was reported on page 1 with a biochemical IC50 of 6.7 uM and 'no detectable cellular effect at 40 uM', but the specific cellular assay/cell line was not identified in the text, so 2 was excluded from the paired dataset.
Table 1 compounds 3a-3f and 3h-3k were excluded because only cell-free CENP-E IC50 values were measured; compound 3g was retained because its cellular potency is reported in Table 2.
Compound 4l is reported in both Table 2 and Table 4 with identical potencies (0.19 uM biochemical, 4.4 uM cellular) and is linked to both table sources in a single measurement record.
No machine-readable SMILES were supplied in the PDF; structure representations rely on image and fragment tables.

Added claim_carboxylate_permeability (Grade 1) capturing the authors' initial hypothesis on page 2 that poor permeability of the carboxylate moiety in fragment hit 2 caused its lack of cellular activity, leading to synthesis of neutral phenylalaninamide analogues such as 3g.

Expanded interventions for claim_atp_competition to include the Table 4 C-terminal modification series (4l -> 6a, 4l -> 6d, and the matched homologation pair 6b -> 6d) alongside the mechanistic kinetic pair 4g -> 6d.

claims.author_explanation: Macrocyclic peptide 1 contains the negatively charged ETGE motif (-3 overall charge at physiological pH) and lacks a cell-penetrating motif, resulting in poor membrane permeability, endosomal entrapment, and weak cytosolic delivery, which severely limits its potency in activating Nrf2 in cellular assays.

evidence.experiment: Literature assessment of cyclic peptidyl Keap1 inhibitors containing the E-T-G-E motif
evidence.result: Peptides containing the E-T-G-E motif carry a -3 net charge and are generally impermeable to mammalian cell membranes.

evidence.experiment: Live-cell confocal microscopy of HeLa cells treated with 5 µM fluorescein-labeled peptide 1 or 2 for 2 h
evidence.result: Cells treated with peptide 1 showed weak punctate fluorescence trapped in endosomal/lysosomal compartments, whereas peptide 2 showed strong diffuse cytoplasmic fluorescence.

evidence.experiment: Naphthofluorescein (NF) pH-sensitive dye flow cytometry in HeLa cells after 2 h incubation in 10% FBS
evidence.result: Peptide 1 gave an MFI of only 10% relative to CPP9, whereas peptide 2 gave 980%, representing a 98-fold improvement in cytosolic delivery upon CPP9 conjugation.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of Nrf2-driven luciferase reporter activation and endogenous Nrf2/HO-1 protein induction between peptide 1 and CPP9-conjugated peptide 2
evidence.result: Peptide 2 achieved an EC50 of ~1.1 µM in the ARE-luciferase reporter assay (and 4-fold Nrf2/7-fold HO-1 induction at 3 µM), whereas peptide 1 exhibited EC50 > 10 µM.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly measured cellular uptake and cytosolic entry using live-cell confocal microscopy and a pH-sensitive naphthofluorescein flow cytometry assay, demonstrating a 98-fold difference in cytosolic entry between peptide 1 and peptide 2. Furthermore, conjugating peptide 1 to the cyclic CPP motif rescued cellular potency (EC50 improved from >10 µM to ~1.1 µM) despite a modest reduction in cell-free Keap1 binding affinity. Controlled causal rescue and direct mechanistic delivery quantification support grade 4.

classification.rationale: Poor cell membrane permeability and weak cytosolic entry (due to negative charge and endosomal trapping) are directly measured and shown to limit cellular potency.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports cell-free Keap1 binding potencies (fluorescence polarization competition IC50 and direct binding KD) and cellular Nrf2 activation potencies (ARE-HepG2 luciferase reporter EC50) for the macrocyclic peptide 1 and its cyclic CPP conjugate peptide 2.

insights.text: Conjugation of a cyclic cell-penetrating peptide (CPP9) to the impermeable cyclic peptide 1 via a flexible linker increased cytosolic entry efficiency by 98-fold and translated an in vitro binder into a micromolar cellular activator of Nrf2.

Although CPP9 conjugation caused an ~8-fold reduction in cell-free Keap1 competition binding affinity (IC50 19 nM to 153 nM), it enabled cellular activation (EC50 ~1.1 µM vs >10 µM for the unconjugated peptide).
Intracellular target engagement was further corroborated downstream by dose-dependent accumulation of Nrf2 and transcriptional induction of HO-1 protein in HEK293T cells.

review_notes: No explicit machine-readable SMILES strings were supplied in the manuscript; structures are defined via chemical drawings in Scheme 1.
Biochemical direct KD was determined using fluorescein-labeled peptides (FAM-peptide 1 and FITC-peptide 2), whereas competition IC50 values were obtained with unlabeled peptides 1 and 2.
Cellular luciferase reporter assay EC50 for peptide 1 was right-censored at >10 µM due to low induction at up to 5 µM.
Cytosolic entry was independently quantitated by pH-sensitive naphthofluorescein flow cytometry (MFI: peptide 1 = 10%, peptide 2 = 980% relative to CPP9).

claims.author_explanation: The authors hypothesize that active transporter efflux (e.g., MDR1/P-gp and BCRP), membrane permeability, or other cellular mechanisms may influence intracellular concentrations or the ternary PRMT5+MTA complex in cells, leading to a substantial loss of cellular viability potency relative to biochemical potency.

evidence.experiment: MDCKII-MDR1 and MDCKII-BCRP transwell permeability and efflux ratio assays for AM-9959, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11
evidence.result: AM-9959 showed poor A-B Papp (0.3 and 1.2 μcm/s) and high efflux ratios (132 and 21), whereas replacing the 1°-amide with EWG and pyridine in 11 improved Papp (6 and 18 μcm/s) and reduced efflux (8 and 1).

evidence.experiment: Comparison between biochemical MTase-Glo potency and HCT116 cell viability potency for compound 11
evidence.result: Compound 11 was 100-fold less potent in cell viability (IC50 = 3.2 μM) than in biochemical MTA+ assay (<35 nM), despite having improved permeability and reduced efflux in MDCKII cells, indicating other transporters, permeability, or intracellular mechanisms may influence cellular potency.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors measured MDCKII-MDR1 and MDCKII-BCRP permeability and efflux ratios for multiple analogues and showed that EWG replacements reduced efflux in 11. However, 11 still exhibited poor cellular potency, and the authors did not perform a controlled causal rescue (such as testing cell viability in the presence and absence of an efflux pump inhibitor).

classification.rationale: Authors invoke multiple mechanisms (active transporter efflux, membrane permeability, and intracellular ternary complex factors), and reducing efflux/improving permeability in MDCKII assays failed to rescue cellular potency.

claims.author_explanation: The authors hypothesize that introducing small alkyl substituents into the quinolin-2-amine RHS pocket establishes favorable hydrophobic interactions predicted by energy-grid modeling, thereby enhancing cellular inhibitory potency to below 1 μM.

evidence.experiment: Energy-grid docking modeling followed by a methyl scan of the RHS quinolin-2-amine core (positions 3, 4, 5, 7, 8) and evaluation in HCT116 viability
evidence.result: Methyl substitution at position 4 (12, IC50 = 320 nM) or position 3 (AM-9934, IC50 = 290 nM) improved cellular potency below 1 μM compared to the parent des-methyl analogue 11 (3200 nM), while 5-, 7-, and 8-methyl analogues remained >5 μM.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free PRMT5 methyltransferase inhibition (MTase-Glo IC50) and cellular viability inhibition (CellTiter-Glo IC50 in HCT116 MTAP-del and MTAP-WT cells) for the same series of quinolin-2-amine PRMT5 inhibitors (compounds 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, and AM-9934).

insights.text: Early quinolin-2-amine lead AM-9959 exhibited significant efflux by MDR1 and BCRP in MDCKII transwell assays, which was ameliorated by replacing the primary carboxamide with electron-withdrawing groups such as trifluoromethyl-pyridinyl.

Despite achieving biochemical MTA+ IC50 values below the 35 nM assay detection limit and eliminating transporter efflux in compound 11, cellular viability potency remained modest (~3.2 μM), indicating that cell permeability or unmeasured intracellular factors dampened cellular translation.

Computational energy-grid mapping of the PRMT5:MTA binding pocket guided the introduction of 3- or 4-methyl substituents on the quinolin-2-amine core (compounds 12 and AM-9934), which successfully drove cellular viability potency below 1 μM without altering MDCKII permeability or efflux.

review_notes: The lead compound AM-9747, although thoroughly profiled in cellular viability (Table 3), cellular SDMA imaging (Figure 7), mouse PK (Table 4), and multiple in vivo xenograft models (Figures 8-11), lacks a cell-free biochemical potency measurement in the text or tables, and was therefore excluded from the paired measurement set.

A minor discrepancy was noted in the MTA concentration for the biochemical MTA+ assay: Table 1 and Table 2 footnotes specify 5 μM MTA, whereas the Experimental Section MTase-Glo protocol text states 1 μM MTA.
Several biochemical IC50 values (compounds 9, 11, 12, AM-9934) are censored as <35 nM because of the theoretical assay limit resulting from poor curve fitting below or near 35 nM.

Compounds from the RHS methyl scan at positions 5-, 7-, and 8- (mentioned in the text on page 7 as having MTAP-del viability >5 μM and not increasing potency in biochemical assays) lack individual compound numbers, structures, and quantitative biochemical IC50 values (reported as 'data not shown'), and thus are not included as paired compounds.

On page 14 (Conclusions), the authors state an SDMA IC50 of 2.7 nM in HCT116 MTAP-del and 520 nM in MTAP-WT for AM-9747, whereas page 10 (text and Figure 7B) reports 0.2 nM and 50 nM, respectively; since AM-9747 has no reported cell-free biochemical potency, it remains excluded from the paired dataset.

claims.author_explanation: The authors hypothesize that poor cell membrane permeability diminishes cellular potency relative to cell-free potency, noting that both compounds demonstrated poor permeability in Caco-2 assays (with a modest ~2-fold increase for UNC9512 over UNC8531).

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 bidirectional cell permeability assay measuring Papp values (Ap->Bl and Bl->Ap) in the absence and presence of P-gp inhibitor PSC833
evidence.result: Both compounds demonstrated poor permeability, with an approximate 2-fold increase for UNC9512 over UNC8531.

evidence.experiment: Evaluation of cellular target engagement by NanoBRET and foci formation in U2OS cells
evidence.result: Compounds exhibited IC50 values in the 6.9-8.5 uM range in NanoBRET and required 50 uM dosing in foci formation assays, attributed by authors to low cellular permeability.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors specifically measured Caco-2 bidirectional permeability and found both compounds had poor permeability (Table S1), with an ~2-fold increase for UNC9512 over UNC8531 after removing one hydrogen bond donor via cyclic amide formation. They also showed cellular target engagement (NanoBRET IC50 8.5 uM and 6.9 uM) was substantially weaker than in vitro TR-FRET IC50 (0.47 and 0.46 uM), and high doses (50 uM) were needed to inhibit foci formation and failed to alter DNA repair in PathSig-ddPCR due to low permeability/potency. However, no controlled non-structural permeability-modulating rescue was tested.

classification.rationale: Poor cell membrane permeability measured in Caco-2 assays is used to explain the drop from cell-free to cellular potency.

insights.text: DNA-encoded library screening followed by SAR optimization yielded UNC9512, which retained submicromolar in vitro affinity (TR-FRET IC50 0.46 uM, SPR Kd 0.17 uM) while demonstrating cellular target engagement in NanoBRET assays (IC50 6.9 uM).
Cellular target engagement IC50 values in NanoBRET (8.5 uM for UNC8531 and 6.9 uM for UNC9512) were substantially higher than biochemical TR-FRET IC50 values (0.47 uM and 0.46 uM, respectively).
The authors attributed the drop in cellular potency to poor membrane permeability, as confirmed by Caco-2 transwell permeability assays.

Conformationally constraining the amide into an isoindolinone core in UNC9512 eliminated one hydrogen bond donor and increased Caco-2 permeability approximately 2-fold without sacrificing 53BP1 TTD affinity.

review_notes: In NanoBRET characterization, the text (pages 9 and 10) cites IC50 values of 8.5 ± 2.0 uM for UNC8531 and 6.9 ± 3.0 uM for UNC9512, whereas the inset in Figure 4A reports 8.5 ± 4.5 uM and 6.9 ± 6.0 uM. Both numbers reflect the same experiments, and the difference is noted in precision_note.

Compounds 2-18, 20-25, 27-34, and 35-37 were evaluated biochemically by TR-FRET but were not profiled for quantitative cellular potency (IC50/EC50) in intact cells, and were therefore excluded from the compound extraction list per scope rules.

Foci formation in U2OS cells was tested at discrete concentrations (50 uM in Fig 4B, and 11-100 uM in Fig S11) showing dose-dependent reduction in foci, but no fitted numerical EC50 was reported in the main text.

claims.author_explanation: While biochemical catalytic inhibition of PARP1/2 is within 3- to 8-fold across inhibitors, cellular cytotoxic potency in HR-deficient cells varies by orders of magnitude (up to >10,000-fold). Authors hypothesized this might involve activities unrelated to catalytic inhibition, but showed strict enantiomeric stereospecificity (BMN 673 vs inactive trans-isomer LT-00674) and linked the enhanced cellular DNA damage / cytotoxicity to much slower dissociation rate (longer target residence time) and replication fork stalling / trapping.

evidence.experiment: Surface plasmon resonance (Biacore T200) kinetics of PARP1 binding comparing BMN 673 and veliparib
evidence.result: BMN 673 off-rate was 1.05 x 10^-4 /s with KD 0.29 nM, nearly 40-fold slower than veliparib (koff 4.10 x 10^-3 /s, KD 2.39 nM)

evidence.experiment: Comparison of active enantiomer BMN 673 with inactive trans-enantiomer LT-00674 and cis-isomers for enzyme inhibition, Capan-1 cell killing, and temozolomide potentiation
evidence.result: PARP1 enzyme inhibition tightly correlated with Capan-1 cytotoxicity and temozolomide potentiation across chiral isomers, confirming on-target mechanism

evidence.experiment: Confocal microscopy of nuclear gamma-H2AX foci formation after 24 h treatment with BMN 673 vs olaparib
evidence.result: BMN 673 induced gamma-H2AX foci at concentrations as low as 100 pM, whereas 100 nM olaparib was required to elicit a similar response

claims.grade_rationale: Authors tested chiral enantiomer pairs to confirm that cellular cytotoxicity tightly tracks PARP1 biochemical potency rather than non-specific off-target toxicity, and demonstrated Biacore off-rate differences (~40-fold slower off-rate for BMN 673 vs veliparib) and gamma-H2AX induction at 100 pM vs 100 nM for olaparib, representing mechanistic measurements with strong stereochemical controls (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: Differences in cellular cytotoxicity vs catalytic inhibition are explained by drug-target residence time (dissociation kinetics) and PARP DNA trapping, which fall outside the standard taxonomy categories.

coverage.note: Clonogenic survival dose-response curves in isogenic mouse ES (BRCA1+/+ vs BRCA1-/-) and human DLD1 (BRCA2+/+ vs BRCA2-/-) cells; low-resolution multi-panel log plots without reported numerical SF50 values in text/tables, so graph estimation was not performed.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free enzymatic potency (PARP1 IC50 and Ki) and cellular potency (intracellular PAR synthesis EC50 in LoVo cells, cytotoxicity SF50/IC50 across multiple cell lines) for BMN 673, LT-00628, veliparib, rucaparib, and olaparib.

insights.text: Cellular PAR synthesis inhibition (EC50) in LoVo cells closely mirrors biochemical PARP1 enzyme IC50 for all compounds (2.5-5.9 nM cellular vs 0.57-4.73 nM biochemical), indicating rapid cell permeability and target engagement.

In contrast to acute intracellular PAR synthesis, long-term cytotoxicity (SF50) in BRCA-deficient tumor cells shows orders-of-magnitude divergence between BMN 673 and earlier generation inhibitors (e.g. 8.57 pM vs 0.818 uM in SUM149).

Surface plasmon resonance demonstrated an approximately 40-fold slower PARP1 dissociation rate (koff = 1.05 x 10^-4 /s) for BMN 673 compared to veliparib (koff = 4.10 x 10^-3 /s), correlating with markedly enhanced replication fork stalling and gamma-H2AX induction.

review_notes: Supplementary tables (Suppl Tables 1-6) were not included in the main manuscript PDF. LT-00674 cellular potency is in Suppl Table 5 and therefore LT-00674 was excluded from full paired extraction per eligibility criteria.
Table 1 reports Capan-1 IC50 as 5 nM for BMN 673, whereas Table 2 reports SF50 as 0.005 uM (5 nM), confirming concordance across both tables.
SUM149 SF50 for BMN 673 is stated as 8 x 10^-12 M in text (page 5) and 8.57E-6 uM (8.57 pM) in Table 2; the exact raw string from Table 2 is preserved.

All 5 eligible paired compounds (BMN 673, LT-00628, veliparib, rucaparib, olaparib) and all biochemical (PARP1 IC50, PARP1/2 Ki, Biacore KD) and cellular (LoVo PAR EC50, LoVo TMZ GI50, CAL51 SF80, and all 9 cell line SF50/IC50 columns in Tables 1-2) measurements were verified against the PDF and extracted.

claims.author_explanation: The disconnect between biochemical potency and cellular ER reporter assay activity across the series could not be explained by cellular permeability (Caco-2 Papp or efflux ratio) nor by acylsulfonamide linker pKa differences.

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 bidirectional permeability measurement for compound 11
evidence.result: Compound 11 displayed good permeability [Papp (A-B) = 64 nm/s, efflux ratio = 1.0] but had only low micromolar/weak cellular activity in the ER reporter assay (>4600 nM).

evidence.experiment: pKa determination and correlation with MVLN cellular activity across acylsulfonamide variants (Table 2)
evidence.result: Compounds 15 and 17 had the highest pKa values (5.8-6.0 vs 4.3 for 11) but showed no improvement in cellular activity (>17600 nM and 3680 nM, respectively).

evidence.experiment: Correlation analysis of biochemical KAT6A vs MVLN reporter activity across series (Figure 5)
evidence.result: The authors noted that observed cellular activity differences between subseries could be rationalized neither by pKa differences nor by Caco-2 permeability data, stating 'The reason for the good cellular activity of the N,N-amino-dimethyl subseries remains yet unclear.'

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured Caco-2 bidirectional permeability and experimental/predicted pKa across compounds with disparate cellular potencies, demonstrating that compounds with good permeability (e.g., compound 11, Papp 64 nm/s, efflux ratio 1.0) and high pKa (compounds 15, 17) still exhibited weak or no cellular activity, whereas the N,N-dimethylamino subseries displayed robust cellular activity. However, no controlled causal rescue or mechanistic isolation of cellular uptake was established; the underlying reason remains explicitly unresolved.

classification.rationale: Caco-2 permeability, efflux ratio, and pKa were experimentally tested and explicitly ruled out as explanations for the biochemical-to-cellular potency disconnect.

claims.author_explanation: Introduction of a 6-N,N-dimethylamino group occupies the narrow AcCoA tunnel, establishing weak C-H...O hydrogen bonds and an N-H...pi interaction with Ile649, boosting both biochemical affinity and cellular activity, while bulkier groups (morpholine in 32) cause steric clashes with Phe600.

evidence.experiment: X-ray cocrystal structure of KAT6A with compound 29 (BAY-184, PDB 9FKR)
evidence.result: Cocrystal structure demonstrated that the 6-N,N-dimethylamino group binds deep in the AcCoA tunnel, making weak C-H...O contacts with Ile647, Phe600, Ile649 and an N-H...pi interaction with Ile649 backbone NH, explaining tolerance and potency.

evidence.experiment: SAR exploration at position 6 (compounds 28, 29, 31, 32, 39 in Table 3)
evidence.result: Mono-methylamino 28 (ER IC50 = 2580 nM) gave less cellular activity than dimethylamino 29 (ER IC50 = 168 nM), while bulky morpholine 32 lost all activity (>20,000 nM in both assays).

claims.grade_rationale: The structural interaction of 29 was resolved by X-ray crystallography (PDB 9FKR) and compared with an inactive bulky analogue (morpholine 32) and smaller mono-methyl analogue (28), showing clear SAR association and structural validation of binding pocket engagement, though cellular potency differences between mono- and dimethyl remain partly empirical.

classification.rationale: General SAR optimization of active-site binding interactions increasing both biochemical and cellular potency is not a specific discrepancy mechanism in the taxonomy.

claims.author_explanation: Additional studies were undertaken evaluating the concentration dependence of the unbound partition-coefficient Kpuu on exposure to correct for exposure-related discrepancies between biochemical and cellular potency of KAT6A inhibitors, published in a separate manuscript (Trünkle et al., 2020, Ref 46).

evidence.experiment: Citation of companion Kpuu study (Ref 46) and plasma protein binding measurements for BAY-184 (29)
evidence.result: Authors note that BAY-184 is an acidic compound with high plasma protein binding and that concentration dependence of Kpuu was evaluated in a separate manuscript (Ref 46) to address discrepancies between biochemical and cellular potency.

claims.grade_rationale: In the current paper, the authors briefly cite their companion study (Ref 46) on concentration-dependent unbound partition coefficient (Kpuu) correcting for exposure-related discrepancies between biochemical and cellular potency of KAT6A inhibitors, and report high plasma protein binding for acidic compound BAY-184 (29), but the Kpuu data and causal rescue analysis are in the external reference rather than presented in this PDF.

classification.rationale: Cites an external companion study on unbound intracellular partitioning (Kpuu) and protein binding without presenting direct mechanism-specific data in the current text.

sources.label: Pharmacokinetics (In Vitro/In Vivo) text and Ref 46
sources.paraphrase: Reports high plasma protein binding of acidic compound BAY-184 (fu = 0.31%, 0.042%, 0.048% in mouse, human, rat plasma) and notes separate studies (Ref 46) evaluating the concentration dependence of the unbound partition coefficient Kpuu to correct for exposure-related discrepancies between biochemical and cellular potency of KAT6A inhibitors.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Direct analogue comparison on the N-([1,1'-biphenyl]-2-sulfonyl)-1-benzofuran-2-carboxamide scaffold evaluated in identical KAT6A biochemical and MVLN ER reporter assays; simultaneous change at C4 (Me to H) and C6 (OMe to NMe2) is a structural confounder.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison replacing the 6-methoxy and 4-methyl substituents of compound 11 with a 6-N,N-dimethylamino substituent and 4-H (compound 29, BAY-184), which markedly improved cellular ER reporter potency despite slightly lower biochemical KAT6A potency.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Analogue comparison keeping the 6-methoxy-4-methyl-benzofuran core constant while modulating acylsulfonamide substitution and experimental pKa; failed to substantially rescue cellular potency (3680 nM for 17 and >17600 nM for 15 vs >4600 nM for 11).
interventions.description: Analogue comparison modifying the acylsulfonamide aryl group of compound 11 (pKa 4.30) by introducing ortho-ethoxy and meta-chloro substituents in compound 17 (pKa 6.00) or para-biphenyl in compound 15 (pKa 5.80) to decrease acidity (increase pKa) and explore whether linker pKa drives the cellular potency dropoff.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched molecular pair differing only by N-methylation at the 6-amino position (NHMe in 28 vs NMe2 in 29), improving biochemical IC50 from 123 nM to 71 nM and cellular ER reporter IC50 from 2580 nM to 168 nM.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison between 6-methylamino substituent (compound 28) and 6-N,N-dimethylamino substituent (compound 29, BAY-184) on the unsubstituted C4 benzofuran scaffold.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Matched molecular pair differing by H vs F at position 4 of the 6-N,N-dimethylamino-benzofuran scaffold evaluated in identical biochemical and cellular assays.
interventions.description: Analogue comparison adding a 4-fluoro substituent to 6-N,N-dimethylamino compound 29 (BAY-184) to yield compound 39, boosting both biochemical KAT6A potency (71 nM to 13 nM) and cellular ER reporter potency (168 nM to 60 nM).

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative in vitro biochemical potency (KAT6A / KAT6B TR-FRET IC50) and cellular potency (ER reporter gene assay in MVLN cells IC50, H3K23ac HTRF cellular IC50, and 2D proliferation IC50) for multiple acylsulfonamide-benzofuran analogues.

insights.text: The acylsulfonamide linker serves as an effective bioisostere mimicking the negatively charged pyrophosphate of AcCoA within the deep KAT6A binding pocket.

The early benzofuran series displayed a major disconnect between potent biochemical KAT6A inhibition and weak cellular activity in ER reporter assays that could not be accounted for by Caco-2 permeability or linker pKa.
Introduction of a 6-N,N-dimethylamino group on the benzofuran scaffold (BAY-184) rescued cellular potency, establishing key weak hydrogen bonds and an N-H...pi interaction in the narrow AcCoA tunnel.

BAY-184 (29) demonstrated dual KAT6A/B selectivity over other MYST family members and induced dose-dependent cellular H3K23 deacetylation and proliferation inhibition in ER-positive breast cancer cells.

review_notes: Negative control compound 40 (BAY-644) was reported with in vitro KAT6A IC50 > 20 uM or inactive in Figure 6, and was omitted from the main paired dataset because it lacks a quantitative cellular IC50 value.
Metabolite compound 41 was reported with KAT6A IC50 = 1.1 uM but qualitative 'inactive' in MVLN cells without numerical bound, so it was excluded.
Compounds 4, 6, and 8 had n.a. in the cellular column of Table 1 and were excluded from compound records as unpaired.

Verified all 35 compounds with paired cell-free and cellular potency across Figure 2 and Tables 1-4 and 7 (compounds 22 and N-methylated 13/14 lacked numerical cellular bounds and are in SI), added explicit biochemical-vs-cellular pairs for all 35 compounds (37 total pairs), verified author claims regarding lack of Caco-2/pKa correlation, 6-dimethylamino subpocket engagement, and cited Kpuu work (Ref 46), and verified four SAR/chemical modification interventions.

claims.author_explanation: The carboxylic acids 4 and 11, resulting from ester hydrolysis, are fully charged under physiological conditions, leading to substantially reduced membrane permeability (>10- to >30-fold lower than their parent neutral esters). Consequently, the acids cannot penetrate cell membranes to reach intracellular JAK kinases, rendering them poorly active or inactive in cellular and whole blood assays despite retaining high biochemical potency.

evidence.experiment: Determination of membrane permeability for esters (6, 12, 3(R), 14(S)) and corresponding carboxylic acids (4, 11)
evidence.result: Acids 4 and 11 showed >10- to >30-fold reduced permeability (0.5 and 0.9 x 10^-6 cm/s) compared to parent neutral esters (11 to 28 x 10^-6 cm/s)

evidence.experiment: Masking the charged carboxylic acid as neutral ester prodrugs/analogs and testing biochemical vs cellular potencies
evidence.result: Conversion of acid 11 (IL15 IC50 = 2578 nM) to esters 6 (IL15 IC50 = 24 nM) or 9 (IL15 IC50 = 27 nM), and acid 4 (IL15 IC50 = 7018 nM) to ester 3(R) (IL15 IC50 = 131 nM) restored potent cellular activity while maintaining single-digit nanomolar biochemical JAK inhibition

claims.grade_rationale: The authors provide direct mechanistic measurements of permeability (PAMPA/artificial membrane permeability in Table 2: compound 4 = 0.5 x 10^-6 cm/s vs ester 3(R) = 18 x 10^-6 cm/s; compound 11 = 0.9 x 10^-6 cm/s vs ester 6 = 11 x 10^-6 cm/s), paired with corresponding biochemical vs cellular potencies showing that esterification rescues cellular potency from micromolar (acids 4, 11) to low nanomolar (esters 6, 9, 10, 12, 3(R), 14(S)) without loss of biochemical JAK affinity. This represents a controlled chemical intervention confirming permeability as the causal mechanism (Grade 4).

classification.rationale: Poor passive membrane permeability of charged carboxylic acids compared to neutral esters is directly measured and shown to cause the loss of cellular potency.

claims.author_explanation: In the human whole blood cellular assay (30 min preincubation prior to IL-2 stimulation), neutral esters 3(R), 3(S), 6, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14(R), and 14(S) show a pronounced loss of potency relative to biochemical and Mo7e cellular assays because blood esterases rapidly hydrolyze them (t1/2 = 5-7 min) into their corresponding charged, poorly permeable carboxylic acids (4 or 11). Similarly, carbonate 1 is rapidly hydrolyzed (t1/2 ~ 4 min) to hydroxypyridine 2, which tautomerizes into an inactive pyridone conformation.

evidence.experiment: LC-MS determination of compound stability (half-life of ester cleavage and acid formation at 1 uM) in fresh human blood at 37 °C
evidence.result: Labile esters 1, 3(R), 6, 9, 12, and 14(S) were rapidly hydrolyzed with half-lives of 4 to 7 min, whereas branched isopropyl ester 10 had a half-life of 65 min and CEE321 was stable (>240 min)

evidence.experiment: Comparison of sterically hindered isopropyl ester 10 vs unhindered methyl/ethyl esters 9 and 6 in human blood stability and whole-blood IL-2 P-STAT5 cellular potency
evidence.result: Branching increased human blood half-life from 5-7 min (esters 9 and 6) to 65 min (ester 10) and improved whole-blood IL-2 IC50 from 7854-12178 nM to 1201 nM while maintaining similar biochemical and Mo7e cellular potency

claims.grade_rationale: The authors directly measure ester cleavage and acid formation half-lives in human blood by LC-MS (Table 1: t1/2 = 4-7 min for labile esters 1, 3(R), 6, 9, 12, 14(S) vs >240 min for CEE321 and acids 4, 11) and demonstrate through steric branching (isopropyl ester 10, blood t1/2 = 65 min vs ethyl ester 6, t1/2 = 7 min) that slowing esterase hydrolysis restores whole-blood cellular potency (IL-2 IC50 = 1201 nM for 10 vs 12178 nM for 6).

classification.rationale: Rapid metabolic hydrolysis by blood esterases converts active neutral esters into poorly permeable acids or inactive tautomers, explaining the loss of potency in whole blood.
