insights.text: Esterification of the inactive charged carboxylic acid metabolite 4 into neutral ester 3(R) masks the negative carboxylate charge, increasing permeability >30-fold and restoring cellular JAK inhibitory potency.

Carboxylic acids 4 and 11 retain potent single-digit nanomolar biochemical affinity against JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, and TYK2, proving that the lack of cellular activity is solely pharmacokinetic (poor cellular uptake) rather than lack of target engagement.

In human blood, neutral ester 3(R) is rapidly hydrolyzed by blood esterases with a half-life of 6 min to carboxylic acid 4, causing a loss of cellular potency (>40 uM in whole blood) to disarm the drug outside the skin.

review_notes: immersion culture data (% inhibition) and blood/skin S9 half-lives in Table 1 are single-dose/kinetic readouts rather than concentration-based potencies and were not extracted as potency measurements.

Stereochemical differences at the ester alpha-carbon in compounds 3(R)/3(S) and 14(R)/14(S) significantly influence blood and skin S9 esterase hydrolysis rates without impacting biochemical JAK inhibition.
The paper confirms the prodrug/soft-drug mechanism by directly measuring artificial membrane permeability in Table 2, supporting an intervention grade of 4.

pairs.rationale: Both measurements assess BA24 inhibition of human COMT-catalyzed 3-BTD-O-methylation, comparing the cell-free competitive inhibition constant (Ki) with the intact-cell IC50 in U87-MG cells.

claims.author_explanation: The authors attribute the relatively weak cellular anti-COMT activity of BA (22.65 μM vs 165.4 nM biochemically) and the ~26-fold enhancement in cellular inhibition of BA24 over BA primarily to superior cell membrane permeability and cellular uptake of BA24.

evidence.experiment: Cellular membrane permeability/uptake assay in U87-MG glioblastoma cells and NCM-460 colon epithelial cells after 30 min incubation with 10 μM of BA, BA24, or EN, determined by HPLC-UV analysis of cell pellets versus supernatant.
evidence.result: BA exhibited low intracellular penetration (<5%), whereas BA24 showed ~40-52% intracellular accumulation (approximately 10-fold higher than BA and 18-fold higher than EN).

evidence.experiment: Comparison of cellular COMT IC50 between BA and BA24 in U87-MG cells using 3-BTD fluorogenic substrate.
evidence.result: BA24 demonstrated an IC50 of 0.86 μM (~26-fold increase in potency) compared to BA (22.65 μM), paralleling the ~10-fold improvement in intracellular membrane penetration.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors quantitatively measured cellular uptake and membrane permeability in U87-MG and NCM-460 cells using HPLC-UV, demonstrating approximately 10-fold higher cellular uptake for BA24 compared to BA, which correlates with improved cellular activity. However, BA24 was synthesized with multiple simultaneous modifications (4'-pyrrolidine on ring B and 7-methoxy on ring A), representing an analogue comparison rather than an isolated single-mechanism causal intervention (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: Low intracellular penetration/membrane permeability of BA vs BA24 was directly measured and shown to account for the difference in cellular potency.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative biochemical COMT inhibition IC50 values and intact-cell COMT inhibition IC50 values in U87-MG cells for both baicalein (BA) and its optimized derivative BA24.

insights.text: Natural flavone baicalein exhibits potent biochemical COMT inhibition (IC50 = 165.4 nM) but exhibits poor cellular potency (IC50 = 22.65 μM) in U87-MG cells.
Poor intact-cell activity of baicalein is primarily attributed to low cellular membrane penetration, as measured by low relative intracellular uptake (<5%) in U87-MG glioblastoma cells.
Dual optimization introducing a 4'-pyrrolidine group on ring B and a 7-methoxy group on ring A (compound BA24) improved intracellular uptake by ~10-fold and resulted in a cellular IC50 of 0.86 μM.

review_notes: Only BA and BA24 possess both cell-free biochemical IC50 and cellular IC50 determinations in intact cells; all other synthesized BA analogues were evaluated only in the cell-free biochemical assay and microsomal stability assay.
Entacapone was included as a positive control in the biochemical assay and evaluated for membrane permeability, but its cellular COMT IC50 was not quantitatively determined in this paper.
Added BA24 cell-free competitive inhibition constant (Ki = 89.28 nM from Figure 4A and Section 3.6) and paired it with its cellular COMT IC50 (0.86 μM).

claims.author_explanation: The methylated product inhibitors and SAH-uncompetitive hits are charged cations that exhibit high biochemical affinity/potency for the NNMT-SAH complex but have modest or poor cellular potency (averaging ~40-fold lower in cells than in biochemical assays) due to poor cell membrane permeability of the positively charged species.

evidence.experiment: Authors note that methylated products are charged and possess modest cellular potency, whereas utilizing uncharged substrate precursors combines substrate cell permeability with high product potency.
evidence.result: Product inhibitors are charged and display modest cellular potency, while neutral substrate analogs show equal or greater potency in cells relative to biochemical assays.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of biochemical pIC50 and cellular pIC50 across 11 matched substrate-product pairs in human NNMT assays (Table 2 vs Table 3 and Figure 5).
evidence.result: Substrate inhibitors were slightly more potent in cellular than biochemical assays, while cation products showed an average of 40-fold weaker potency in cellular than biochemical assays (ΔpIC50,cell = -1.1 ± 0.4 on average).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors propose that the positive charge impairs cell permeability and support this with systematic SAR comparing 11 neutral substrate analogs to their charged methylated counterparts (Grade 2/3), demonstrating that neutral substrates achieve superior cellular potency because intracellular NNMT-mediated biotransformation generates the charged product in situ.

classification.rationale: Poor cell membrane permeability of positively charged methylated product inhibitors vs neutral substrate precursors explains the ~40-fold drop in cellular potency.

claims.author_explanation: Substrate turnover rate (kcat) is a key determinant of cellular and biochemical potency. Halogenated analogs (27s, 28s) suffer from reduced ring-nitrogen reactivity (due to halogen electron-withdrawing deactivation), and 4-methylamine (17s) suffers from a steric clash with Ala247 in the NNMT active site that lowers its catalysis rate (pkcat = 2.2 vs 0.8 for 20s), resulting in poor cellular potency despite good binding affinity to NNMT.

evidence.experiment: SPR biosensor determination of substrate binding, turnover rate (kcat), and product dissociation rate (koff,P) for 20s, 27s, 28s, and 17s.
evidence.result: Substrates 27s and 28s have similar binding affinity and product off-rates to 20s but 5-6 fold slower kcat (Δpkcat = 0.8 and 0.7), directly matching their lower cellular potencies (ΔpIC50,cell = 2.4 and 1.8). Substrate 17s exhibits ~25-fold slower kcat (pkcat = 2.2) than 20s.

evidence.experiment: DFT transition-state energy barrier calculations and molecular docking of 16s vs 17s into the NNMT active site.
evidence.result: DFT calculations match experimental rate constants; docking reveals that the 4-methylamine in 17s clashes with the side chain of Ala247, shifting the pyridine ring into an offset pose with a suboptimal S-Me-N angle (148° vs 157° for 16s).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors perform quantitative surface biosensor kinetic measurements (measuring kon,S, koff,S, kcat, and koff,P) across 13 inhibitors and correlate these with DFT transition-state calculations and X-ray/docking structures, demonstrating a strong correlation between pkcat and cellular pIC50 (R2 = 0.72) (Grade 3 mechanistic measurement).

classification.rationale: The compounds are prodrug-like substrates requiring enzymatic biotransformation (methylation turnover kcat by NNMT) to form the active inhibitor in situ; slower catalytic turnover reduces cellular potency.

insights.text: Methylated nicotinamide analog products are charged cations with nanomolar to sub-nanomolar affinity for NNMT-SAH (pKd up to 9.8), but display an average of 40-fold lower cellular potency due to low membrane permeability.

Uncharged nicotinamide substrate analogs function as turnover inhibitors by readily penetrating cell membranes and undergoing in situ enzymatic N-methylation into the charged product, yielding equal or superior cellular vs biochemical potency.

Substrate catalysis turnover rate (kcat) strongly correlates with cellular potency (R2 = 0.72); substrates with deactivated ring nitrogens (4-fluoro 27s and 4-chloro 28s) show poor cellular potency despite good binding affinities.

Steric hindrance can severely suppress turnover rate without disrupting ground-state binding: 4-methylamino analog 17s binds NNMT with similar affinity to 16s and 20s, but clashes with Ala247, slowing turnover by ~25-fold and drastically reducing cellular activity.

Product off-rate (koff,P) is primarily dictated by the 6-position substituent (-NHCH3 exhibits significantly longer residence time than -OCH3), and slower product release translates into prolonged target engagement in vivo.

review_notes: Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3 report potencies as pIC50, cell pIC50, and pKd with explicit units of -log10(M), which have been preserved directly.

Table 4 provides rat cell pIC50 in NRK-49F cells alongside human MCF7 cell pIC50; human cell values are nearly identical to those in Table 2 (minor re-measured differences like 6.7 vs 6.6 for 11s are noted).
Figure 2 compound 2s (citing literature pIC50 = 7.4) and NS1 were not evaluated for cellular potency in this paper and are excluded from the dataset.
Compounds 3a, 4, and 5 from Figure 3 were included because they have both cell-free biochemical pIC50 and cellular pIC50 values (<4.5).

Verified all 39 compounds with paired cell-free and cellular potency across Figure 3 and Tables 1-4, refined chemical structure descriptions for screening hits 3a, 4, and 5, and confirmed complete coverage of author explanations and interventions for both cation permeability dropoff and turnover kinetics.

claims.author_explanation: Excessive lipophilicity (LogD7.4 >= 3.2 for 3 and 4) impedes nuclear membrane permeation and leads to predominant cytoplasmic trapping, uncoupling DNA binding affinity in solution from cellular antiproliferative efficacy; in contrast, lower lipophilicity (LogD7.4 = 0.60 for 6) driven by higher basicity/ionization allows efficient nuclear penetration and accumulation at target DNA.

evidence.experiment: Two-photon and confocal fluorescence microscopy measuring subcellular localization and nucleus-to-cytoplasm integrated fluorescence intensity ratios in MCF7 cells.
evidence.result: Compound 6 (LogD7.4 = 0.6) exhibited a nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio near 3 (predominantly nuclear), whereas lipophilic compounds 3 and 4 (LogD7.4 >= 3.2) were largely retained in the cytoplasm (ratio < 0.25). Compound 5 (LogD7.4 = 1.5) had an intermediate ratio (~0.35) and lower IC50 than 4 despite identical in vitro DNA binding affinity.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of octanol/PBS LogD7.4 with antiproliferative IC50 values in MCF7 and HepG2 cells.
evidence.result: Cellular potency correlates negatively with LogD7.4 (6 > 5 > 4 ~ 3), whereas in vitro DNA binding constants (ds-DNA and G4) do not distinguish 4 from 5.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors propose that differences in nuclear versus cytoplasmic distribution, dictated by LogD7.4, explain why compounds with identical or similar in vitro DNA affinity (e.g. 4 vs 5) differ significantly in cellular potency. They perform direct mechanistic measurements of subcellular distribution using two-photon and confocal fluorescence microscopy, quantifying nuclear vs cytoplasmic intensity ratios (Fig. 5F), which correlate with cellular potency (Grade 3). Because structural differences (chlorination, chain length) are matched analogue comparisons rather than dynamic causal rescues/interventions, it does not achieve grade 4.

classification.rationale: Excessive lipophilicity (high LogD7.4) impedes nuclear membrane permeation and causes cytoplasmic trapping of the compound, preventing access to nuclear DNA.

claims.author_explanation: In previous studies on related indolo[3,2-b]quinolines (quindoline 1 vs cryptolepine 2), neutral quindoline 1 is retained in the cytoplasm with weak cytotoxicity whereas cationic cryptolepine 2 accumulates preferentially in the nucleus; however, additional structural features such as halogenation or nitro substitution can preclude nuclear accumulation.

evidence.experiment: Prior two-photon fluorescence microscopy and cytotoxicity studies of quindoline (1), cryptolepine (2), and halogenated/nitro derivatives in HEK 293T and cancer cells (cited from refs [2, 16, 17, 19]).
evidence.result: Cationic cryptolepine (2) accumulates in the nucleus and shows strong cytotoxicity, whereas neutral quindoline (1) and certain halogenated/nitro analogues are retained in the cytoplasm.

claims.grade_rationale: Cited background literature [16, 19] on parent scaffolds 1 and 2 motivating the investigation of ionization and halogenation effects on nuclear localization in the present series (3-6).

classification.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
classification.rationale: Cites prior findings showing that compound ionization state (neutral vs cationic) and structural substituents govern cytoplasmic retention versus nuclear accumulation of the compound.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 4 and 5 are structural analogues differing solely by the presence or absence of a single aromatic chlorine on position 7 of the indole core.
interventions.description: Removal of the 7-chloro atom on the indole moiety (comparing dichlorinated 4 to monochlorinated 5) while keeping the same 11-(3-aminopropylamino) side chain, which reduces LogD7.4 from 3.20 to 1.50 and improves MCF7 IC50 from 6.5 uM to 3.8 uM despite nearly identical cell-free DNA binding affinities.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 5 and 6 are monochlorinated analogues differing only by one methylene unit in the 11-NH alkylamine chain (propyl vs butyl).
interventions.description: Lengthening the 11-NH alkylamine side chain from propyl (5) to butyl (6) in monochlorinated derivatives, which increases side-chain basicity, lowers LogD7.4 to 0.6, increases nuclear accumulation threefold, and improves MCF7 IC50 from 3.8 uM to 1.8 uM.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 3 and 4 are matched dichlorinated analogues differing by one methylene unit in the 11-NH alkylamine chain (ethyl vs propyl), demonstrating that chain extension from 2 to 3 carbons is insufficient to overcome high lipophilicity from indole chlorination.
interventions.description: Lengthening the 11-NH alkylamine side chain from ethyl (3) to propyl (4) in the 7,quinoline-dichlorinated series leaves LogD7.4 high (>= 3.20), fails to promote nuclear accumulation, and does not significantly improve cellular potency (MCF7 IC50 7.0 uM vs 6.5 uM).

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free equilibrium DNA binding association constants (K for ds-DNA and MYC-G4) alongside cellular antiproliferative IC50 values in MCF7 cancer cells for compounds 3, 4, 5, and 6.

insights.text: Indolo[3,2-b]quinolines with near-identical in vitro DNA binding affinity (e.g. dichlorinated 4 vs monochlorinated 5) show divergent cellular cytotoxic potencies, demonstrating an uncoupling between cell-free affinity and cellular efficacy.
Cellular potency correlates inversely with physiological lipophilicity (LogD7.4) and directly with nuclear accumulation, rather than in vitro DNA binding constants.

Higher lipophilicity (LogD7.4 >= 3.2) caused by aromatic chlorination traps compounds in the cytoplasm, whereas lower lipophilicity (LogD7.4 = 0.6) allows nuclear membrane permeation and access to genomic DNA targets.

review_notes: Table 2 reports binding association constants (K, 10^6 M^-1) rather than dissociation constants; these were preserved exactly in their original unit.

Table 2 also reports delta Tm (°C) for kRAS-G4 and Telo-G4 from FRET melting assays; these are thermal stabilization shifts rather than concentration-based potencies and were not extracted as potency endpoints.
HepG2 IC50 values listed in Table 3 were cited from previous literature (reference [28]), while MCF7 IC50 values were measured de novo in the current work.

Added missing biochemical_after_id and cellular_after_id links to the interventions, added the 3-to-4 dichlorinated chain-length comparison intervention, added HepG2 pairing records, and added cited background claim clm_2 for parent scaffolds 1 and 2.

classification.rationale: Extracellular sequestration by serum albumin (FBS/BSA/HSA) reduces free compound concentration; serum protein binding is outside the specific listed taxonomy causes.

eligibility.reason: Compound 1 is evaluated in both a cell-free TR-FRET Mcl-1 binding assay (Ki = 0.5 nM) and an intact-cell NCI-H929 caspase 3/7 activation assay (IC50 = 0.1 uM in 0% FBS, 1.4 uM in 1% FBS, and 6.0 uM in 10% FBS), presented quantitatively in Table 1.

insights.text: Compound 1 exhibits subnanomolar cell-free affinity for Mcl-1 (Ki = 0.5 nM in 0% FBS), which right-shifts to 1.4-1.5 nM upon addition of 1% FBS or 200 ug/ml delipidated BSA/HSA.
Cellular caspase 3/7 activation by compound 1 in NCI-H929 cells displays a dramatic serum shift from IC50 = 0.1 uM in serum-free conditions to 1.4 uM in 1% FBS and 6.0 uM in 10% FBS.

The cellular potency loss in the presence of serum is caused by compound sequestration by serum albumin, as demonstrated by the near-identical shift produced by purified HSA or BSA in biochemical assays.
X-ray crystallography (2.7 A) revealed that compound 1 binds predominantly to drug site 3 in domain IB of HSA, anchored by deep hydrophobic insertion near I142 and polar contacts with R117 and R186.

Structural superposition indicates compound 1 is more deeply buried in HSA than in Mcl-1, suggesting steric additions to the indole headpiece, lactam bridge, or 7-pyrazole could selectively disrupt albumin binding.

review_notes: Only compound 1 is quantitatively evaluated for both biochemical and cellular potencies in the main text and tables; earlier analogues mentioned as having improved plasma shifts are located in supplementary material.
Table 1 includes a predicted albumin Ka (1.8 uM) calculated from the Copeland shift equation rather than measured directly.
Caspase 3/7 activation was measured at 3 h rather than 24-72 h to minimize confounding effects of cell viability changes under serum-starved conditions.

claims.author_explanation: Differences in cellular potency relative to biochemical potency (in cellulo/in vitro IC50 ratio) are caused by differences in passive cell membrane permeability, driven by linker-dependent molecular folding in nonpolar environments to shield solvent-accessible 3D polar surface area (SA 3D PSA) and reduce radius of gyration (Rgyr).

evidence.experiment: PAMPA permeability assay for PROTACs 1-9
evidence.result: PAMPA log Pe values correlate well with the in cellulo/in vitro IC50 ratio: high-permeability PROTACs 2 and 9 have high PAMPA log Pe (-5.42 and -6.30), whereas low-permeability PROTAC 1 has low PAMPA log Pe (-8.29).

evidence.experiment: NMR conformational ensemble determination in CDCl3 (NAMFIS) to calculate SA 3D PSA and Rgyr
evidence.result: Compounds with higher permeability (e.g., 2 and 9) adopt folded conformations with lower population-weighted mean SA 3D PSA and Rgyr compared to less permeable analogues (e.g., 6 and 3).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors perform mechanistic measurements of passive artificial membrane permeability (PAMPA) that correlate with cellular/in vitro ratios across compounds 1-9, and determine 3D conformational ensembles in CDCl3 by solution NMR (NAMFIS) for compounds 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 9 to measure SA 3D PSA and Rgyr. While structural linker modifications modulate permeability, these are analogue comparisons rather than controlled on/off rescue interventions of a single compound.

classification.rationale: Passive membrane entry is the primary stated bottleneck, supported by PAMPA differences that track cellular/biochemical ratios. CDCl3 folding and polar shielding provide an upstream explanation of entry differences; the supplied evidence does not isolate defective environment-dependent adaptability as a separate cause. Overlap with molecular chameleonicity warrants review.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Both PROTACs 1 and 2 share identical ERK5 and VHL ligands and an 8-atom linker length, varying only in linker composition (aliphatic vs PEG-like ether).
interventions.description: Replacement of two methylene groups in the linear aliphatic 8-carbon linker of PROTAC 1 by oxygen atoms to form a PEG-like linker in PROTAC 2.

interventions.comparison_rationale: PROTACs 1 and 7 share identical ligands and linker length, evaluating the effect of introducing a basic/polar N-methyl amino group into an otherwise flexible linker.
interventions.description: Replacement of one methylene group in the 8-atom linker of PROTAC 1 by an N-methylated tertiary amine in PROTAC 7.

interventions.comparison_rationale: PROTACs 5 and 6 are explicitly designed as a matched molecular pair differing only by a CH-to-N substitution in the aromatic ring of the 8-atom linker.
interventions.description: Replacement of the 1,4-phenylene ring in the linker of PROTAC 5 with a pyridine-2,5-diyl ring in matched molecular pair PROTAC 6 to enable potential intramolecular hydrogen bonding with the VHL amide NH.

interventions.comparison_rationale: PROTACs 7 and 8 are explicitly designed as a matched molecular pair retaining the tertiary amine and 8-atom linker length while varying linker rigidity.
interventions.description: Replacement of the flexible N-methylated tertiary amine linker in PROTAC 7 with a rigidified piperidine-containing 8-atom linker in matched molecular pair PROTAC 8.

interventions.comparison_rationale: PROTAC 9 was explicitly included for comparison to PROTAC 3, as both contain an amide and ether moiety in their linker but differ in linker length (10 atoms vs 8 atoms).

coverage.file_name: Abeje et al. - 2025 - Impact of Linker Composition on VHL PROTAC Cell Permeability.pdf
coverage.label: Table 2
coverage.note: Extracted all 9 PROTAC compounds having paired biochemical (in vitro) and cellular (in cellulo) VHL IC50 values.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports both cell-free biochemical VHL binding potencies (TR-FRET IC50) and cellular intact-cell VHL engagement potencies (NanoBRET IC50 in live cells) for the same series of nine VHL PROTAC compounds (1-9).

insights.text: Linker flexibility and composition strongly govern passive cell permeability in VHL PROTACs; introducing ether oxygens in place of methylene units in an 8-atom linker dramatically improves cellular permeability and PAMPA flux.
The ratio between in cellulo and in vitro IC50 for VHL target engagement serves as a functional surrogate for cellular permeability that correlates qualitatively with PAMPA log Pe.

Solution-state conformational ensembles in apolar solvent demonstrate that high permeability correlates with the capacity to adopt folded conformations that shield solvent-accessible 3D polar surface area (SA 3D PSA) in the VHL ligand.
In addition to intramolecular hydrogen bonds (IMHBs), pi-pi and NH-pi interactions between POI and VHL ligands provide critical stabilization of low-polarity folded states.

review_notes: Table 2 reports both in vitro biochemical IC50 and in cellulo intact-cell IC50 for human VHL target binding for all nine PROTACs (1-9), providing 9 matched pairs.

ERK5 biochemical binding is referenced in text for compound 9 (IC50 1.23 uM, ref 20) but not systematically tested across the series; VHL binding was chosen as the paired biochemical/cellular target engagement axis.
Uncertainties are explicitly reported as +- SEM in Table 2 with n=3 (in vitro) and n=6 (in cellulo).

claims.author_explanation: The drop in VHL potency from biochemical to cell-based assay reflects cellular permeability limits of the large, flexible PROTAC, which is partially mitigated by molecular chameleonicity (conformational folding, IMHB formation, and polar surface shielding in apolar environments).

evidence.experiment: NMR conformational deconvolution (NAMFIS) in CDCl3, DMSO-d6, and DMSO-d6-D2O to evaluate radius of gyration, solvent accessible 3D polar surface area, and intramolecular hydrogen bonding
evidence.result: In CDCl3 mimicking the apolar membrane interior, compound 1 adopts folded conformations with reduced SA 3D PSA (<=207 A2) and Rgyr (5.4-6.2 A) through intramolecular hydrogen bonds and amide shielding, explaining its ability to permeate cells despite bRo5 properties

evidence.experiment: PAMPA artificial membrane permeability assay, logD (pH 7.5), and PBS (pH 6.5) aqueous solubility measurements for PROTAC 1 (Table 1)
evidence.result: PROTAC 1 displays medium-to-high passive membrane permeability in PAMPA (-logPe = 5.85 cm/s), drug-like lipophilicity (logD = 2.68), and low aqueous solubility (7.0 mg/L), consistent with medium cellular permeability underlying the moderate biochemical-to-cellular VHL potency shift

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors performed detailed conformational analysis using solution NMR (NAMFIS) across apolar and polar solvents to mechanistically demonstrate conformational compaction and polar shielding, but no causal rescue or perturbation in cellular assays was tested.

classification.rationale: The claim attributes the cellular shift to membrane entry, with PAMPA and conformational measurements supporting that interpretation. Chameleonic folding and polar shielding are described as mitigating this limitation rather than causing the loss. Moderate PAMPA permeability does not independently establish the magnitude of the cellular shift.

eligibility.reason: The main article provides paired cell-free and cellular potencies for compounds 4, 7, 8, and 9. Compound 9 has an exact human whole-blood CD69 IC50 (240 ± 20 nM; 146 ± 10 ng/mL), graph-estimable Ramos B-cell BTK occupancy IC50 (~8 nM, Fig. 4c) and off-target cellular reporter bounds (>1,000 nM, Fig. 4c), paired with graph-estimable BTK enzymatic IC50 (~2.0 nM, Figs. 2d and 4b) and off-target enzymatic bounds (>3 uM, p. 4). Compounds 4 (text BTK IC50 = 1.4 ± 0.2 nM), 7, and 8 (Fig. 2d) also pair with the reported cellular BTK occupancy IC50 range (5 to 27 nM, p. 3).

insights.text: Compound 9 exhibits potent cell-free BTK enzymatic inhibition (~1.8 nM, Figs. 2d and 4b), intact-cell Ramos B-cell BTK occupancy (~9 nM, Fig. 4c; within the 5-27 nM series range), and human whole-blood B-cell CD69 inhibition (240 ± 20 nM / 146 ± 10 ng/mL), while sparing off-target Cys481 kinases ITK and EGFR in both enzymatic (>3 uM) and cellular (>1,000 nM) assays.

The authors do not state a mechanistic explanation for concentration-based IC50 dropoff between biochemical, Ramos cell, and whole-blood assays, noting instead that standard IC50 measurements fail to capture true affinity for slow off-rate reversible covalent inhibitors.

Regarding residence time (washout durability) rather than IC50 dropoff, the authors state that faster apparent recovery of unoccupied BTK in cells relative to biochemical off-rate assays reflects higher temperature (37 vs. 23 C) and intracellular BTK turnover/resynthesis, supported by cycloheximide cotreatment (Supplementary Fig. 16).

Structural optimization from compound 3 to compounds 4-9 replaced the piperidine linker with a methylpyrrolidine linker, monofluorinated the scaffold, and added polar branched-alkyl capping groups (morpholine in 8, oxetane in 9) to improve aqueous solubility (126 uM for 9) and oral bioavailability while extending BTK residence time to 167 ± 21 h.

review_notes: Updated eligibility to has_paired_compounds=true and extracted paired cell-free and cellular potencies for compounds 4, 7, 8, and 9 from the main text, Figure 2d, and Figure 4b-c.

For compound 9, exact numerical whole-blood cellular potency (240 ± 20 nM; 146 ± 10 ng/mL) and off-target enzymatic bounds (>3 uM for ITK and EGFR) are explicitly stated in the text, while BTK enzymatic IC50 (~1.8 nM from Fig. 4b / ~2.2 nM from Fig. 2d), Ramos B-cell AlphaScreen BTK occupancy IC50 (~9 nM from Fig. 4c, consistent with the 5-27 nM text range), and cellular ITK/EGFR reporter bounds (>1,000 nM from Fig. 4c) are well-calibrated graph estimates.

For compounds 4, 7, and 8, biochemical BTK IC50 values (1.4 ± 0.2 nM in text for 4; ~0.55 nM and ~3.2 nM in Fig. 2d for 7 and 8) pair with the aggregate cellular BTK AlphaScreen IC50 range (5 ± 1 nM to 27 ± 11 nM) reported on p. 3; individual cellular IC50s and full tables for compounds 10-26 and 28-38 reside in the unprovided Supplementary Information.

No claims or interventions were extracted for IC50 cell potency dropoff because the authors do not attribute concentration-based cellular or whole-blood IC50 shifts to a specific mechanism; their mechanistic discussion and cycloheximide experiment (p. 3, p. 5) address apparent target dissociation rate / BTK resynthesis during washout durability assays rather than equilibrium IC50 dropoff.

claims.author_explanation: Previous reports claiming potent ACVR1 inhibition by pacritinib and momelotinib were performed at subtherapeutic, low ATP concentrations (such as 3 to 10 uM), which overestimates cellular kinase inhibition because millimolar intracellular ATP outcompetes these type 1 ATP-competitive inhibitors.

evidence.experiment: Enzymatic ACVR1 IC50 titration at 3 uM, 100 uM, and 1000 uM ATP compared to cellular pSMAD1/5 and hepcidin IC50 in HeLa and HUH-7 cells
evidence.result: Pacritinib and momelotinib ACVR1 IC50 shifted from 6 nM and 21 nM at 3 uM ATP to 644 nM and 2184 nM at 1 mM ATP, aligning with weak cellular IC50s (717 nM and 5173 nM for pSMAD1/5)

claims.grade_rationale: The authors systematically measured ACVR1 enzymatic inhibition across multiple ATP concentrations (3, 100, and 1000 uM ATP), demonstrating a shift in IC50 values that aligns with the Cheng-Prusoff model and matches the micromolar cellular potencies (pSMAD1/5 and hepcidin) observed in intact cells.

classification.rationale: ATP titration from low-micromolar to millimolar concentrations reduces inhibitor potency and brings biochemical estimates closer to cellular pSMAD potency. The causal explanation is competition from intracellular ATP; low-ATP assay overestimation is its assay-level consequence.

claims.author_explanation: Alongside intracellular ATP concentration, cell membrane permeability and plasma protein binding must be considered when translating biochemical potencies of kinase inhibitors to cellular and clinical pharmacological effects.
claims.category: cell membrane permeability and plasma protein binding

evidence.experiment: General statement citing Jansson-Lofmark et al. (ref. 14) on factors affecting biochemical-to-cellular/clinical potency translation.
evidence.result: Authors note that intracellular ATP concentration, cell membrane permeability, and plasma protein binding must be accounted for when interpreting biochemical IC50 values.

claims.grade_rationale: Stated as general background citing external literature (ref. 14) for translating biochemical kinase potency; permeability is not experimentally measured in this study, while plasma protein binding is used to calculate clinical free Cmax/Cavg.

classification.rationale: The claim jointly invokes membrane permeability and plasma protein binding as general considerations, citing external background without a permeability experiment establishing the drop-off in these compounds. No single primary mechanism can be separated from the supplied claim, and plasma protein binding has no dedicated specific cause in this taxonomy.

eligibility.reason: The paper evaluates clinical JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib, fedratinib, pacritinib, momelotinib, and metabolite M21) in cell-free enzymatic kinase assays (JAK family and full kinome profiling) as well as cellular signaling (pSTAT5, pSMAD1/5) and viability/cytotoxicity assays.

insights.text: ATP concentration in cell-free assays strongly dictates measured IC50 values for ATP-competitive type 1 kinase inhibitors; testing at subphysiological ATP can dramatically overestimate potency relative to cellular conditions.

Ruxolitinib demonstrated the highest JAK2 potency and kinome selectivity, displaying on-target cellular pSTAT5 suppression and selective antiproliferative effects in JAK2-dependent cells over JAK2-independent cells.
Pacritinib and momelotinib show only micromolar cellular inhibition of ACVR1 downstream signaling (pSMAD1/5 and hepcidin), consistent with enzymatic IC50 shifts at 1 mM physiological ATP.
Momelotinib major metabolite M21 showed weaker JAK2 and STAT5 inhibitory activity than parent momelotinib but exhibited strong activity against TYK2 and other off-target kinases.

review_notes: Zilurgisertib was evaluated in cellular assays in Table 6 as an ACVR1 reference inhibitor, but was not characterized in cell-free assays in this paper and is therefore excluded from the paired compound dataset.
Momelotinib + M21 combination data in Figures 3, 4, and 5 were excluded as combination treatments rather than single chemical entities.

Verified all 5 compounds with paired cell-free and cellular potency (ruxolitinib, fedratinib, pacritinib, momelotinib, and M21). Added 3 uM and 100 uM ATP ACVR1 enzymatic measurements (Table 5), additional JAK2 WT Baf3 cellular pairs (Figure 2), low-ATP ACVR1 pairs, before/after links for ATP titration interventions, and the cited background claim on cell membrane permeability and plasma protein binding (page 2).

claims.author_explanation: Masked polar group incorporation (MPGI) via intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the amino NH and adjacent methoxy oxygen permits high aqueous solubility in water while presenting an apolar profile in the hydrophobic tubulin colchicine site, allowing high antiproliferative and tubulin polymerization inhibitory potencies.

evidence.experiment: Thermodynamic aqueous solubility determination at pH 7.0 buffer by shake-flask method
evidence.result: Amino derivatives (e.g., 8 at 164 µg/mL and 60Z at 52 µg/mL) showed substantial solubility improvements over parent CA-4 (1 µg/mL).

claims.grade_rationale: The authors demonstrate improved thermodynamic solubility and DFT-calculated intramolecular hydrogen bonds, supported by consistent cellular and biochemical tubulin inhibition, but without controlled rescue of a bond-deficient mutant.

classification.specific_cause: Imbalanced Molecular Chameleon Characteristics (Abnormal Conformational Adaptability/Polarity Regulation)
classification.rationale: The explanation specifically invokes environment-dependent polar masking: an amino/methoxy intramolecular hydrogen bond permits aqueous solubility while presenting an apolar profile in the hydrophobic binding site. This compound-side change in exposed polarity is closest to molecular chameleonicity. Direct support is solubility measurement plus calculated hydrogen bonding; conformational switching is not directly demonstrated, so physicochemical properties remain an alternative classification.

claims.author_explanation: Lower sensitivity of HT-29 colon adenocarcinoma cells relative to HeLa/MCF7 was investigated for P-glycoprotein/MDR1 efflux susceptibility using 10 µM verapamil. Using a >=3-fold IC50 reduction cutoff, only 8, 44, and 60Z among submicromolar compounds (plus amide 55Z) are MDR substrates, whereas 9, 25, 43, 48Z, 49Z, 67, CA-4, and ABT-751 are not, indicating a non-MDR origin for HT-29 insensitivity in the latter.

evidence.experiment: Antiproliferative XTT assay in HT-29 cells with and without 10 µM verapamil co-treatment
evidence.result: Verapamil reduced HT-29 IC50 >=3-fold for 8 (410 to 130 nM), 44 (2000 to 600 nM), 55Z (5500 to 987 nM), and 60Z (309 to 73 nM), but had <3-fold or no effect on 9, 25, 43, 48Z, 49Z, 67 (303 to 430 nM), CA-4, and ABT-751.

claims.grade_rationale: A controlled intervention adding 10 µM verapamil to HT-29 cells produced a greater than 3-fold decrease in IC50 for 8, 44, and 60Z, specifically testing and demonstrating the causal role of efflux in the potency loss.

classification.rationale: Verapamil improves cellular potency for linked compounds 8, 44, 55Z and 60Z, supporting active transporter efflux for that subgroup. Linked compound 67 instead changes from 303 to 430 nM and has no rescue. A single supported label across all supplied compound links would propagate the mechanism to a negative comparator; retain mixed status until compound-specific assertions are curated.

claims.author_explanation: Nanomolar cytotoxicity despite micromolar turbidimetric TPI values, especially in sulfonamides, arises because cytotoxicity is driven by disruption of microtubule polymerization dynamics rather than large changes in total polymer mass.

evidence.experiment: Immunofluorescence confocal microscopy of alpha-tubulin in HeLa and MCF7 cells treated with 8, 60Z, or 67
evidence.result: Compounds caused drastic disruption of microtubule networks and multi-lobulated nuclei consistent with mitotic arrest at cellular concentrations.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors propose this mechanistic rationale based on cited work and support it with immunofluorescence confocal microscopy showing severe cellular microtubule disruption at cytotoxic concentrations.

classification.rationale: Cellular microtubule disruption and mitotic arrest support a distinction between effects on microtubule dynamics and the bulk polymerization assay endpoint. This is an endpoint/biological-response explanation, not an explicit Ki/IC50 miscalculation, target PTM, or target localization mechanism. It falls outside the named specific causes.

claims.author_explanation: Lower cellular potency of dimethylaniline 49Z (despite potent 1.1 µM cell-free TPI) and reduced potency in HeLa versus MCF7 cells (>3-fold difference) for polar amino derivatives (43, 48Z, 49Z, 60Z) are attributed to reduced cellular uptake in HeLa due to higher polarity; ortho-substituted dimethylanilines are less planar and more basic, favoring protonation and increased polarity.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of cell-free TPI IC50 and cellular antiproliferative IC50 across HeLa, MCF7, and HT-29 alongside aqueous solubility and DFT conformational analysis
evidence.result: Dimethylaniline 49Z potently inhibits tubulin polymerization (IC50 1.1 µM) and MCF7 growth (57 nM) but is >4-fold less potent in HeLa (260 nM), matching the >3-fold HeLa vs MCF7 potency drop seen for soluble polar amines 43, 48Z, and 60Z; permanent ammonium salt 50Z loses both TPI (>5 µM) and cellular potency (4870 nM in HeLa, 973 nM in MCF7).

claims.grade_rationale: Supported by comparison of cell-free TPI potency (where 49Z is at least as potent as 43 and 48Z) with cellular antiproliferative SAR across HeLa and MCF7 and aqueous solubility/DFT conformational analysis, without direct intracellular accumulation measurements.

classification.rationale: The authors attribute the potency pattern to reduced cellular uptake associated with polarity, protonation and nonplanarity. The biochemical/cellular SAR and weak permanently charged analogue support that attribution, although neither intracellular concentration nor permeability was directly measured in the supplied evidence. The explicit uptake explanation takes priority over a generic physicochemical label.

coverage.file_name: González et al. - 2023 - Novel amino analogs of the trimethoxyphenyl ring in potent colchicine site ligands improve solubilit.pdf
coverage.label: Table 1
coverage.note: Extracted all 44 compounds with quantitative biochemical TPI and cellular antiproliferative data; compound 36 was excluded because TPI was n.d.

eligibility.reason: The study reports quantitative cell-free tubulin polymerization inhibition (IC50 in µM) and quantitative cellular antiproliferative activity (IC50 in nM against HeLa, MCF7, and HT-29 cells) for the same series of synthetic compounds and reference agents.

insights.text: Introducing a 3-methylamino substituent onto the 4,5-dimethoxyphenyl A ring effectively replaces the classical 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl group, substantially enhancing aqueous solubility via the masked polar group incorporation (MPGI) mechanism while retaining nanomolar antiproliferative potency and submicromolar tubulin polymerization inhibition.

The discrepancy between micromolar turbidimetric cell-free tubulin polymerization inhibition and nanomolar cellular antiproliferative potency varies markedly by scaffold, being pronounced in sulfonamides compared to stilbenes, consistent with cellular cytotoxicity driven by perturbation of microtubule dynamics rather than net reduction in polymer mass.

Co-treatment with the MDR inhibitor verapamil in HT-29 colon adenocarcinoma cells demonstrated that cellular potency loss is selectively caused by Pgp/MDR1 efflux for certain methylanilines (8, 44, 60Z), while other potent analogs such as phenstatin 67 are non-substrates.

review_notes: Compound 36 was omitted from compound and measurement extraction because its tubulin polymerization inhibitory IC50 was reported as n.d. (not determined).
Censored measurements (>1000 nM in cellular assays and >10 or >5 µM in biochemical TPI assays) are retained as quantitative upper bounds as per guidelines.
Only explicit SMILES present in the PDF text are captured in provided_smiles; none were provided in the manuscript, so null was used.

Verified all 44 compounds in Table 1 with paired cell-free TPI and cellular antiproliferative IC50 values (compound 36 correctly excluded due to n.d. TPI). Added claim cl_4 covering the authors' explanation that higher polarity and basicity/protonation (especially for ortho-substituted dimethylaniline 49Z and polar amino analogs 43, 48Z, 60Z) reduce cellular uptake in HeLa cells, and expanded MDR1/Pgp efflux interventions (verapamil co-treatment for 44, 55Z, and negative control 67) and MPGI analogue comparison (49Z vs 60Z).

claims.author_explanation: For orthosteric inhibitors, higher physiological concentrations of intracellular ATP (1 mmol/L) compete with inhibitor binding at the ATP pocket, causing a shift to higher IC50 values compared to assays at Km,ATP.

evidence.experiment: Biochemical kinase mobility shift assays performed at Km,ATP versus 1 mmol/L physiological ATP
evidence.result: Orthosteric inhibitors displayed higher IC50 values at 1 mmol/L ATP than at Km,ATP, while the allosteric inhibitor JBJ-09-063 maintained similar potency across both ATP concentrations.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors explicitly tested kinase inhibition at both Km,ATP and 1 mmol/L ATP, demonstrating consistent right-shifts for orthosteric inhibitors (osimertinib, BLU-945, silevertinib), whereas allosteric JBJ-09-063 was ATP-independent. Grade 4: controlled intervention varying ATP concentration demonstrates causal potency modulation.

classification.rationale: Orthosteric inhibitor potency worsens at physiologically relevant ATP concentration, whereas the allosteric control is relatively insensitive. This directly supports ATP competition at the intracellular binding pocket as the reported mechanism.

eligibility.reason: The paper evaluates four EGFR inhibitors (osimertinib, BLU-945, JBJ-09-063, and silevertinib) side-by-side in both cell-free biochemical kinase activity assays across multiple EGFR variants and cellular viability assays across EGFR-mutant NSCLC cell lines.

insights.text: Fourth-generation EGFR inhibitors display markedly divergent selectivity and resistance profiles against T790M and C797S mutations.
Orthosteric inhibitors experience a substantial drop in potency at physiological 1 mM ATP compared to Km,ATP, whereas allosteric JBJ-09-063 maintains ATP-independent potency.
Silevertinib retains sub-nanomolar affinity and biochemical potency against C797S-containing double mutants despite losing the cysteine required for its covalent warhead.
In the triple mutant L858R + T790M + C797S setting, allosteric inhibitor JBJ-09-063 shows the strongest cellular antiproliferative activity among tested inhibitors.

review_notes: Assay concentration for ATP at 1 mmol/L was used to reflect intracellular ATP levels and explains the loss of apparent potency of orthosteric inhibitors in cells.
Table 2 notes that for the EGFR L858R + T790M + C797S mutant, biochemical kinase assay was not available at Km,ATP because it did not meet predefined assay criteria.
Table 4 includes three distinct clones of CRISPR-engineered NCI-H1975 C797S; measurements from clone 1 were extracted as representative for pairing.

claims.author_explanation: Differences in intracellular CRBN binding relative to biochemical affinity reflect membrane permeability, driven by linker flexibility and conformational folding in apolar environments: the flexible PEG linker in 1 enables folded, spherical conformations that shield polar surface area (via intramolecular hydrogen bonding, pi-pi and van der Waals interactions), whereas more rigid or alkyl-amide linkers (2 and 3) favor extended conformations with high solvent-accessible 3D polar surface area and poorer cell penetration.

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 passive permeability (Ppassive) and PAMPA (-LogPe) determinations alongside cell/bio CRBN binding ratios.
evidence.result: Permeability ranking across Caco-2 monolayers (Ppassive: 30 nm/s for 1, 10 nm/s for 2, 5 nm/s for 3) and PAMPA (-LogPe: 6.56 for 1 vs >7.37 for 3) matches the CRBN cell/biochemical potency ratio ranking (4 for 1, 12 for 2, 27 for 3).

evidence.experiment: Solution NMR spectroscopy (NAMFIS deconvolution of NOESY build-ups in CDCl3) and unrestrained MD simulations in explicit chloroform.
evidence.result: PROTAC 1 populates folded conformations with lower radius of gyration (Rgyr) and lower solvent-accessible 3D polar surface area (SA 3D PSA) stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonds and pi-pi stacking, whereas 2 and especially 3 populate more extended, higher SA 3D PSA conformations.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured the cellular-to-biochemical potency ratio as a surrogate for permeability and confirmed the permeability differences orthogonally via PAMPA and Caco-2 assays, supported by extensive solution-phase NMR conformational analyses and MD simulations. However, they did not perform a direct causal rescue test (such as chemical formulation, prodrug cleavage, or membrane perturbation) on the exact same chemical series in the cell assay.

classification.rationale: Caco-2 passive permeability and PAMPA measurements track cellular/biochemical potency ratios across the compounds. Linker-dependent folding, intramolecular hydrogen bonds and polar shielding explain the entry differences upstream. Passive entry is the explicitly measured bottleneck; separating an additional chameleonicity cause from the same claim would require a secondary annotation rather than duplicate primary classification.

eligibility.reason: The study reports cellular GPCR antagonism (beta-arrestin recruitment IC50s in Table 1 and inverse agonism IC50s in Figure 5) for clotrimazole, itraconazole, quercetin, and TIPT, but their cell-free enzyme potencies are only cited from prior literature (TIPT has only a single-dose 10 uM % beta-lactamase activity reading in Table 2). Conversely, cell-free IC50s against beta-lactamase and cruzain are measured for genistein and luteolin (Table 3), whose GPCR activities are only cited from external literature. Thus, no compound has both quantitative cell-free and cellular potencies measured in this paper.

insights.text: Known small-molecule aggregators (clotrimazole, itraconazole, quercetin, TIPT) inhibit live-cell GPCR signaling at micromolar concentrations commensurate with their critical aggregation concentrations.

The cellular inhibitory activity of colloidal aggregators against GPCRs can be attenuated or eliminated by pre-centrifugation of stock solutions or by the addition of 0.025% nonionic detergent (Tween-80).
Colloid formers can directly suppress basal GPCR signaling in the absence of agonist, functioning as apparent inverse agonists, and can also sequester peptide ligands onto colloidal surfaces.

review_notes: Verified against the PDF that no compound has paired quantitative cell-free and cellular potency measurements in this study: clotrimazole, itraconazole, quercetin, and TIPT have cellular GPCR IC50s (Table 1, Figures 2, 4, 5; TIPT has only a single-dose 10 uM % beta-lactamase reading in Table 2), whereas genistein and luteolin have only cell-free counter-screen enzyme IC50s (Table 3). claims.author_explanation: Low aqueous solubility caused compounds to precipitate out of assay media, interfering with accurate biological evaluation in both biochemical and cellular assays upon N-methylation of the lariat nitrogen in the spirocyclic series.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of kinetic solubility (KSol) and potency of spirocyclic-capped compounds vs difluorocyclobutyl-capped compounds (17 vs 18).
evidence.result: Difluorocyclobutyl-capped 18 maintained potency and had higher solubility (Compound 3 KSol = 109 uM vs Compound 2 = 18.9 uM), overcoming the potency loss observed for 14 and 16.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors measured kinetic solubility (KSol) and observed a correlation between low solubility and anomalous potency loss upon methylation in the spiro-cap series (Compound 2 KSol 18.9 uM vs Compound 3 KSol 109 uM), leading to rescue when introducing the more soluble difluorocyclobutyl cap (18 vs 17), but they did not directly quantify precipitate in the well.

classification.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
classification.rationale: Measured aqueous solubility, observations of precipitation and analogue comparisons support limited soluble compound availability after lariat N-methylation. The supplied evidence supports a solubility limitation rather than an independently measured membrane entry defect; the analogue comparison is not an isolated causal rescue.

claims.author_explanation: Increasing steric bulk and lipophilic character with branched isopropyl (31) or isobutyl (32) groups on the pyridone-ether negatively impacted cellular potency despite retaining biochemical potency.

evidence.experiment: Alkyl scan on the pyridone-ether moiety comparing methyl, ethyl, isopropyl, isobutyl, and cyclopropyl groups for FP IC50 and NCI-H1048 GI50.
evidence.result: 31 and 32 showed Cyclin A FP IC50 values of 0.033 and 0.027 uM, but cellular GI50 dropped to 0.100 and 0.057 uM, respectively.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 2: The authors observed a discrepancy between maintained biochemical potency and reduced cellular potency for bulkier alkyl ethers (31, 32 vs 29, 30, 33) across an SAR series without direct intracellular concentration or permeation rescue assays.

classification.specific_cause: Physicochemical Defects (Excessive Hydrophobicity, Poor Membrane Permeability)
classification.rationale: The supplied explanation reports bulkier, more lipophilic substituents associated with poorer cellular potency while biochemical potency remains similar. Excessive hydrophobicity/steric physicochemical properties are the stated factors. Passive entry is not explicitly established by this claim or its SAR evidence, so the recorded permeability label should not automatically become the specific permeability cause. The underlying cellular mechanism remains unresolved.

claims.author_explanation: Passive membrane permeability (measured by MDCK Papp) and substituent volume modulate cellular potency across the macrocycle series; specifically, matched pair 12 (phenyl ether) and 13 (pyridone-ether) have identical biochemical potency (0.073 vs 0.071 uM), but conversion to the pyridone-ether increases MDCK permeability (1.1 to 1.9 x 10^-6 cm/s) and improves cellular GI50 (0.107 to 0.019 uM), an advantage also observed when converting 24 to pyridone-ether 29 and when optimizing the lariat linker and cap (19-24).

evidence.experiment: MDCK monolayer permeability (Papp) and NCI-H1048 cellular proliferation (GI50) measurements for matched pair 12 (A = CH) and 13 (A = N, pyridone-ether) as well as 24 and 29.
evidence.result: Despite equivalent Cyclin A FP IC50 (0.073 vs 0.071 uM), pyridone-ether 13 exhibited higher MDCK Papp (1.9 vs 1.1 x 10^-6 cm/s) and >5-fold more potent cellular GI50 (0.019 vs 0.107 uM) than phenyl ether 12; similarly, 29 improved MDCK Papp to 14.0 x 10^-6 cm/s and cellular GI50 to <0.01 uM relative to 24 (MDCK 9.0, GI50 0.026 uM).

evidence.experiment: Matched-pair comparison of spirocyclic cap vs difluorocyclobutyl cap and alkene hydrogenation in extended lariat compounds (19-24 and Figure 6) across Cyclin A FP IC50, NCI-H1048 GI50, and MDCK Papp.
evidence.result: Swapping from the spiro-cap to the difluorocyclobutyl-cap (19 to 20; 21 to 22) and saturating the extended lariat alkene (20 to 23; 22 to 24) simultaneously improved biochemical binding, MDCK permeability (e.g., 2.9 in 21 to 6.5 in 22 and 9.0 in 24), and cellular GI50 (0.244 uM in 21 to 0.098 uM in 22 and 0.026 uM in 24).

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors measured passive permeability in MDCK monolayers across matched pairs (e.g., 12 vs 13, 19 vs 20, 21 vs 22, 24 vs 29) showing that improved MDCK Papp correlates with stronger cellular antiproliferative GI50 even when biochemical FP IC50 is unchanged (12 vs 13, 24 vs 29).

classification.rationale: Matched-series MDCK Papp measurements improve alongside cellular potency, including comparisons retaining similar biochemical potency. This supports membrane entry as the reported mechanism; other cap/linker comparisons also change affinity and do not isolate permeability causally.

eligibility.reason: The paper evaluates macrocyclic peptide inhibitors of Cyclin A/B with both cell-free biochemical binding assays (fluorescence polarization and surface plasmon resonance) and cellular proliferation assays (MTT GI50 in NCI-H1048, NCI-H69, and NCI-H446 small-cell lung cancer cells).

insights.text: Macrocyclic peptides targeting the Cyclin A/B RxL Hydrophobic Patch achieved sub-50 nM biochemical and cellular potency by optimizing backbone N-methylation and replacing peptide bridging segments with extended alkyl chains.
Replacement of the spirocyclic N-terminal cap with a difluorocyclobutyl cap significantly enhanced kinetic solubility while preserving low-nanomolar potency and high passive MDCK permeability.

Introduction of a 2-pyridone cyclopropyl ether on the phenylalanine residue yielded advanced lead 33, displaying oral bioavailability of 27.2% in mice while retaining sub-20 nM cellular potency against SCLC lines.

Potent cellular antiproliferative activity tracked target-specific Cyclin A/B inhibition, demonstrating >100-fold selectivity for Rb-dysregulated cancer lines (NCI-H1048, NCI-H69) over nontransformed WI-38 fibroblasts.

review_notes: Compound 1 (Compound 6 in ref. 39, Figure 4) was excluded from paired compounds because its cellular activity is stated qualitatively as 'Cell Inactive' without a numerical concentration bound (Cyclin A FP IC50 = 12.7 uM).
Compound 14 in Table 3 was excluded because its cellular GI50 was reported as 'NC' (not calculated).
Compounds 4, 5, and 6 in Table 1 were excluded from pairing because cellular potencies were not reported in Table 1.
Compounds 19, 21, and 22 were tested as alkene isomer mixtures; their isomeric identities were not separated or fully elucidated as stated in Table 4 footnotes.

Corrected R-group chemical structure descriptions for compounds 8, 9, 11, 12, 13 (Table 2) and 25, 26, 27, 28 (Table 6) based on visual inspection of the PDF tables, and added Cyclin B/E biochemical measurements (FP IC50 and SPR KD), NCI-H69 GI50 for Compound 2, and passive permeability claims/interventions.
The clinical candidate CID-078 is mentioned in the conclusions as structurally related to 33, but its chemical structure and individual quantitative data were not disclosed in this manuscript.

claims.author_explanation: The low cellular degradation efficacy of triazole-ester-linked degraders AP2 and AP5 (which prevented DC50 determination despite nanomolar cell-free HDAC6/10 inhibition) is in very good agreement with their low stability in human plasma and BSA control solutions; ring-opened bicyclic analogs AP3 and AP6 also showed lower stability than tricyclic tubastatin A-based degraders AP1 and AP4.

evidence.experiment: 24 h stability assay of AP1-AP6 and tubastatin A at 50 nM and 1 µM in human plasma and 1 µM in 4% BSA control (Figure 4).
evidence.result: Triazole-ester linked AP2 and AP5 showed the lowest stability in both human plasma and BSA; tubastatin A-based AP1 and AP4 were more stable than ring-opened analogs AP3 and AP6, with AP1 remaining stable over 24 h.

evidence.experiment: Western blot HDAC6 and HDAC10 degradation and DC50 determination in MM.1S cells for hexyl-amide-linked AP1/AP4 versus triazole-ester-linked AP2/AP5 and tricyclic AP1/AP4 versus bicyclic AP3/AP6 (Table 2, Figure 5, Figure 6).
evidence.result: Stable hexyl-amide-linked AP1 and AP4 achieved potent cellular degradation (HDAC6 DC50 = 13 nM and 1.3 nM; HDAC10 DC50 = 29 nM and 1.7 nM), whereas unstable AP2 and AP5 showed weak or minimal degradation (DC50 not determinable).

claims.grade_rationale: Authors directly measured compound stability over 24 h in human plasma (50 nM and 1 µM) and 4% BSA control (Figure 4) and compared structural analogs with more stable hexyl-amide linkers (AP1, AP4 vs AP2, AP5) and tricyclic warheads (AP1, AP4 vs AP3, AP6), showing substantially stronger cellular degradation, although linker length and warhead structure also influence ternary complex formation.

classification.rationale: AP2/AP5 show poorer chemical/plasma stability and weaker cellular degradation despite biochemical inhibition; stable amide comparators retain stronger degradation. Compound degradation/conversion falls under metabolism and efflux. Concurrent linker changes limit causal attribution but do not negate the supplied supporting measurements.

claims.author_explanation: The diminished cellular degradation potencies of AP2 and AP5 compared with AP1, AP3, AP4, and AP6 may also be attributed to their longer triazole-containing linkers, potentially affecting the formation of a productive ternary complex.
claims.category: Unfavorable Linker Length / Ternary Complex Formation

evidence.experiment: Comparison of cellular HDAC6/10 degradation in MM.1S cells (Table 2) between longer triazole-ester linkers (AP2, AP5) and shorter hexyl-amide linkers (AP1, AP4).
evidence.result: Shorter hexyl-amide degraders AP1 and AP4 potently degraded HDAC6 and HDAC10 with nanomolar DC50 values, whereas longer linker analogs AP2 and AP5 exhibited diminished cellular degradation.

claims.grade_rationale: Supported by SAR comparison between longer triazole-ester linked degraders (AP2, AP5) and shorter hexyl-amide linked degraders (AP1, AP4), which is confounded by the concurrent difference in chemical and plasma stability.

classification.rationale: The proposed bottleneck is PROTAC linker geometry and formation of a productive target–degrader–E3 ternary complex. Consistent with the existing Pal2021 classifier assignments, induced ternary-complex assembly is treated as outside the dedicated target localization/oligomerization cause. The supplied SAR supports the attribution weakly and is confounded by stability; it does not directly measure ternary-complex formation.

claims.author_explanation: All PROTACs exhibited single- or double-digit micromolar IC50 values in the intact-cell CRBN NanoBRET target engagement and cell permeability assay (with AP3 weakest at <=80.8 µM); pomalidomide-based degraders AP1-AP3 had higher TPSA and weaker cellular CRBN engagement than phenylglutarimide-based degraders AP4-AP6, which achieved lower cellular DC50 values.
claims.category: Low Cell Permeability / Weak Intracellular E3 Ligase Engagement

evidence.experiment: Intact-cell NanoBRET CRBN target engagement competition assay in HEK293T NanoLuc-CRBN cells and physicochemical profiling (Table 1).
evidence.result: Phenylglutarimides AP4 (IC50 = 2.2 µM), AP5 (2.5 µM), and AP6 (15.6 µM) had lower TPSA (142.0-169.9 Å²) and stronger cellular CRBN engagement than pomalidomide analogs AP1 (*7.5 µM), AP2 (*4.4 µM), and AP3 (*80.8 µM; TPSA 182.2-210.1 Å²).

evidence.experiment: Comparison of 24 h cellular HDAC6 and HDAC10 DC50 values in MM.1S cells between pomalidomide-based (AP1, AP3) and phenylglutarimide-based (AP4, AP6) degraders (Table 2, Figure 6).
evidence.result: Replacing pomalidomide with phenylglutarimide improved HDAC6/10 DC50 from 13/29 nM (AP1) to 1.3/1.7 nM (AP4) and from 16/50 nM (AP3) to 4.5/7.9 nM (AP6), though introducing a hook effect at higher concentrations.

claims.grade_rationale: Supported by intact-cell CRBN NanoBRET target engagement/permeability measurements (Table 1), experimental elogD7.4 and calculated TPSA values, and consistent cellular DC50 improvements for phenylglutarimide analogs AP4 and AP6 over pomalidomide analogs AP1 and AP3 (Table 2).

classification.rationale: The extracted claim interprets poorer intact-cell CRBN engagement and higher TPSA as limited cellular access, with corresponding cellular DC50 differences. This makes permeability the closest primary stated mechanism. NanoBRET engagement is an intracellular availability proxy that also depends on CRBN affinity, which changes with E3-ligand chemistry; it is not a direct isolated measurement of passive entry and requires review.

eligibility.reason: The study reports quantitative cell-free biochemical IC50 values against recombinant human HDAC6 and HDAC10 alongside quantitative intact-cell degradation potencies (DC50) in MM.1S multiple myeloma cells for compounds AP1, AP3, AP4, and AP6.

insights.text: Degraders AP1, AP3, AP4, and AP6 all maintain nanomolar cell-free catalytic inhibition of both HDAC6 and HDAC10 while also achieving single- or double-digit nanomolar degradation (DC50) in MM.1S cells.
Phenylglutarimide-based degraders AP4 and AP6 demonstrated lower DC50 degradation values than pomalidomide-based degraders AP1 and AP3, but exhibited prominent hook effects at higher concentrations.

For compounds AP1, AP4, and AP6, cellular DC50 values for HDAC6 degradation were equal to or more potent than cell-free enzyme inhibition IC50 values, consistent with sub-stoichiometric event-driven degradation.
Triazole-linked degraders AP2 and AP5 displayed low degradation efficacy and did not yield measurable DC50 values, which correlated with reduced stability in human plasma.

review_notes: All six PROTACs (AP1-AP6) with cell-free HDAC6/10 enzymatic IC50 values and intact-cell CRBN NanoBRET IC50 values in Table 1 (pages 15-16) were extracted; AP1, AP3, AP4, and AP6 also have paired cellular HDAC6/10 degradation DC50 values in MM.1S cells (Table 2, page 19).

Compounds AP2 and AP5 were evaluated for cellular HDAC6/10 degradation at 1 and 5 µM (Table 2), where their DC50 values were not determined (n.d.) due to weak/minimal degradation; their cell-free HDAC6/10 IC50 and cellular CRBN NanoBRET IC50 values are retained.

Authors explicitly attribute the low cellular degradation efficacy of AP2 and AP5 to low plasma/chemical stability (Figure 4, page 17; text page 18) and longer triazole-containing linkers affecting productive ternary complex formation (page 19), and discuss differences in cellular CRBN target engagement/permeability (Table 1) and warhead structure across AP1-AP6 (page 20).

Reference compounds (Vorinostat, Quisinostat, Lenalidomide, and Tubastatin A) lacked paired cell-free and cellular potencies measured in this study, and analogs AP7-AP10 and AP1-N were tested only at single concentrations (1 and 5 µM) in western blots without IC50 or DC50 determination.

claims.author_explanation: The authors explain that low cellular permeability (low Caco-2 Papp), active efflux (efflux ratio 26-34), and high topological polar surface area (tPSA = 122-167 A^2, needing reduction to <120 A^2) prevent sufficient cell penetration, accounting for the potency drops between enzymatic CatD and cellular/ex vivo cartilage GAG release assays (e.g., 3-fold for 27 and 40-fold for 32).

evidence.experiment: In vitro Caco-2 cell permeability assay measuring Papp (A to B) and efflux ratio
evidence.result: Compound 27 had Papp of 5 x 10^-6 cm/s with an efflux ratio of 26; compound 32 had Papp of 0.25 x 10^-6 cm/s with an efflux ratio of 34, showing low passive permeability and active efflux.

evidence.experiment: Author synthesis and interpretation linking permeability/efflux measurements with biochemical vs explant potency gaps
evidence.result: Authors conclude that compounds 27 and especially 32 were unable to show sufficient cell penetration, which explains the observed drops between enzymatic and cellular potencies.

evidence.experiment: Calculation of topological polar surface area (tPSA) in MOE and SAR comparison across analogues 24, 27, 30, 32, and 38
evidence.result: Higher tPSA in tetrazole 32 (167 A^2) compared to fluorinated analogue 27 (122 A^2) was associated with 20-fold lower Caco-2 permeability (0.25 vs 5 x 10^-6 cm/s), higher efflux (34 vs 26), and a larger biochemical-to-cellular potency drop (40-fold vs 3-fold); authors state tPSA must be reduced below 120 A^2.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured Caco-2 permeability (Papp A to B) and efflux ratio directly for representative compounds 27 and 32 (Table 3), demonstrating low Papp (5 x 10^-6 and 0.25 x 10^-6 cm/s) and significant efflux (ratios 26 and 34). This mechanistic measurement correlates with the potency drop between biochemical CatD and cartilage explant GAG assays. However, no controlled rescue experiment (such as co-treatment with an efflux pump inhibitor or formulation/prodrug rescue) was conducted in the cartilage assay. Therefore, this is graded as mechanistic measurement without controlled causal rescue (Grade 3).

classification.rationale: The explanation combines low passive permeability (low Caco-2 Papp, high tPSA) and strong active efflux (efflux ratio 26-34) as co-central causes of poor cell penetration.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Compounds 32 and 27 are matched analogues sharing the exact acylguanidine core, P1/P3 3,4-dimethoxyphenyl ring, and P3' cyclohexyl substituent, differing only in the S2/S3' benzyl amide substitution (4-tetrazolyl vs 4-fluoro-3-methoxy). interventions.description: Analogue comparison on the shared 3,4-dimethoxyphenyl P1/P3 and cyclohexyl P3' scaffold between para-tetrazole amide 32 (tPSA = 167 A^2) and 4-fluoro-3-methoxybenzyl amide 27 (tPSA = 122 A^2), showing higher Caco-2 permeability (5 vs 0.25 x 10^-6 cm/s), lower efflux (ratio 26 vs 34), improved GAG cellular potency (0.5 vs 1.8 uM), and a smaller potency dropoff (3-fold vs 40-fold) for the lower-tPSA fluorinated analogue 27.

interventions.comparison_rationale: The authors explicitly describe replacing one or both methoxy groups of the S2/S3' benzyl amide substituent with fluorine (24 -> 27, 30) to reduce PSA, though simultaneous replacement of the P3' benzyl group with cyclohexyl confounds a single-point comparison.
interventions.description: Analogue modification reducing topological polar surface area (tPSA from 131 A^2 in 24 to 122 A^2 in 27) by replacing one methoxy group on the S2/S3' benzyl amide with fluorine (alongside benzyl-to-cyclohexyl replacement at P3'). While the enzymatic-to-cellular dropoff ratio narrowed (~3-fold for 27 vs ~5.7-fold for 24), absolute GAG cellular potency did not improve (0.5 uM vs 0.33 uM) as tPSA remained >120 A^2.

interventions.comparison_rationale: Authors explicitly linked replacement of methoxy by fluorine in 27-30 to PSA reduction and enhanced biochemical CatD affinity (30: IC50 = 24 nM), while noting that this did not translate into GAG assay potency gains (30: IC50 = 0.62 uM); simultaneous P3' benzyl-to-isobutyl replacement is a structural confounder.
interventions.description: Analogue modification reducing tPSA from 131 A^2 (in 24) to 122 A^2 (in 30) by replacing one methoxy group of the S2/S3' benzyl amide substituent with fluorine (4-fluoro-3-methoxybenzyl amide, alongside an isobutyl group at P3'). Despite >2-fold improved biochemical CatD potency (0.024 uM vs 0.058 uM), cellular GAG potency did not improve (0.62 uM vs 0.33 uM).

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free human Cathepsin D IC50 values and quantitative ex vivo cellular bovine cartilage explant GAG release IC50 values for the same series of acylguanidine analogues (compounds 24, 27, 30, 32, and 38).

insights.text: Acylguanidine Cathepsin D inhibitors achieved single-digit nanomolar biochemical IC50 values (e.g., compound 38, IC50 = 8.6 nM), but exhibited substantially attenuated micromolar to submicromolar potencies in the ex vivo bovine cartilage explant GAG release assay.

The authors identified poor cellular permeability (Papp down to 0.25 x 10^-6 cm/s) and substantial active efflux (efflux ratios of 26 to 34 in Caco-2 cells) as the primary explanation for the 3-fold to 40-fold potency drop between enzymatic and cellular/ex vivo explant assays.

Elevated topological polar surface area (tPSA > 120 A^2) arising from the polar acylguanidine core and hydrogen-bonding substituents was proposed as a key structural liability limiting passive cell permeability.

X-ray crystallography of CatD-inhibitor complexes revealed that the acylguanidine moiety adopts a pseudo-6-membered ring conformation making essential H-bonds with the catalytic dyad Asp33 and Asp231, guiding subpocket-filling optimizations.

review_notes: Pepstatin A was tested as a reference inhibitor in the cartilage explant assay (IC50 = 1.5 nM), but its biochemical CatD potency in this paper was only cited from external literature (<1 nM), so it was not included as an extracted pair.
Earlier HTS compounds 5-9 and reference inhibitor 2 were stated in the text to show no inhibition of GAG release below 1 uM, but lacked explicit numerical IC50 determinations in Table 1 or Table 2.
Caco-2 Papp and efflux ratio data from Table 3 were captured as mechanistic evidence for claim_permeability_efflux rather than potency measurements.

No controlled non-chemical rescue interventions (such as co-dosing with an efflux inhibitor or prodrug conversion) were tested in the cartilage explant assay, and the authors' proposed cyclization of the acylguanidine core to reduce tPSA < 120 A^2 was a future design direction rather than a synthesized compound in this paper; however, author-discussed chemical modifications / analogue comparisons exploring PSA reduction and permeability/efflux differences (32 vs 27, 24 vs 27, and 24 vs 30) were recorded as interventions with mechanism_isolated=false.

claims.author_explanation: Discrepancies observed for the PROTACs between biochemical assays using isolated enzymes and the cellular NanoBRET assay likely result from limited cellular permeability due to high molecular weight.

evidence.experiment: Cellular HDAC inhibition assay measuring substrate deacetylation in both intact and lysed (0.05% IGEPAL CA-630) HeLa HDAC6-HiBiT cells treated with FF2014, A6, and vorinostat
evidence.result: FF2014 and A6 showed reduced cell permeability in intact cells compared to lysed cells, whereas small molecule inhibitor vorinostat did not show reduced permeability

claims.grade_rationale: Authors measured permeability directly by comparing cellular HDAC inhibition in intact vs lysed HeLa cells for PROTACs FF2014 and A6 versus vorinostat (Figure S2), demonstrating reduced cellular permeability for PROTACs. However, no controlled causal rescue of target engagement IC50 was performed with a permeabilizing agent for the PROTACs, warranting Grade 3.

classification.rationale: Reduced inhibition in intact versus lysed cells supports limited cellular membrane permeability of the high-MW PROTACs.

claims.author_explanation: Tracer 4 has lower apparent affinity in whole cells compared to permeabilized cells due to limited cell permeability conferred by its PEG linker, whereas tracer 5 with a shorter propylene linker has favorable permeability.

evidence.experiment: NanoBRET saturation binding assay of tracer 4 in whole cells compared to digitonin-permeabilized (50 µg/mL) cells
evidence.result: Digitonin permeabilization reduced the Kd of tracer 4 from 0.12 ± 0.04 µM to 0.046 ± 0.021 µM, establishing cell permeability limitation in intact cells

claims.grade_rationale: The authors performed a controlled intervention by permeabilizing cells with 50 µg/mL digitonin, which rescued the Kd of tracer 4 from 0.12 µM in whole cells to 0.046 µM in permeabilized cells, matching the biochemical potencies, isolating the membrane barrier as the cause (Grade 4).

classification.rationale: Digitonin permeabilization rescues the apparent affinity of tracer 4 in whole cells, directly supporting a passive membrane permeability limitation.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative cell-free biochemical HDAC inhibition IC50 values (Table 1 and Table 2) and quantitative cellular potency endpoints, including NanoBRET target engagement Kd/IC50/Ki values in whole HeLa cells and HiBiT live-cell degradation Dmax50 values for the same compounds (Table 2 and Table 3).

insights.text: Cellular permeability represents a major driver of potency loss when comparing PROTAC cell-free target affinity to cellular target engagement, as demonstrated by the comparison of PROTACs FF2014 and A6 with parent inhibitor vorinostat in intact versus lysed cell deacetylation assays.

Membrane permeabilization with digitonin directly isolated cell permeability as the factor lowering intact-cell apparent affinity (Kd) for tracer 4, whereas tracer 5 with a shorter propylene linker exhibited equal affinity in intact and permeabilized cells.

Endogenously tagged HDAC6 in HeLa cells via CRISPR/Cas9 HiBiT knock-in avoids overexpression artifacts and allows direct assessment of binary target engagement in a near-native environment using NanoBRET displacement.

Degradation efficiency (Dmax50 and degradation rate) does not directly mirror binary target engagement IC50; for example, A6 had a higher NanoBRET IC50 than FF2007 or FF2014 but elicited the fastest initial degradation rate.

review_notes: Table 2 reports HDAC6 enzyme inhibition IC50 values where certain values for previously published compounds (tubastatin A, BK1, ricolinostat, A6, B4, Gue3821, Gue3822) are annotated with citation superscripts to prior publications from the authors' laboratory using identical assay protocols, while vorinostat, FF2007, FF2014, and HDAC6 degrader 1 represent freshly evaluated measurements.

Compounds Gue3821 and HDAC6 degrader 1 exhibit autofluorescence at concentrations >= 2.34 µM that interferes with the NanoBRET signal, meaning their reported IC50 and Ki values in Table 2 represent upper estimates as noted by the authors.
PROTAC MM-47 in Figure 6 has reported degradation potency (Dmax50 = 0.014 µM) but lacks a biochemical potency measurement in this publication, so it was excluded from the paired compound dataset.

Added explicit cross-assay pairs linking cell-free HDAC6 IC50 to permeabilized-cell Kd (tracers 4 and 5), Cheng-Prusoff cellular Ki (Table 2), and live-cell degradation Dmax50 (Table 3), as well as interventions for tracer 5 digitonin permeabilization, the tracer 4 to 5 PEG-to-propylene linker modification, the intact vs IGEPAL-lysed cellular HDAC assay for PROTACs FF2014 and A6 (Figure S2), and the A6 to FF2014 CRBN-recruiter analogue comparison.
