claims.author_explanation: Rapid sequential enzymatic degradation of the exocyclic L-arginines at both termini leads to loss of cellular potency over time. Enantiomeric replacement with D-arginines provides proteolytic stability and confers cellular KRAS inhibition.

evidence.experiment: MetID profiling of KRpep-2d after incubation in homogenized THP-1 cells using high-resolution mass spectrometry.
evidence.result: Rapid sequential cleavage of terminal arginines from one or both termini within 10 min was detected.

evidence.experiment: Substitution of all eight terminal L-arginines in MP-6483 with D-arginines to yield MP-4090, followed by pERK inhibition assay in AsPC-1 cells.
evidence.result: MP-4090 demonstrated robust pERK and pAKT inhibition (1 h EC50 = 3.6 uM), rescuing cellular activity relative to MP-6483 (1 h EC50 = 15.9 uM; 18 h >50 uM).

claims.grade_rationale: Controlled intervention: MetID in THP-1 cell homogenate identified rapid arginine truncation within 10 min. Replacing L-Arg with D-Arg (MP-6483 -> MP-4090) preserved biochemical affinity (172.4 vs 140.7 nM) and improved 1 h cellular pERK EC50 from 15.9 uM to 3.6 uM, establishing sustained cellular target engagement (CETSA) and on-target activity.

classification.rationale: MetID and D-arginine replacement demonstrate that proteolytic degradation of terminal L-arginines causes the loss of cellular potency.

claims.author_explanation: Proteolytic cleavage between Tyr8 and Ile9 within the macrocycle causes an 8-fold drop in cellular potency between 1 h and 18 h for MP-4090. Incorporation of an alpha-methyl group at Ser10 stabilizes the backbone against degradation and rescues 18 h potency.

evidence.experiment: MetID in THP-1 cell homogenate on the macrocyclic core and stability profiling of alpha-methylated analogs in HeLa cell homogenate.
evidence.result: Tyr8-Ile9 was identified as a proteolytic cleavage site. Alpha-methylation at Ser10 increased homogenate t1/2 from 37 min (parent MP-1687) to 154 min.

evidence.experiment: Incorporation of alpha-methyl-Ser10 into MP-4090 to generate MP-3995, followed by pERK inhibition measurement at 1 h and 18 h in AsPC-1 cells.
evidence.result: MP-3995 maintained pERK EC50 of 1.2 uM at 1 h and 1.5 uM at 18 h, fully eliminating the 8-fold potency drop observed for MP-4090 (3.6 uM at 1 h vs 30.5 uM at 18 h).

claims.grade_rationale: Controlled intervention: Authors identified the Tyr8-Ile9 proteolytic soft spot by MetID in cell homogenate. An alpha-methyl scan identified alpha-Me-Ser10 as maintaining biochemical potency (62 nM vs 60 nM) while increasing HeLa homogenate half-life from 37 min to 154 min. Translating this into MP-4090 to produce MP-3995 rescued 18 h cellular pERK EC50 (1.5 uM vs 30.5 uM for MP-4090).

classification.rationale: Proteolytic cleavage of the macrocycle at Tyr8-Ile9 causes time-dependent potency loss, which is rescued by metabolic stabilization via alpha-methylation at Ser10.

claims.author_explanation: Cellular activity is strictly dependent on membrane translocation mediated by at least 8 exocyclic arginine residues. Truncating the arginine tails abrogates cellular permeability (measured by NanoClick) and abolishes cellular pERK inhibition (>50 uM) despite retaining high biochemical KRAS binding affinity.

evidence.experiment: Systematic arginine truncation series (8, 6, 4, 2, 1, 0 Arg residues) tested in KRAS(G12D) TR-FRET and AsPC-1 pERK assays.
evidence.result: Biochemical TR-FRET EC50 remained between 59.4 and 409.5 nM, but cellular pERK EC50 dropped from 3.6 uM (8 Arg) to >50 uM for all peptides with 6 or fewer arginines.

evidence.experiment: NanoClick bioorthogonal intracellular click permeability assay across the arginine truncation series.
evidence.result: Permeability EC50 weakened from 251 nM (8 Arg) to 3314 nM (6 Arg), 4552 nM (4 Arg), 6939 nM (2 Arg), and >10 000 nM (0-1 Arg), correlating directly with the loss of cellular pERK inhibition.

claims.grade_rationale: Systematic SAR association and mechanistic measurement: A series with 8, 6, 4, 2, 1, and 0 arginines was evaluated for biochemical binding, NanoClick permeability, and cellular pERK inhibition. Diminishing arginine content below 8 caused a loss of intracellular delivery and cellular potency without impacting cell-free KRAS binding.

classification.rationale: NanoClick permeability assays across the arginine truncation series show that loss of membrane translocation explains the loss of cellular activity.

claims.author_explanation: The disulfide bridge of the parent peptide KRpep-2d is reduced in the intracellular environment to a non-binding linear form, obviating cellular activity. Replacement with a redox-insensitive D-Cys5-CH2-L-Cys15 thioacetal crosslink (MP-6483) preserves KRAS binding under reducing conditions and enables initial cellular pERK inhibition.

evidence.experiment: SPR and TR-FRET binding assays of KRpep-2d and thioacetal analog MP-6483 in oxidizing vs reducing (1 mM DTT) conditions.
evidence.result: KRpep-2d lost all binding in the presence of 1 mM DTT (TR-FRET EC50 shifted from 1916 nM to >50,000 nM), whereas MP-6483 maintained binding in 1 mM DTT (EC50 = 93 nM vs 172 nM).

claims.grade_rationale: Mechanistic measurement and SAR: Authors demonstrated by SPR and TR-FRET that parent KRpep-2d loses all binding in 1 mM DTT (TR-FRET EC50 >50,000 nM vs 1916 nM) whereas thioacetal analog MP-6483 retains potency in 1 mM DTT (93 nM vs 172 nM) and gains weak cellular activity (1 h pERK EC50 = 15.9 uM). Graded 3 because parent KRpep-2d lacks a quantitative cellular potency bound in the main text for a formal paired before/after comparison.

classification.rationale: Intracellular reductive cleavage of the peptide disulfide bridge inactivates the compound, representing intracellular chemical/metabolic transformation.

insights.text: Replacement of the KRpep-2d labile disulfide bridge with a D-Cys5-CH2-L-Cys15 thioacetal linkage preserved high-affinity KRAS binding in both oxidizing and reducing conditions, overcoming cytosolic reduction liabilities.

Sequential exopeptidase degradation of terminal L-arginines was demonstrated in cell homogenate, and stereochemical inversion to D-arginines (MP-4090) established on-target cellular pERK and pAKT inhibition.

An internal proteolytic cleavage site at Tyr8-Ile9 caused an 8-fold loss in cellular pERK inhibition between 1 h and 18 h; backbone alpha-methylation at Ser10 (MP-3995) resolved this instability, sustaining cellular potency (EC50 1.2-1.5 uM).

Cellular membrane permeability strictly required at least eight exocyclic arginines; truncating the arginine tails (compounds 23, MP-1687, MP-9903, 24, 25) eliminated cell entry and cellular activity despite maintaining high biochemical affinity.

Cationic poly-arginine tails induced potent IgE-independent mast cell degranulation in an ex vivo assay, uncovering a critical dose-limiting safety liability inherent to arginine-mediated cellular uptake.

review_notes: Table 3 and Table 5 both report data for MP-4090 and MP-6483; values are concordant except 18 h pERK EC50 for MP-4090 which is reported as 30.5 uM in Table 3 and 30.8 uM in Table 5.

LDH cytotoxicity and NanoClick permeability EC50 values from Table 3 and Table 5 are extracted as assays/measurements where appropriate, but pairs strictly compare biochemical target engagement to cellular functional pERK pathway inhibition.
Parent KRpep-2d and truncation/alanine analogs in Tables 1, 2, and 4 lack quantitative cellular potency measurements in the manuscript and were therefore excluded from the paired compound dataset.

claims.author_explanation: The substantial potency shift between biochemical AVP inhibition and cellular CPE assay for glycine nitrile derivatives (such as 13) is attributed to low to moderate passive permeability and high active efflux.

evidence.experiment: Caco-2 and PAMPA permeability measurements for glycine nitrile series compounds including 13.
evidence.result: Compounds 7-13 displayed low to moderate permeability with high efflux ratios (compound 13 Caco-2 A-B/B-A = 7.3/12.2 x 10^-6 cm/s), consistent with the large shift from biochemical IC50 (10-20 nM) to cellular EC50 (2.5 μM).

evidence.experiment: Replacement of the P1/P2 glycine nitrile amide bond with a 4-(aminomethyl)pyrimidine-2-carbonitrile core (compounds 14-17) and profiling in Caco-2, PAMPA, biochemical FLT, and HEK293 CPE assays.
evidence.result: Pyrimidine nitriles 14-17 showed high Caco-2 permeability (12.2-23.2 x 10^-6 cm/s) and no efflux while improving biochemical potency (IC50 down to 2-3 nM for 16-17), yet cellular CPE EC50 values remained in the micromolar range (1.2-7.2 μM), leaving a substantial residual potency shift.

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 3: The authors measured Caco-2 and PAMPA permeability and efflux ratios for glycine nitriles, correlating these mechanistic transport properties with the cell-free to cellular potency gap, but did not perform a controlled causal rescue (e.g., efflux inhibition) on the same compounds.

classification.rationale: Combines low passive permeability and high active efflux as co-equal causes, and replacement with permeable, non-effluxed pyrimidine nitriles still left a large cellular potency shift.

claims.author_explanation: Despite excellent drug-like properties, high Caco-2 permeability, and lack of efflux, pyrimidine nitriles 16 and 17 still displayed EC50 values of 3.2 and 1.2 μM in the CPE assay; the authors explicitly state that the reasons for this moderate cellular activity remain to be elucidated.

evidence.experiment: Comparison of single-digit nanomolar biochemical IC50s with micromolar cellular CPE EC50s in pyrimidine nitriles 16 and 17 possessing high Caco-2 permeability.
evidence.result: The authors state: 'Unfortunately, however, despite their drug-like properties, 16 and 17 displayed EC50s of only 3 and 1 μM, respectively, in the CPE assay. The reasons for this moderate cellular activity remain to be elucidated.'

claims.grade_rationale: Grade 1: Explicit author statement acknowledging that the residual biochemical-to-cellular potency shift in pyrimidine nitriles 16 and 17 remains unexplained despite resolved permeability and efflux.

classification.rationale: Authors explicitly state that the reason for the residual biochemical-to-cellular potency drop remains unknown despite good permeability and lack of efflux.

eligibility.reason: The paper reports both cell-free biochemical protease inhibition (IC50 against adenoviral proteases AVP8 and AVP5 in a fluorescence lifetime assay) and cellular antiviral efficacy (EC50 in a cytopathic effect [CPE] assay in HEK293 cells) for compounds 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17.

insights.text: For peptidic glycine nitrile adenain inhibitors, low passive permeability and active efflux were identified by the authors as major contributors to the substantial potency shift between biochemical FLT assays and cellular viral replication inhibition.

Replacement of the peptidic P1/P2 glycine nitrile with a 4-(aminomethyl)pyrimidine-2-carbonitrile scaffold eliminated efflux and yielded high Caco-2 permeability while retaining single-digit nanomolar biochemical adenain potency.

Despite overcoming the permeability and efflux liabilities of the peptidic series, optimized pyrimidine nitriles 16 and 17 still displayed micromolar cellular CPE activity, an effect the authors noted remains unexplained.

review_notes: Hit compound 1 was noted to be completely inactive in viral replication assays, but without an exact quantitative numerical boundary, so it was excluded from paired extraction.
Compounds 3-12 only have cell-free biochemical IC50 and physicochemical/transport data reported in Table 1; cellular CPE EC50 was only reported for compound 13 in the accompanying text.
Table 2 reports CPE EC50 values for compounds 14-17 with n >= 5 independent assays.

claims.author_explanation: Carrier-mediated efflux selectively affects compound 1 (but not its enantiomer compound 2), decreasing its intracellular bioavailability (Fic) and thereby limiting its cellular potency relative to compound 2 despite identical biochemical potency.

evidence.experiment: Measurement of Fic in PBMCs for compounds 1 and 2 in the absence and presence of cyclosporine A
evidence.result: Fic of compound 1 increased threefold in the presence of cyclosporine A (P = 0.05), whereas compound 2 showed no change (P = 0.95)

evidence.experiment: Comparison of Fic and cellular pIC50 between enantiomers compound 1 and compound 2 in PBMCs
evidence.result: Compound 2 had 2.3-fold higher Fic and 2.5-fold higher cellular potency (IC50 4.5 nM vs 12 nM) than compound 1, despite identical biochemical IC50 (12 nM)

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured intracellular bioavailability (Fic) in the presence and absence of cyclosporine A (a pan-transporter inhibitor), demonstrating that efflux inhibition increased Fic of compound 1 threefold while compound 2 was unaffected (mechanistic measurement). However, they did not perform a controlled functional rescue test showing that cyclosporine A restored cellular potency (IC50) of compound 1.

classification.rationale: Cyclosporine A-sensitive carrier-mediated efflux selectively lowers intracellular bioavailability and cellular potency of compound 1 relative to its enantiomer.

claims.author_explanation: Cell drop-off (lower cellular potency than biochemical potency) across p38alpha inhibitors is explained by low intracellular bioavailability (Fic), which reflects the combined effects of cellular permeability, binding, and transport, whereas artificial membrane permeability (PAMPA) fails to correlate with cellular drop-off.

evidence.experiment: Correlation of predicted cellular pIC50 (log Fic + biochemical pIC50) versus measured cellular PBMC pIC50 across 35 p38alpha inhibitors
evidence.result: Predicted cellular pIC50 strongly correlated with measured cellular pIC50 (rS = 0.79) and brought predicted potencies to the same numerical level as experimental ones

evidence.experiment: Correlation between PAMPA permeability and Fic or cell drop-off for p38alpha inhibitors
evidence.result: PAMPA permeability showed poor correlation with Fic (rS = 0.03) and did not explain the cell drop-off (rS = 0.21)

claims.grade_rationale: The authors measured Fic and PAMPA across 35 p38alpha inhibitors, showing that correcting biochemical pIC50 by Fic successfully predicted cellular potency (rS = 0.79) and explained the drop-off, whereas PAMPA did not correlate with Fic (rS = 0.03) or cell drop-off.

classification.rationale: Attributes drop-off to composite intracellular bioavailability (combining permeability, binding, and active transport) while explicitly ruling out passive artificial membrane permeability (PAMPA) as a correlate.

claims.author_explanation: For kinase inhibitors (such as the p38alpha inhibitors), the drop in potency from biochemical to cellular assays is commonly attributed to high cellular ATP concentrations competing with the inhibitor compared with the lower ATP concentrations used in biochemical assays, in addition to limited intracellular bioavailability (Fic).

evidence.experiment: Cited literature statement regarding ATP competition for kinase inhibitors in cellular versus biochemical assays
evidence.result: High cellular ATP concentrations relative to biochemical assay ATP (50 uM) are cited as a known contributor to lower cellular potency of kinase inhibitors

claims.grade_rationale: The authors mention high cellular ATP competition as a commonly attributed background mechanism for kinase inhibitor cell drop-off citing prior literature (refs. 3, 49, 50), without experimentally varying ATP concentrations in this study.

classification.rationale: Cites high intracellular ATP competition as a common literature explanation for kinase inhibitor potency drop-off without experimental testing in this study.

interventions.description: Inversion of configuration at the single stereocenter (compound 1 to enantiomer compound 2) avoids carrier-mediated efflux, increasing intracellular bioavailability (Fic) 2.3-fold and improving cellular potency 2.5-fold (IC50 12 nM to 4.5 nM) while maintaining identical biochemical target potency (IC50 12 nM).

eligibility.reason: The paper reports quantitative biochemical IC50 (12 nM / pIC50 7.9) and cellular IC50 (12 nM and 4.5 nM / pIC50 7.9 and 8.4) for an enantiomeric pair of p38alpha (MAPK14) inhibitors (compounds 1 and 2) in human PBMCs.

insights.text: Intracellular bioavailability (Fic), defined as the ratio of intracellular unbound to extracellular concentration, directly bridges the gap between biochemical and cellular potencies.

For an enantiomeric pair of p38alpha inhibitors with identical cell-free potency (IC50 = 12 nM), stereoselective carrier-mediated efflux lowered the cellular bioavailability and cellular potency of compound 1 relative to compound 2.
Transporter pan-inhibition by cyclosporine A selectively increased Fic of compound 1 threefold while compound 2 was unaffected, confirming the role of active efflux in cellular disposition.

Artificial membrane permeability (PAMPA) failed to correlate with Fic (rS = 0.03) or explain cellular drop-off, demonstrating that rate-based permeability does not equate to steady-state unbound intracellular drug concentration.

review_notes: The manuscript contains three datasets: 35 p38alpha inhibitors, 51 PKIS kinase inhibitors, and 30 BACE-1 inhibitors. However, individual compound identities and numerical potency values are only reported in the main text and figures for the enantiomeric pair (compounds 1 and 2); the remaining compounds reside in Supplementary Datasets S1-S3, which are not included in the PDF.
Both IC50 (in nM) from page 3 text and pIC50 from Fig. 2E/2F labels were captured for completeness.

Cyclosporine A was tested for its effect on Fic (mechanistic measurement), but its effect on functional cellular potency (IC50 rescue) was not measured; thus claim-carrier-mediated-efflux is graded 3.

claims.grade_rationale: Intact-cell CETSA directly measured intracellular target engagement across multiple concentrations, confirming that compound 4 readily penetrates cells and binds eIF4E with single-digit micromolar potency.

classification.rationale: Intact-cell CETSA confirmed robust intracellular target engagement matching lysate potency, ruling out lack of cellular target engagement.

claims.author_explanation: The authors established that the drop-off in cellular functional activity (lack of cap-dependent translation inhibition and lack of anti-proliferative effect) occurs because eIF4G engages eIF4E via an extended protein-protein interface; small-molecule binding to site 2 (non-canonical interface) alone is insufficient in intact cells, and simultaneous disruption of both the canonical interface (e.g. via W73F mutation) and non-canonical site 2 (via compound 4 or L85R mutation) is required to drive strong cellular functional inhibition.

evidence.experiment: Genetic rescue of eIF4E-dTAG degraded H1299 cells with canonical and site 2 mutants alone and in combination with compound 4 (25 µM)
evidence.result: Neither compound 4 alone nor W73F alone impaired proliferation, but compound 4 combined with the W73F mutant caused significant inhibition of cell proliferation, matching the genetic W73F/L85R double mutant phenotype.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors performed a controlled causal genetic-pharmacological intervention: in an eIF4E-dTAG degradation model rescued with eIF4E variants, compound 4 had no functional effect alone, and the W73F canonical mutant rescued proliferation normally, but combining compound 4 treatment with the W73F mutant produced a profound synthetic loss of proliferation, fully phenocopying the W73F/L85R double mutant.

classification.rationale: Intracellular eIF4G binds eIF4E via a multipartite PPI interface (canonical + non-canonical sites), so small-molecule inhibition at site 2 alone cannot overcome the full complex interaction in intact cells.

eligibility.reason: Compound 4 has quantitative cell-free binding affinities determined by ITC (Kd = 0.017 µM for D127N and 0.09 µM for D127), quantitative protein-protein interaction disruption in cell lysates (EC50 = 1.4 µM in HeLa, 2.6 µM in SW620, and ~1.5 µM in H1299 lysates), and quantitative intact-cell target engagement determined by cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA EC50 = 2 µM in H1299 cells).

insights.text: Structure-guided lead compound 4 binds eIF4E with sub-micromolar affinity (Kd = 17–90 nM) and disrupts eIF4E:eIF4G complex formation in cell lysates with low-micromolar potency (EC50 = 1.4–2.6 µM).
Compound 4 successfully engages eIF4E in intact H1299 cells, producing dose-dependent thermal stabilization with CETSA EC50 = 2 µM, closely aligning with its cell-free lysate potency.

Despite confirmed intracellular target engagement and good passive permeability (Caco-2 Papp = 9.0 x 10^-6 cm/s), compound 4 fails to inhibit cap-dependent translation or cell proliferation in intact cells.

Genetic rescue in an eIF4E-dTAG degradation model revealed that perturbing the non-canonical site 2 alone (via compound 4 or the L85R mutation) does not abrogate eIF4E function, whereas combining site 2 disruption with canonical PPI perturbation (W73F mutation) causes profound loss of cell proliferation.

The findings establish that small-molecule inhibition of an extended protein-protein interaction such as eIF4E:eIF4G may necessitate simultaneous disruption of both canonical and non-canonical binding sites to achieve cellular phenotypic efficacy.

review_notes: Compound 4 is the only compound in the paper with both quantitative cell-free potency (ITC Kd and lysate EC50) and quantitative cellular potency (intact-cell CETSA EC50 = 2 µM).

Negative control diastereomer 5 was profiled biochemically (ITC Kd = 3.0 µM for D127 variant; HeLa lysate PPI EC50 > 100 µM) and in intact cells at fixed doses (50 µM), but no quantitative intact-cell potency (IC50/EC50) or bound was reported.
Fragments 1, 2, and 3 were characterized only biophysically by ITC (Kd = 400 µM, 7400 µM, and 20 µM, respectively) and lack intact-cell data.

In intact cells, compound 4 was inactive in cap-dependent dual luciferase reporter assays (tested at 10 and 25 µM) and viability assays (tested up to 50 µM), but explicit numerical bounds (e.g. >50 µM) were not reported as fitted potency endpoints.
Caco-2 permeability (Papp = 9.0 x 10^-6 cm/s, efflux ratio 1.5) was measured to investigate potential causes for the cellular drop-off and ruled out permeability limitations.

claims.author_explanation: The observed drop-off in cellular potency relative to biochemical potency (averaging 73-fold) in ZR75-1 cells is primarily driven by reduced intracellular target exposure caused by saturable active drug efflux (e.g., via ABCB1 and ABCC1) and nonspecific cellular binding, rather than differences in intrinsic cellular target pharmacology. When cytosolic exposure is corrected using concentration-dependent Kpuu,cyto, the potency disconnect is reconciled down to an average 5.4-fold difference.

evidence.experiment: Total cellular accumulation ratio (Kp) was measured in ZR75-1 cells across concentrations from 0.1 to 100 µM, demonstrating lower accumulation at unsaturated concentrations (Kpunsat) and saturation at high concentrations (Kpsat) consistent with active efflux.
evidence.result: All 12 compounds exhibited Kpunsat lower than Kpsat, with high recovery ruling out extensive metabolism, confirming active efflux reduces unbound cytosolic concentration at nonsaturating extracellular concentrations.

evidence.experiment: Mathematical prediction of cytosolic IC50 using Kpuu,cyto derived from intact-cell Kp saturation compared against biochemical IC50 across 12 inhibitors.
evidence.result: Accounting for cytosolic target exposure using Kpuu,cyto bridged the average disconnect between biochemical and cellular IC50 from 73-fold down to 5.4-fold.

claims.grade_rationale: The authors perform detailed mechanistic measurements (concentration-dependent cellular accumulation Kp, equilibrium dialysis binding in medium and cell homogenate, and model fitting of saturable cellular accumulation Kpunsat and Kpsat) that correlate exposure correction with reconciled potency across 12 compounds. However, no controlled causal rescue experiment (such as pharmacological transporter inhibition with an ABCB1/ABCC1 inhibitor or genetic knockdown/knockout) was performed to test whether blocking efflux directly shifts the cellular IC50.

classification.rationale: Saturable active drug efflux ( alongside nonspecific cellular binding) primarily drives reduced unbound cytosolic exposure and the cellular potency drop-off.

insights.text: Cellular accumulation (Kp) of KAT6A inhibitors in ZR75-1 breast carcinoma cells is concentration-dependent, transitioning from an unsaturated lower plateau (Kpunsat) to a saturated upper plateau (Kpsat) consistent with active efflux.

Intact-cell Kp saturation provides an alternative estimate of the fraction of unbound drug in the cytosol (fu,cyto = fu,med / Kpsat) that avoids cellular disruption and artificial binding artifacts observed in cell homogenates.

Correcting cellular potency using cytosolic unbound partition coefficients (Kpuu,cyto) reduces the average potency disconnect between biochemical KAT6A inhibition and ZR75-1 cellular activity from 73-fold down to 5.4-fold.

Cell homogenate binding methods (Kpuu,cell,hom) caused severe underpredictions of intracellular IC50 for highly bound compounds (up to 105-fold lower than biochemical IC50), which is biologically implausible in cells subject to efflux.

review_notes: Chemical structures for Compounds 1-10 and literature compounds WM-8014 and WM-1119 were not drawn in the main manuscript text or figures (referenced to Supplemental Fig. 1), so structure_mode is set to 'name_only'.

Table 3 reports measured biochemical IC50 and cellular IC50 alongside calculated/predicted 'Cytosolic IC50' and 'Intracellular IC50'. Only the experimentally measured IC50 values were extracted as measurements, as the predicted values are model-derived exposure corrections (eq. 15 and 16).

No pharmacological or genetic intervention (such as an efflux inhibitor or transporter knockout) was conducted in the paper; the study evaluated a profiling panel to demonstrate exposure correction methodology. Hence, interventions is empty and claim_efflux_exposure is assigned grade 3.
